itable, strand based fur geometry. We utilize fur thickness cues from learned volumetric surface
representations to estimate fur depth and an estimate of the unseen defurred body.
ABSTRACT
Realistic and editable animal fur reconstruction from multi-view images is chal-
lenging: fine-scale detail, self-occlusion and obfuscation, and, unlike human hair,
the lack of animal fur datasets. Fur usually covers most of an animal’s body, with
large inter- and intra-species variability. We presentFurE, an efficient strand-
based animal fur reconstruction method that recovers a per-strand, editable groom
by optimizing a root-conditioned latent field, decoded into strand geometry via a
PCA-based decoder. We reconstruct a defurred animal body using local fur thick-
ness cues from surface-constrained Gaussian ”frosting” representation, along with
part-based priors. We next show using a PCA-based decoder using knowledge
from human hair strand data - allows us to alleviate the animal data scarcity, while
allowing for faster optimization. FurE achieves a 10×speedup in strand train-
ing over current SOTA dense per-strand optimization, retaining strand fidelity and
generalizing across synthetic and, more importantly, real-world sequences, with
quantitative and qualitative validation despite this reduction in training time.
1 INTRODUCTION
Strand-based hair and fur is the standard representation for high-quality digital assets. Unlike vol-
umetric or surface-based representations, explicit strands remain directly editable, renderable, and
simulatable in production pipelines. Recovering such a representation from images is difficult, es-
pecially for animal fur where individual fine-scale strands are heavily self-occluded by surrounding
fur, and this occlusion is compounded by fur’s view-dependent appearance and the fact that it covers
most of the animal’s visible body. Moreover, the surface reconstructed from multiview images is
usually the outer furry envelope rather than the underlying skin on which the strand roots should
be placed. This ambiguity is substantially greater than in human hair capture, as animal fur varies
not only across species but also across body parts of the same individual, with different lengths,
densities, directions, and thicknesses around the face, ears, torso, belly, legs, paws, and tail. Disen-

title: FurE: Efficient Instance-Specific 3D Fur Reconstruction without Animal-Fur Datasets

text:
Efficient Instance-Specific 3D Fur Reconstruction without Animal-Fur Datasets
tangling fur from the body also remains crucial for tasks such as pose estimation (Xu et al., 2023),
3D part segmentation, and tracking.
We presentFurE, an efficient method for strand-based animal fur reconstruction from multiview
images, built on two principles. First, the expensive fur strand-learning problem should be solved
in a low dimensional latent space rather than the full 3D strand space. Instead of treating each
fur strand as an unconstrained high-dimensional polyline, FurE predicts compact (low-dimensional)
codec coefficients (vectors) on a defurred body surface, which a lightweight pretrained (using abun-
dant human hair data) PERM (He et al., 2025) style decoder maps to explicit local-frame strand
geometry, scaled by fur-length and rendered with strand-aligned gaussians. This retains the edit-
ing and rendering benefits of strand-based reconstruction while substantially reducing the cost of
per-scene strand learning relative to dense per-strand optimization used in current SOTA methods.
Second, FurE treats defurring (estimating the skin underlying the fur) as a localshell-estimation
problem (outer shell being the visible fur, and inner is defurred). We discovered that we can use
fur-depth cues from Gaussian Frosting (Gu ´edon & Lepetit, 2024), which uses the misalignment of
surface-aligned Gaussians to identify areas where more volumetric rendering is needed.
FurE extracts view-consistent shell statistics as local evidence for fur-bearing volume, then cali-
brates this evidence with part-aware priors to produce a defurred surface mesh. Given this defurred
mesh approximation, FurE samples strand roots and assigns each a local coordinate framework -
TBN basis (Tangent, Bitangent, Normal), semantic part label, and calibrated length; a latent UV
texture is then decoded via a lightweight PCA decoder into normalized canonical strands, scaled
to target length and transformed into world space. FurE then attaches cylindrical Gaussians to the
decoded strand segments and optimizes with multiview photometric loss, yielding explicit poly-
lines and strand-aligned Gaussians compatible with downstream rendering, simulation, and editing
applications.
On multiview inputs from the Artemis dataset (Luo et al., 2022), FurE completes strand training
in under one hour, achieving a10×speedup with comparable or better quantitative results while
retaining explicit, editable strands. We evaluate reconstruction quality and efficiency against animal
fur and strand-based hair baselines, with ablations of the codec representation. We further demon-
strate, to our knowledge, the first instance-specific, strand-based animal fur reconstruction from
noisy real-world multiview images, on which NeuralFur (Sklyarova et al., 2026) struggles.
Our contributions are:
• We introduceFurEfor instance-specific reconstruction of explicit, editable animal fur
from calibrated multiview images. Strand training takes under one hour, achieving a10×
speedup over SoTA methods with comparable or better rendering quality.
• We transfer human-hair priors to animal fur through a compact PCA codec, replacing dense
strand optimization with root-conditioned latent learning without animal-fur training data.
• We introduce shell-based defurring that combines local Gaussian Frosting cues with part-
aware priors to estimate a plausible hidden strand-root surface without SMAL fitting.
• We demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first instance-specific, strand-based animal fur re-
construction from noisy real-world multiview images.
2 RELATEDWORK
Animal reconstruction.SMAL (Zuffi et al., 2017), GenZoo (Niewiadomski et al., 2025), and Ani-
Mer (Lyu et al., 2025) recover animal body shape but not explicit fur strands. NeuralFur, our closest
prior work, combines NeuS geometry (Wang et al., 2021), SMAL-based part localization, and VLM-
derived fur attributes to guide defurring and strand reconstruction. Its defurring depends on template
fitting and part-level semantic estimates, while dense strand optimization remains computationally
expensive. FurE instead uses local Gaussian Frosting cues and part-aware priors to estimate the
hidden strand-root surface. Direct part segmentation (Paul et al., 2026) removes the dependency on
SMAL fitting. Combined with compact strand learning, this achieves a10×strand-training speedup
with comparable rendering quality. We further reconstruct explicit fur from a noisy real-world bison
sequence on which NeuralFur fails.

3.1 DEFURRING ANDFURINITIALIZATION
Given calibrated multiview images and foreground masks, NeuS2 (Wang et al., 2023) reconstructs
the coat’s outer surfaceM outer. We estimate a plausible defurred meshM root beneath it for strand
attachment.
Defurring.Gaussian Frosting surrounds a base mesh with an adaptive layer of 3D Gaussians.
Trained on the same images, its layer width provides local fur-thickness cues, not direct measure-
ments of skin depth or strand length. We label body parts using ALIGN-Parts (Paul et al., 2026),
with manual verification, avoiding SMAL fitting. We transfer nearby shell widths using part labels
and normal agreement, then calibrate them with coarse part-thickness references where available.
Rather than copying the inner shell, we solve for smooth inward vertex displacements that balance
supported local cues with part-level guidance. Weakly supported regions rely more on part-level
estimates, while smoothing is weaker across part boundaries. We keep non-fur regions fixed, bound
displacement near opposing surfaces, and reduce offsets causing face flips, severe collapse, or new
self-intersections. We obtainM root by moving each outer-mesh vertexx i tox root

3.3 RENDERING ANDOPTIMIZATION
Next, in order to integrate the reconstructed strands into the 3DGS differentiable rendering frame-
work, we attach cylindrical Gaussians to the strands with lengths significantly larger than their diam-
eters. Each line segment of a strand is represented by a Gaussian whose length matches the segment
length and orientation aligns with the local tangent direction. Each Gaussian is further associated
with trainable spherical harmonic coefficients for appearance modeling, allowing the photometric
supervision to refine the geometric structure.
Each decoded strand is represented as a continuous chain of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, whose
elongated shapes tightly follow the strand’s local geometry. Specifically, we attach cylindrical Gaus-
sians along the reconstructed strands and integrate them into the 3DGS differentiable rendering
framework. Each line segment of a strand is represented by a Gaussian whose length matches the

5 CONCLUSION
We presented FurE for instance-specific reconstruction of explicit, editable animal fur from cali-
brated multiview images. FurE adapts a human-hair PCA basis to replace dense strand optimization
with compact code learning, without requiring a separate animal-fur training dataset. Local Gaus-
sian Frosting cues and part-aware priors guide defurring, while direct part segmentation removes
the need for SMAL fitting. On Artemis, strand training takes under one hour, achieving a10×
speedup over NeuralFur with comparable rendering quality. We further reconstruct fur from a noisy
real-world bison sequence on which NeuralFur fails. These results demonstrate efficient animal fur
reconstruction while retaining explicit strands for downstream editing, rendering, and simulation.

However, several limitations still remain. Our evaluation lacks ground-truth cases with strong local
variation within body parts, such as shaved patches, injuries, or irregular grooming. Such cases
would better test local Frosting cues against part-level priors. FurE also represents fur as a single
strand layer on one root surface, which is estimated before strand optimization. Modeling multilayer
coats and jointly optimizing root placement and strand geometry under multiview supervision are
important next steps toward more automatic reconstruction.

A.2 CODECSTRANDLEARNINGDETAILS
FurE optimizes a compact strand code rather than dense per-strand control points. For each sampled rootr i,
a root-conditioned encoder predicts a latent codez i, and a decoder maps this code to a normalized strand
curve. The root tangent frame, part label, Frosting density, and initialized strand length scale the decoded curve
into world space. We use a continous latent texture for strand optimization. We train with 15K strand for
every iteration for 2500 iterations and finetune the PCA based decoder. We use the same hyper-parameters as
NeuralFur.
A.3 APPLICATIONS
As we demonstrate in the main and in Fig. 12, the fur strands reconstructed by FurE can be directly imported
into commonly used standard 3D game engines, such as Blender and Unreal Engine. The structural plausibility
of the generated strands enables downstream physics simulations. For example, subjecting the imported strands
to simulated wind dynamics produces realistic and coherent motion.
A.4 LIMITATIONS ANDFUTUREWORK
While FurE enables efficient, fur reconstruction, several limitations still remain. First, our current framework
requires calibrated multi-view images of static animal. Since capturing dense, static multi-view images of living
animals is often very difficult, extending FurE to handle dynamic motion is the next step. Additionally our
defurring process relies on initial Gaussian Frosting cues and dense camera viewpoints. Severe self-occlusions
in the input images and the animal fur can degrade the shell thickness and the fur length estimate and hence the
need for stronger geometric priors for future iterations.

Abstract
Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement
remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-
Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting up-
dates to both a robot’s capabilities and its improvement procedure, making sub-
sequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges
from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible conse-
quences. We present an L0–L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from
meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for in-
dependently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness
adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that gov-
ern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substan-
tial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demon-
strate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priori-
ties in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmark-
ing, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn
while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at
https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.

Learning.

text:
Physical RSI
1 Introduction
Advances in robotics have enabled machines to carry out an expanding range of tasks on their own,
from sorting parcels in logistics centers to performing routine chores at home (Zeng et al., 2018;
Fu et al., 2025). Yet behind this execution autonomy lies a reliance on human support. In data
preparation, robots do not have data as abundant as the internet data available to language models.
Their data is generated through thousands of physical interactions, and humans are needed to collect
and review it (Collaboration et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024). In deployment, when a robot meets
an unfamiliar failure, recovery largely depends on humans to diagnose the problem or demonstrate a
fix (Liu et al., 2023b). In training and optimization, most systems rely on training pipelines designed
by humans, and the final choice of which update to adopt remains a human decision (Zhu et al.,
2020a). Consequently, even highly capable robots lackimprovement autonomy, meaning the ability
to improve themselves without humans driving the loop.
Recent work has begun to narrow this gap by letting systems improve themselves. One line of work
lets language model agents rewrite code or scaffolding, and keep the changes that score better under
automated evaluation (Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026d; Novikov et al.,
2025). Another line improves the model itself, training it on data and feedback that the system
or another language model generates (Yuan et al., 2024b; Zweiger et al., 2025; Ghasemipour et al.,
2025; Ma et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024d). Most of this work achieves self-improvement, in that
the system raises its own task performance by changing what it uses when it performs a task. The
procedure that produces and selects these changes usually stays fixed, so what the system can gain is
limited by how effective that procedure is. Recursive self-improvement goes further. It updates the
improvement procedure itself. Recursive gain is established when the revised procedure produces
better subsequent improvements than its predecessor under matched conditions. Few works however
update the procedure, and fewer show that doing so yields recursive gain.
Moreover, recursive self-improvement is harder for robots in the real world than in simulated or
digital environments. The physical world cannot be monitored as exhaustively as digital environ-
ments. A robot observes only partial and noisy traces of what actually happened, which makes
failures hard to diagnose and improvements hard to verify (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2019). Outcomes
are also less deterministic than in digital environments, and the robot must act through continuous
dynamics under real-time constraints (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2019). Evaluating any change therefore
requires repeated trials under noisy conditions, which is time-consuming on real robots (Zhou et al.,
2025c). Finally, resetting a physical system is expensive, hardware can fail, and many interactions
risk irreversible outcomes, including harm to people who share the workspace, so the cheap trial and
error on which self-improvement in digital environments relies becomes costly and risky (Eysenbach
et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020a). These constraints make it particularly hard on real robots to update
and to verify the changes. Physical robots therefore call for a recursive self-improvement framework
of their own, rather than one carried over from digital settings.
We build this framework aroundPhysical Recursive Self-Improvement(Physical RSI). We say that
a robot performs Physical RSI when it uses evidence from its physical interaction to persistently
update both its task-execution system and its improvement procedure, such that its subsequent
improvement becomes more effective over successive rounds. Here thetask-execution systemis the
models and harness that the robot uses to perform tasks, and theimprovement procedureis the
part that can update the task-execution system and itself. An independent evaluator assesses the
gains of the updated system. Our long-term vision is for robots to operate and evolve autonomously
in real-world physical environments, addressing diverse and unforeseen challenges without human
intervention.
Based on this definition, we introduce six levels, L0 to L5, to describe how much of it a system
meets, as shown in Figure 1. L0 covers systems that make no retained change on their own, either
because they adjust only within a run or because humans still drive the loop. L1 to L4 vary along
two axes. Capability-level updates change the task-execution system, whereas meta-level updates
change the improvement procedure. The second axis is scope. A gain on a single task may be

L5 builds on L4 and requires evidence, from an independent evaluator under the same controlled

Existing surveys cover complementary parts of this framework. Surveys centered on components
and experience examine how agents change their models, prompts, memory, tools, and workflows
(Gao et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026a). RSI-oriented accounts
ask whether the mechanisms that generate, evaluate, and select updates can themselves change (Liu
et al., 2026c; Duan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b), and address safety through
governance, independent evaluation, and the preservation of safeguards across updates (Liu et al.,
2026c; Wang et al., 2026b; Gong et al., 2026). For humanoids, Nguyen et al. (2026) formulate
admissible evolution through layered safety mechanisms. Such safeguards carry more weight in the
physical world, where a failed trial cannot simply be rerun or rolled back (Duan et al., 2026; Nguyen
et al., 2026). We therefore make safety and control explicit in our system framework and dedicate
a section to how they constrain physical interaction and autonomous improvement. And existing
accounts characterize the scope of improvement in different ways. Liu et al. (2026c) reserve a higher
level for broad transfer, Wang et al. (2026b) treat transfer as a separate empirical question, and
Wu et al. (2026b) separately record improvement targets and held-out transfer while cautioning
against collapsing independent dimensions into a single autonomy ladder. For robots, generalization
remains uneven across changes in objects, embodiment, and deployment conditions (Hou et al.,
2026b). We therefore cross two criteria in L0–L5, namely, whether an update changes the task-
execution system or the improvement procedure, and whether its demonstrated effects remain within

text:
Physical RSI
one task or extend across tasks. Finally, the task-execution system and the improvement procedure
play different roles, but both involve models, harnesses, and associated improvement procedures
(Liu et al., 2026c; Ren et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026b). We therefore organize methods into harness
adaptation and model learning. This groups methods that operate on similar components while
preserving the distinction between what the robot can do and how it improves.
This study makes three contributions. First, we propose Physical RSI as a concept and give it a
graded framework from L0 to L5. The framework treats what is updated and how far an update
reaches as orthogonal criteria to define L1–L4. Second, we investigate existing methods along two
implementation paths, harness adaptation and model learning, each covering both the task-execution
system and the improvement procedure, together with the safety and control mechanisms that bound
both, andtheverificationthatdecideswhichupdatesarekept. Third, wereviewhowexistingsystems
are evaluated, set out a protocol for independently evaluating improvement procedures, and identify
the evidence gaps that separate current work from higher levels.
The remainder of the study is organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the framework, including
the definition, the system architecture, the L0–L5 levels, and the boundaries of evidence. Section 3
surveys harness adaptation, and Section 4 surveys model learning. Section 5 addresses safety and
control, and Section 6 examines how Physical RSI is evaluated. Section 7 discusses open problems,
and Section 8 concludes.
2 Foundations of Physical Recursive Self-Improvement
This section establishes the foundations for analyzing Physical RSI. Section 2.1 defines the system
components and the conditions for physical self-improvement and Physical RSI, and relates them
to neighboring research paradigms. Section 2.2 describes the execution, capability-level update,
and meta-level update loops. Section 2.3 specifies task identity and the criteria for assigning levels
L0–L5. This framework also provides a shared terminology for the analysis throughout the study.
2.1 Definition and Scope of Physical RSI
We describe an improving robot by its task-execution system and improvement procedure (Fig-
ure 1(a)), together with two properties of its updates, physical grounding and inheritance.
Task-execution systemThe task-execution system is the pipeline through which the robot turns
a task into action. It has two parts. TheharnessHcomprises the components outside the learned
models, such as prompts, memory, skills and tools, task decomposition and recovery logic, and
interface and controller code. Theparametric modelsare the learned models used during execution,
such as a planner, a vision-language-action policy, or a value function or world model, and we denote
their weights byΘ. Capability can reside in either part, so we track both. Anything used only in the
improvement procedure and not during task execution belongs toΦrather than to the task-execution
system (Section 2.3).
Improvement procedureThe improvement procedureΦis responsible for improving the whole
system, including the task-execution system and the procedure itself. It has three stages. An
adaptation stageAdaptupdatesH. A training stageTrainselects experience and optimizesΘ. A
verification stageVerjudges each candidate change proposed byAdaptorTrainand decides whether
to keep it.Φcan also improve itself by changing these stages, with an update toAdaptorTrain
judged byVerand an update toVerjudged by the independent evaluatorEintroduced below. This
matters because an improvement procedure is designed around particular tasks. When new tasks
arrive, a fixed procedure usually has to be re-engineered by people, whereas one that can update
itself adapts without them. We call changes to the task-execution system capability-level updates
and changes to the improvement procedure meta-level updates, and Section 2.2 describes how each
is carried out.
5

text:
Physical RSI
Physical groundingThe improvement procedure draws its changes from experience, which it
keeps in an experience and feedback storeD.Dstores the records of task execution, together with
the records of improvement. Memory inHholds whatAdapthas distilled fromDfor use inH.
Experience may come from the real world, from a physics simulator, from a learned world model,
from humans, or from signals inside the system. Among these sources, only the real world shows
how the robot’s actions actually play out. A physics simulator reproduces contact and dynamics
only approximately. A learned world model, humans, or internal signals can propose candidates or
supply additional data, but a change drawn only from them is not physically grounded. We therefore
call a changephysically groundedwhen it depends on what happened as the robot acted, either in
the real world or in a physics simulator.
InheritanceA change becomes the starting point of later behavior only if it is inherited. We call

Physical RSI requires real-world grounding, which separates it from RSI in digital environments in
four ways.
1.Continuous, real-time interaction.The robot acts through continuous dynamics under real-time
constraints, and a task counts as done only when it is completed physically, whereas digital
environments can often be paused and replayed.

2.Costly and irreversible trials.Resets are expensive and some actions cannot be undone, whereas
a digital environment can be restored to an earlier state.
3.Partial, noisy observation.The robot sees only local, noisy traces of what happened, whereas
digital environments can often expose the full state. Outcomes are therefore uncertain, failures
are hard to attribute, and evidence from simulation does not fully carry over to the real robot
(the sim-to-real gap).
4.Safety of people and hardware.Robots often work alongside people, and the hardware itself can
fail or be damaged, so safety constraints, and human oversight where people are involved, need
to bound the loops.
These differences are also why our framework requires physical grounding for Physical RSI.

retains that change for subsequent improvement. Such a change may be implemented in code or
learned parameters.
TasksA task is what the experimenter asks the robot to accomplish, such as lifting a cup or
placing it in the sink. We describe it by two factors. The skill sequenceκis the sequence of skills
required to accomplish the task, such as walking to an object, opening a door, grasping, and pouring.
The instance parametersξare the variation that leavesκunchanged, such as the poses of objects,
their arrangement, and the difficulty of a scene as long as the same skills still suffice. This follows
the distinction in Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020). Whether the scene is simulated or real is recorded
as the source of evidence and does not change the task.
Whether a task has changed depends on itsκ, which can change in two ways (Figure 2(b)). The
first is thatκgains a new skill. Lifting a cup that stands in front of the robot and walking to a
table before lifting it are different tasks, because only the second requires navigation. Walking to
a table before lifting a cup and walking to a kitchen counter before lifting it are the same task,
because both require only navigation and grasping. The second is thatκis a new combination
of skills that the system already has, which is what a long-horizon task usually is. Going from
the kitchen to the bedroom and fetching a pair of socks runs navigation, opening the door, and
grasping, whereas picking up a piece of clothing in the kitchen and carrying it into the bedroom
runs grasping, navigation, and opening the door. The skills are the same but the order differs, so
the two are different tasks. This matches the hardest level of GemBench (Garcia et al., 2025), where
the robot must compose several skills learned during training.
We apply this distinction to evaluation protocols from seven surveyed systems. Five of these pro-

(Zhang et al., 2025d) fine-tunes on a task variation new to the pretrained model but evaluates on
that same variation. Eureka (Ma et al., 2024a) separately optimizes a reward for each of 29 tasks
and evaluates the resulting policy on the corresponding task. In these four cases, improvement and
evaluation concern the sameκ. Eurekaverse (Liang et al., 2025) trains on diverse generated parkour

The capability improvement loop uses execution feedback and prior modification history to produce
persistent updates to memory, skills, and workflows. Feedback interpretation identifies modification
targets and scope, guiding the construction of candidate changes. Adopted updates become available
for subsequent execution, while attempted changes and their outcomes accumulate as improvement
history to inform future updates.
3.1 Feedback Interpretation and Update Target Identification
Execution records and improvement histories support diagnosis by relating observed deviations to
the actions, conditions, and previous interventions associated with them. In simulated robot tasks,
primitive-level traces in ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026), workflow-node diagnostics in HarnessPAI (Wang
et al., 2026c), and visual keyframes in Act-Observe-Rewrite (Kumar, 2026) connect execution out-
comes to specific operations and observations. Comparisons across attempts provide additional
grounds for interpreting these deviations. In digital agent studies, ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) con-
trasts successful and failed attempts, while AutoGuide (Fu et al., 2024) relates their differences to
the contexts in which corrective guidance applies. Modification histories in WikiSkill (Tang et al.,
2026b) and language corrections in DROC (Zha et al., 2024) supplement these comparisons with
evidence from previous edits and clarification of task requirements. Together, these sources support
hypotheses about the causes of observed failures and the conditions under which they recur.
Selecting a modification target requires determining which harness component should change in
response to the diagnosis. When failures concern the use of guidance, AutoManual (Chen et al.,
2024) and EmbodiSkill (Ju et al., 2026) distinguish defective instructions from failures to follow
valid instructions, directing intervention toward the instructions themselves or reminders of their
use. Dynamo (Sun et al., 2026) distinguishes reasoning from perceptual gaps to target textual
skills or perception tools. These judgments must then be grounded in editable implementations.
HarnessFix (Chen et al., 2026b) links failed trajectory steps to harness code, while RACaP (Li
et al., 2026e) identifies interventions involving interfaces, exposed parameters, reporting, routing,
or memory. Once the component is identified, the proposal must delimit both the extent of the
change and its intended applicability. Self-Harness (Zhang et al., 2026b) favors bounded changes,
and SkillAdam (Li et al., 2026a) uses prior editing outcomes to regulate their scope, while Robo-
Foundry (Liang et al., 2026b) distinguishes task-specific repairs from changes intended for broader
reuse. With the diagnosed problem linked to a concrete implementation and a defined scope, the
next step is to construct a modification that addresses it within these bounds.
3.2 Memory, Skill, and Workflow Adaptation
Execution memory updates add experiential guidance, organize its application, and revise outdated
content (Figure. 5). In digital agent tasks, Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) retains feedback-derived re-
flections, while ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) extracts reusable insights across attempts. These additions
can be organized into context-specific guidance, as in AutoGuide (Fu et al., 2024), or maintained
as editable rule collections, as in AutoManual (Chen et al., 2024). Related execution guidance can
also be maintained through tool documentation. ContDA (Wu et al., 2026a) revises tool documen-
tation, usage preferences, and fallback guidance as toolsets evolve. In robotics, memory revision
additionally concerns the physical explanations underlying action selection. PhysMem (Li et al.,
2026b) develops interaction-derived hypotheses and tests their applicability, while KnowBody (Lou
et al., 2026) revises action-relevant body relations and rechecks dependent knowledge. Together,
these mechanisms update what subsequent execution can draw on and the conditions under which
it applies.
Individual capabilities can be updated through changes to their implementation or interface, or
supplemented by newly constructed skills and tools. CREATOR (Qian et al., 2023) uses execution
errorstoguidetool-codecorrection, whileASPIRE(Luetal.,2026)repairsrobottaskprogramsusing

tic Robot Learning (Zhang et al., 2026f) extracts reusable helpers from successful robot programs
in simulation. Such changes concern individual capabilities, but shared implementations and callers
can require coordinated modification.
Coordinated updates change related capabilities together when they share functionality or depend
on common interfaces. ReGAL (Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024) couples the introduction of helper func-
tions with refactoring of the programs that use them, linking library construction to changes in
callers. In simulation with human demonstrations and hints, Lifelong Robot Library Learning (Tzi-

and rewrites existing examples to use the resulting library. In both cases, introducing an abstrac-
tion is accompanied by changes to existing programs that previously implemented the functionality
separately. Coordination also concerns the maintenance of these shared structures. ReGAL edits
or prunes abstractions that perform poorly on their associated tests. Playful (Zhang et al., 2026f)
extends library-level modification through periodic consolidation of redundant helpers, with depen-

4 Model Training of Physical RSI
As illustrated in Figure 1, model learning provides another pathway for improvement alongside
adaptation of the model-external harness. Physical experience can support updates to policies,
reward models, and world models. A frozen foundation model may assist with failure analysis
and training decisions. Figure 8 zooms into this pathway and shows how model learning can form a
continuousimprovementloop: Physicalinteractionprovidesexperiencefortraining, andtheresulting
model updates shape subsequent interactions, forming a feedback loop that may eventually extend to
the training procedure itself. This distinction between improving a learnable model and modifying

the process that produces future model updates parallels the L0–L5 distinction between task-level
improvement and adaptation of the improvement mechanism. Section 6 examines the reliability of
the feedback on which both pathways depend.
4.1 Data Preparation
Data preparation couples experience generation with selection for learning. Physical practice prior-
itizes weak capabilities under scene and reset constraints (Sharma et al., 2023c; Fang et al., 2026b).
Simulation generators construct tasks, scenes, rewards, and demonstrations (Wang et al., 2024a; Hua
et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024e), expanding coverage and adjusting difficulty to
learner performance (Choi et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026). Real2Sim2Real workflows further connect
environment preparation to deployment by reconstructing observed scenes in simulation and using
the resulting spatial context for physical execution. HomeBody illustrates this route: a foundation-
model agent builds a digital twin from robot observations and SLAM geometry to support reasoning
and skill execution (Huh et al., 2026). Selection determines how this experience is used. Shared
control, active querying, and correction memory provide human guidance (Liu et al., 2023b; Luo
et al., 2025a; Hoque et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026a), while recovery demonstrations cover failure
states (Ge et al., 2026); dependence on essential human corrective judgments places these workflows
at L0. Autonomous selection admits verified successes for imitation and uses failures for value learn-
ing or recovery (Zhou et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2026); prioritizing failure-prone states focuses scarce
trials on weak behavior (He et al., 2026a). Data preparation contributes to mechanism improvement
when a data sampler, curriculum generator, or selection model is revised and reused in subsequent
learning (Chebotar et al., 2019; Muratore et al., 2021; 2022; Sekar et al., 2020).
4.2 Training Methods
Model training typically begins with pretraining on diverse data to establish behavioral, visual, or
dynamics priors, followed by post-training with task-specific experience or feedback (Kawaharazuka
et al., 2025). Across pretraining and post-training, we review three learning paradigms: imitation
learning (IL), self-supervised learning (SSL), and reinforcement learning (RL).
Imitation learning(IL) learns behavior from demonstrations or teacher-generated targets; selected
self-generated experience can also supervise later updates (Bousmalis et al., 2023). Behavior cloning
can fit continuous actions by regression or predict discrete action tokens autoregressively (Mandlekar
et al., 2021b; Kim et al., 2024; Pertsch et al., 2025). Generative imitation instead fits an action
distribution: diffusion learns iterative denoising, while flow matching learns a velocity field that
transforms noise toward action samples (Chi et al., 2024; Black et al., 2026). Policy distillation
instead transfers a teacher’s behavior to a student (Wang et al., 2024f). And adversarial distribution
matching provides another route to imitation (Ho and Ermon, 2016). The learning objective can also
be the improvement target (Yu et al., 2018), which provides a methodological basis. But evidence
of physically grounded, persistent adaptation of IL mechanisms remains limited.
Self-supervised learning(SSL) derives training targets from observations and trajectories by
delving into their internal structure and relationships. Reconstruction and latent-action objectives
learn visual or motion representations without expert action labels, although mapping them to robot
control may require supervised adaptation (Radosavovic et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2025). Predictive
learning extends this approach to environmental dynamics (Mendonca et al., 2023). In a physical
improvement loop, robot trajectories provide self-supervised targets for updating a predictive model,
which then generates imagined experience for subsequent policy training (Wu et al., 2023; Guo et al.,
2026a). Self-supervised updates can also adapt policy memory during execution: RoboTTT updates
fast weights to incorporate incoming observations into the context used for subsequent actions (Jiang
etal.,2026b). Atthemechanismlevel, AutoSSLsearchescombinationsandweightsofself-supervised
objectives, but does not incorporate a physical robot learning loop (Jin et al., 2022).
Reinforcement learning(RL) enables robots to improve through repeated interaction: execution
outcomes guide policy or value updates, which influence subsequent actions and learning (Hirose

demonstrations provide a starting point, while online interaction and human corrections support
later updates (Nakamoto et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025c; Amin et al., 2025). The learned compo-
nent may be the base policy or a steering policy around a frozen behavioral prior (Ren et al., 2024;
Wagenmaker et al., 2025). In the improvement loop, the reward signal can be adjusted through
online reward-model updates or iterative reward-code revision (Zhang et al., 2026g; Huang et al.,
2024a). Mechanism-level improvement further targets how learning updates or rewards are gen-
erated: DiscoRL learns the rules for updating policies and predictions, while DERL uses policy
validation performance to train the meta-optimizer that generates future rewards (Oh et al., 2025;
Cheng et al., 2026).
4.3 Learning Models
The learning methods above apply to diverse models used in robot policies and their training. This
section focuses on VLA models, world models, and reward models, which have a strong influence on
continual improvement by shaping execution and subsequent learning. VLA updates change actions
and collected experience; world-model updates change predictions used for planning or imagined
training; reward-model updates change the rewards or value estimates guiding subsequent policy
learning.
Vision-language-action(VLA) models generate robot commands from visual observations, lan-
guage instructions, and optional sensory inputs (Kawaharazuka et al., 2025). Continual adaptation
incorporates demonstrations, corrective interventions, and deployment trajectories into IL or RL
updates (Chen et al., 2025c; Amin et al., 2025). One route updates internal components, including
action heads, adapters, backbone layers, or the full model (Kim et al., 2024). Action heads map
multimodal representations to discrete tokens or action chunks (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Black et al.,
2026); continuous generators include diffusion heads and diffusion Transformers (Ghosh et al., 2024;
Liu et al., 2025b). Updating these components changes action generation, while backbone adapta-
tion can also change visual and instruction grounding. Knowledge Insulation controls this coupling
by adapting the backbone through discrete-action supervision while blocking gradients from the
continuous-action expert (Driess et al., 2025). Within hierarchical VLAs, internal adaptation may
target task interpretation, action generation, or both (Belkhale et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025; NVIDIA
et al., 2025). A second route keeps a frozen VLA and learns a lightweight controller from physical
experience. FIND learns residual corrections using outcome assessment and human assistance for
scene recovery (Fang et al., 2026b). RLT instead trains a lightweight actor critic on an RL token
from the frozen VLA, refining action chunks while anchoring the actor to VLA recommendations (Xu
et al., 2026b). Here, improved behavior is carried by the controller instead of the VLA weights.
World modelslearn action-conditioned predictions of future observations, latent states, or object
relations (Hou et al., 2026a). Robot interaction can adapt predictive priors learned from human
video to the deployment environment (Mendonca et al., 2023). Their role in continuing improve-
ment depends on whether these predictions remain fixed or are updated with new experience. A
fixed world model can support repeated policy optimization through imagined rollouts (Yang et al.,
2026a). Alternatively, new policy rollouts update the world model, which then provides predictions
for subsequent policy training (Liu et al., 2026d). The predictor then becomes an evolving source of
training experience. Updated predictions can change the actions inferred through inverse dynam-
ics (Du et al., 2023), the ranking of plans or candidate behaviors (Hansen et al., 2024; Li et al.,
2025b), and the synthetic experience used for policy training (Yang et al., 2024). These uses require
accurate predictions of action outcomes, beyond visually realistic observations (Guo et al., 2026b).
In WAMs, prediction and action generation are integrated within a single model, so world-model
adaptation can also affect control (Bi et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026).
Reward modelslearn to score task progress, success, or relative behavior quality from videos, out-
come labels, and trajectory comparisons (Ma et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026a). They
support continuing improvement through two distinct paths. A fixed evaluator supplies rewards for
successive policy updates, with dense progress estimates complementing sparse task outcomes (Chen

feedback. Reward-model updates can alternate with policy learning, requiring stored experience to
be rescored as the learned rewards change (Lee et al., 2021). In physical deployment, reward mod-
els can be adapted by human confirmed success used for subsequent policy training (Zhang et al.,
2026g). Adaptation to new preferences can be confined to low-rank modules, reducing interference
with earlier reward knowledge while keeping the base reward-model weights fixed (Marta et al.,
2025). Critic updates provide another form of evaluator adaptation: new successful and failed roll-
outs refine expected-return estimates used to select actions. This can improve value-guided action
selection while the underlying action-generating policy remains frozen (Giridhar et al., 2026).
4.4 Knowledge Transfer and Training Procedure Improvement
Across learning rounds, accumulated knowledge can support new tasks, while feedback from training
and execution can inform how subsequent models are trained. We review these routes through cross-
task transfer from learned capabilities, followed by feedback-driven improvements to data prepara-
tion and training methods.
Cross task transferuses knowledge acquired on source tasks to support target task learning, while
preserving the previously acquired capabilities. Policy initialization starts target task training from
a multi-task generalist or a source task policy selected using predicted zero shot success (Bousmalis
et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2025). Skill and module reuse instead incorporates learned skill policies
or temporal action representations into the target policy, with learning focused on their selection,
composition, or adaptation (Zhang et al., 2025c; Zheng et al., 2024a). To adapt these reusable
components to a target task, learning can focus on skill selection, expert routing (Wan et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2024c), or controller composition (Feng et al., 2025). Throughout updates, replay,
modular adaptation, and parameter merging help preserve earlier knowledge while incorporating
target-task experience (He et al., 2026b; Yadav et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zhu et al., 2026).
Data preparation improvementuses learning and execution outcomes to revise what experience
is prepared for subsequent training. Successful demonstrations do not guarantee robots can reliably
learn the demonstrated behaviors. Feedback from policy learning and execution can help identify
suitable demonstrations for subsequent training (Chen et al., 2025a; Agia et al., 2025a; Dass et al.,
2026). Learning feedback can also guide how data from different sources are mixed for subsequent
policy training (Hejna et al., 2024) and informs future experience generation: real-world policy
returns guide simulation distributions, while fresh rollouts update predictors that direct collection
toward current failure regions (Muratore et al., 2021; He et al., 2026a). These approaches connect
data decisions to learner performance. Extending this feedback to autonomous strategy revision,
RSIBench-Data evaluates agents that use training and evaluation results to revise data sources,
coverage, trajectory representations, and curation strategies in digital tasks (Meng et al., 2026a).
Training method improvementchanges training methods for later learning, including revisions
to reward code, the training distribution, the update rule, or the organization of training experi-
ments (Ma et al., 2024b; Chebotar et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). Robot rollout
results can guide revisions to training code and recipes (Xiao et al., 2026), while records of ear-
lier tuning attempts can guide later training decisions (Li et al., 2026d). These changes enter the
self-improvement loop when the system retains and uses them to train subsequent models. Physical
RSI additionally requires training-mechanism revisions to bephysically grounded: feedback from the
robot’s interaction with its environment must inform how the training method changes. Retaining
and reusing such a revision can support L2 on the same task or L4 across tasks. L5 further requires
showing that the revised mechanism yields better subsequent improvements than its predecessor
under matched starting capabilities and resources. Section 6 describes how to test this gain.

5 Safety and Control of Physical RSI
Physical RSI must preserve safety as both the task-execution systemM= (Θ,H)and the improve-
ment procedureΦevolve. System updates can change which states the system visits and alter its
hazard estimates and action interfaces. Environmental drift can change the dynamics and available
control responses. Revisions toΦcan further change how trials are chosen and updates are accepted,
allowing errors in safety assessment to influence later generations.
The reviewed literature mainly provides component results, with limited evidence on safety across
inherited revisions ofΦ. Following Section 2.2, safety constrains the execution, capability-level up-
date, and meta-level update loops. Safety requirements and the independent evaluatorEwith its
scoring criterionQremain protected fromΦeven when safeguard implementations change. Under
these constraints, control includes restricting actions and trials, specifying permitted operating con-
ditions, and retaining the ability to interrupt execution or improvement. The question throughout
this section is which safety evidence remains valid after a change and what must be checked before
further physical operation (Figure 9).
5.1 Safe Exploration and Continual Adaptation
Safety during learning.A policy that is safe after training may still cause harm while collect-
ing experience. Safe reinforcement learning (RL) therefore distinguishes the constrained quantity,
the stage at which it is constrained, and the supporting evidence (Gu et al., 2024b; 2023). In a
constrained Markov decision process, rewards measure task performance and costs represent safety
violations. Constrained Policy Optimization approximately maintains expected-cost limits during
policy updates (Achiam et al., 2017). SafeVLA applies constrained learning to unsafe behaviors
of vision-language-action models (Zhang et al., 2025a). Other methods address conflicts between
reward and safety gradients (Gu et al., 2024a), balance multiple objectives under safety constraints
(Gu et al., 2025c), or incorporate risk measures into safety bounds (Gu et al., 2025b). Expected-cost

text:

limits can still permit individual violations, and their meaning depends on whether the cost captures
the physical hazard.
Retaining safety while adapting.Safe Continual Domain Adaptation (SCDA) combines safe
RL with a penalty on changes to important policy parameters after pretraining across varied sim-
ulated conditions (Josifovski et al., 2025). Its robot experiments show adaptation with reduced
forgetting and controlled average costs under the tested conditions. The penalty constrains the
policy, while learned estimates of reward and safety cost continue adapting. Fitting these estimators
to prescribed targets does not by itself establish a meta-level update, even when their parameters
persist across rounds (Section 2.3).
Retaining task performance does not necessarily retain safety. In simulated non-stationary bench-
marks, Coursey et al. (2026) find that reducing forgetting does not reliably preserve safety per-
formance, while stronger cost penalties can reduce task success. Post-update evaluation should
therefore cover both previous and current operating conditions. Historical safety labels should also
be reassessed against current dynamics and sensing conditions.
Exploration within a supported region.Gaussian-process controller optimization restricts
quadrotor trials to settings predicted to meet a safety threshold (Berkenkamp et al., 2016). Se-
quential safe exploration additionally checks reachability and return paths (Turchetta et al., 2016).
Stability certificates support joint improvement of a controller and its estimated safe region under
regularity and uncertainty assumptions (Berkenkamp et al., 2017).
These results rely on assumptions that may no longer hold after an update toMorΦ, or a change
in the environment. Before further exploration, the affected cost estimates, uncertainty bounds,
and return paths must therefore be checked against current physical conditions. The supported
region may need to shrink under drift. If no available trial supports safe continuation under these
assumptions, physical exploration must pause.
5.2 Safe Transfer and Update Acceptance
What transfers with a policy.Transfer of capability does not establish that safety evidence
transfers with it. Sim-to-Lab-to-Real combines a learned backup policy with restrictions on unsafe
actions and statistical bounds on expected performance and safety (Hsu et al., 2023). Its generaliza-
tion argument assumes that laboratory and deployment environments follow the same distribution.
Robust safe transfer instead uses a guide policy whose tolerance to uncertainty covers the target
environment (Zubia et al., 2025). Its expected-cost guarantee requires compatible action spaces and
a state mapping that preserves safety conditions.
These assumptions concern the system and environment together. A new encoder can invalidate
the state mapping, while an interface change can invalidate the guide’s actions. Neither change
necessarily alters the required skill sequenceκ, so safety reassessment also applies within a task as
defined in Section 2.3.
Evidence for accepting an update.Under Sections 2.2 and 6.1,Verinternally judges changes
toMand toAdaptorTrain. The independent evaluatorE, using the protected criterionQ,
measures gains in the updated task-execution system and assesses revisions toVerby evaluating the
systems retained under each verifier. Acceptance determines inheritance. Establishing improvement
requires independent outcome evaluation (Section 6.2). Release is the separate authorization for
physical operation under specified conditions and safeguards, including restricted trials used to
collect evidence.
High Confidence Policy Improvement bounds the probability of accepting a policy below a return
threshold (Thomas et al., 2015). The Seldonian framework tests specified behavioral constraints
and can return no solution when evidence is insufficient (Thomas et al., 2019). Constrained offline
learning and risk-sensitive objectives account for costs and severe outcomes beyond average return

text:
Physical RSI
(Lee et al., 2022; Chow et al., 2015). Logged data can support policy evaluation and limit policy
changes where evidence is sparse (Jiang and Li, 2016; Laroche et al., 2019). The validity of these
guarantees and estimates depends on data coverage and estimation assumptions, which must be
reconsidered under non-stationarity (Chandak et al., 2020). A gain over an unsafe baseline alone is
insufficient.
Releasing a compatible system.The policy, observation processing, action interface, monitor,
and backup controller should be assessed together. Harness changes require checks of skill precondi-
tions, invocation timing, and handover states (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). Changes to execution models
require checks of compatibility with the retained harness (Section 4.2). Hardware checks include
sensing errors, actuator limits, and control timing. Safety filters can account for bounded sensing
errors, as demonstrated by measurement-robust barrier functions in camera-based Segway control
(Cosner et al., 2021).
Definitions 1 and 2 allow physical grounding through interaction in a physics simulator or the real
world. This grounding condition is distinct from evidence that a particular hardware deployment
is safe. Learned world-model predictions can help screen candidates but cannot supply physical
grounding on their own. Simulation evidence alone does not establish hardware safety, which requires
assessment of the deployed system under its intended physical conditions.
After a system or procedure update, release requires evidence covering the intended conditions and
the complete component combination. Improving the score onEdoes not supply this evidence by
itself. The assessed conditions must remain explicit so that runtime monitoring can detect when
they no longer hold.
5.3 Runtime Assurance under Environmental Drift
Preserving a feasible response.Runtime assurance restricts actions or invokes a backup con-
troller when continued execution threatens safety. Safeguards used during task execution belong
toM: learned model weights are part ofΘ, while filter, switching, and controller code belong to
H. Components used only within the improvement procedure belong toΦ, while the independent
evaluatorEremains outside it (Section 2.1).
Control barrier functions preserve a safe region under model and control-feasibility assumptions
(Ames et al., 2017). Action filters can incorporate learned dynamics and uncertainty estimates
(Dalal et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2019). Reachability methods account for modeled disturbances
(Fisac et al., 2019), while predictive filters check future constraints and safe continuation (Wabersich
and Zeilinger, 2021; Tearle et al., 2021). Shielding restricts actions to satisfy logical specifications,
including checks that those specifications can be met with the available controls (Alshiekh et al.,
2018;Kimetal.,2025). Removingafilteraftertrainingremovesitsdirectruntimeenforcement(Yang
et al., 2026c). Logs must distinguish proposed and executed actions, since frequent corrections can
conceal an unsafe policy.
Detecting failure and invalid evidence.Failure prediction supplies warning signals but does
not itself enforce physical constraints. Visual predictors can bound false alarms and missed failures
for defined outcomes (Farid et al., 2022). Uncertainty in language-model judgments can support de-
ferring uncertain decisions (Zheng et al., 2024b). Sentinel checks execution consistency and progress
(Agia et al., 2025b). SAFE detects task failures from VLA features. Under the exchangeability
assumption, its conformal calibration bounds false alarms on successful trajectories, but does not
guarantee detection of failures or the safety of intervention (Gu et al., 2025a).
DoReMi and Code-as-Monitor connect execution deviations to replanning or geometric checks (Guo
et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a). Other detectors distinguish unusual observations from likely failures
(Römer et al., 2025; Rolland et al., 2026). Policy and encoder updates can change both the visited
states and the features used by these detectors. Recalibration needs evidence from the updated
system. Raising alarm thresholds merely to reduce interventions can conceal declining safety.

Recovery after change.SOTER and Neural Simplex combine switching rules with backup con-
trol (Desai et al., 2019; Phan et al., 2020). Recovery RL learns recovery behavior from estimates
of future violations (Thananjeyan et al., 2021). Such methods require a recoverable state and an
effective controller. Restoring an earlier policy cannot reverse a mechanical fault or changed friction.
Learned resetting and return behaviors support autonomous practice but also require physical trials
and can fail (Eysenbach et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2022; 2023b). In shared workspaces, coordinated
control must remain feasible when other robots change their behavior (Wang et al., 2017).
Changes to a policy, monitor, or backup controller require joint checks of detection errors, response
delays, and recovery feasibility. Revisions toΦmust carry these checks into subsequent updates.
Monitoring must track the physical assumptions as well as task failures, and restrictions must act
before recovery becomes infeasible. Abrupt changes outside the assumed disturbance bounds remain
outside the guarantee.
5.4 Oversight of an Evolving Improvement Procedure
Constraining how successors are produced.Changes toAdapt,Train, orVeraffect the trials
used to develop later systems and the decisions that retain them. Omitting intervention records
fromDcan make assisted task success appear to show that a policy is safe on its own. Procedure
assessment must therefore include the physical trials and subsequent systems it produces, rather
than only the final policy’s performance.
Formal guarantees cover some structured updates. Fulton and Platzer (2019) revise models, control
logic, and associated proofs, then eliminate inconsistent models during operation. Their safety result
requires an accurate model to remain in the candidate set. This supports the specified model and
controller updates, not arbitrary revisions ofΦ.
Preserving requirements and evaluation.A revised cost estimator must still measure the
hazards specified by the protected requirements. If one learned model both proposes actions and
assesses their safety, shared prediction errors can affect both decisions. A verifier can also drift
toward accepting updates that pass its local checks while increasing physical risk. Changes toVer
therefore require assessment through protectedE,Qand evidence from the systems retained under
the competing verifier versions (Section 6.1). The safety criteria for accepting a revision ofVershould
be specified before testing and protected from modification by the candidate verifier. Passing these
safety checks does not by itself establish downstream recursive gain, which requires the controlled
comparisons of Section 6.2.
Instructions embedded in external content can redirect an agent (Greshake et al., 2023). WhenΦ
reads logs or edits code, this content must not acquire permission to change protected requirements
or disable stopping mechanisms.
Human control and autonomous inheritance.Human demonstrations and corrections may
enterDunder the system description in Section 2.1. Their use must nevertheless be distinguished
from the autonomy required for a level claim. Section 2.3 assigns workflows whose retained changes
depend on human intervention or labeling during improvement to L0. Direct human edits toΘ,H,
orΦalso violate the self-inheritance condition, and human selection of retained updates replaces
autonomous retention. Authorization for physical operation is a separate safety decision. Its role,
and any interventions that contribute to learning or update selection, must be recorded explicitly
(Section 6.2).
Human interventions provide experience for policy learning (Kelly et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023b;
Luo et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025b), although uncertain or suboptimal guidance needs additional
care (Zhao et al., 2025). Emergency stops should remain distinguishable from demonstrations of
successful behavior. Methods for allocating human attention and requesting clarification can reduce
supervisiondemands(Hoqueetal.,2022;2023;Renetal.,2023), butdonotensurehelparrivesbefore

Revisiting previous conditions tests safety retention. Comparing fixed and updated systems under

6 Verification and Evaluation of Physical RSI
Evaluating Physical RSI requires assessing both whether candidate updates pass verification and
whether their subsequent use improves task performance or the improvement procedure. Following
Section 2.1, verification within the improvement procedureΦexamines whether proposed updates
should be accepted and inherited, while independent evaluation uses an externalEand criterionQ
to assess the updated task-execution systemM= (Θ,H). Passing internal verification does not by
itself establish subsequent improvement, which requires independent evaluation. As illustrated in
Figure 10, this section reviews verification practices for candidate updates (Section 6.1), evaluation
of improvement outcomes (Section 6.2), and related benchmarks (Section 6.3).
6.1 Verification of Candidate Updates
Verification checks whether a candidate update is ready for adoption by examining its implementa-
tion, its effect on the target problem, and its impact on existing capabilities. Following Section 2.1,
Veris part of the improvement procedureΦ = (Adapt,Train,Ver)and informs which updates to
M= (Θ,H)or to the improvement procedure are accepted and inherited. These internal checks use
development evidence, instead of replacing the protected external evaluationEunder criterionQ.
Implementation Validity.Implementation checks examine whether a candidate can run correctly
within the system, including syntax, interfaces, formats, and execution outputs. Checks at stage
boundaries or before task execution identify implementation errors before more costly task tests, as
illustrated by HARBOR and HarnessPAI (Li et al., 2026d; Wang et al., 2026c). Passing these checks
establishes that the candidate can be tested; its task effect still requires execution evidence.
Repair Effectiveness.Repair checks assess whether a modification resolves the targeted problem.
Re-execution on failed cases and comparison with preceding versions on matched task instances
provide evidence through outcomes and execution traces (Lu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026).
These tests connect the proposed correction to its measured effect within tested conditions. Applying
an update to other tasks requires evidence of its effectiveness beyond the original case: RoboFoundry
checks general updates by generating repair proposals from other pre-repair records and assessing
them against previously successful repair updates and their execution outcomes (Liang et al., 2026b).
Capability Preservation.Preservation checks revisit successful tasks or conditions to detect
losses caused by a shared modification. Acceptance criteria may require previously successful tasks
to remain successful or restrict performance losses on individual tasks. RPG and HarnessPAI retest
the updated systems before accepting changes to check that previously successful tasks remain
successful (Wang et al., 2026d;c). Preserving existing capabilities also requires checking whether
previously learned knowledge remains valid after an update: KnowBody suspends rules that depend
on revised body estimates until they are revalidated (Lou et al., 2026).
Meta-verification.WhenVeritself is revised, its acceptance rules become part of the object
under examination. This evaluation matters because verification mechanisms used to assess can-
didate updates can themselves make incorrect judgments, as documented by FailBench andNo
Free Checker(Navasardyan et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026). VERSE provides a digital example of
developing verification-related tools around fixed checking primitives (Wang et al., 2026f). Such
revisions cannot be judged solely by their own acceptance standards: accepting more updates does
not establish that a revised verifier is better. Independent evaluation should therefore compare the
subsequent performance of systems produced under the original and revised verification procedures,
using a common external evaluation setEand scoring criterionQ.
6.2 Evaluation of Improvement Outcomes
Whereas verification determines which candidate updates are accepted, independent evaluation uses
the protected evaluatorEand scoring criterionQ(Section 2.1) to assess the effects of changes
retained in later task-execution systemsM= (Θ,H). Revisions to the improvement procedure

Φare assessed indirectly through the subsequent systems they produce. We review how existing
studies assess performance across improvement rounds, identify the contributions and transferability
of updates, and report resource costs and human involvement.
Performance and Retention.Existing evaluations examine both the gains from a single learning
update and how performance evolves across successive improvement rounds. Before–after compar-
isons measure changes in task success (Zhou et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026). Multi-round evaluations
extend this comparison to successive policy checkpoints or updated agent systems, tracking whether
gains accumulate, persist, or temporarily decline (Lang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d). To assess
these changes independently, updated systems are evaluated under initial conditions that were not
used for debugging or selecting candidate updates (Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d).
Attribution and Transfer.Controlled comparisons identify which changes contribute to im-
provement, while transfer tests examine their usefulness beyond single tasks. EmbodiRSI compares
adaptive and static collection with matched trajectory counts, initial data, policy architectures, and
training recipes (Lang et al., 2026). RPG ablates diagnostic inputs and separately compares skill-
library versions with the runtime model, prompt, perception, and execution budgets fixed (Wang
et al., 2026d). ASPIRE evaluates library snapshots accumulated from different numbers of source
tasks, including an empty-library baseline on unseen tasks; it also tests simulation-discovered skills
on a different physical embodiment (Lu et al., 2026). These evaluations connect gains to specific
changes and assess whether their benefits can be reused beyond the original tasks and embodiments.
Efficiency and Autonomy.Several studies report the resources behind improvement and distin-
guishautonomousexecutionfromassistanceduringdevelopment. ENPIREmeasuresrobotandGPU
utilization, token consumption, and time and tokens needed to reach success, exposing trade-offs
between faster improvement and resource efficiency (Xiao et al., 2026). KnowBody reports plan-
ner rounds alongside task completion and tracks decision effort during continual interaction (Lou
et al., 2026). F4R compares methods under matched data-preparation time budgets and itemizes
reconstruction, collection, and training costs (Yu et al., 2026). Autonomy is assessed through ex-
plicit execution conditions: EmbodiRSI disables human correction and agent takeover during policy
evaluation, while RPG distinguishes autonomous practice updates from human setup and hardware
adaptation, then evaluates frozen physical systems without human assistance (Lang et al., 2026;
Wang et al., 2026d). These reports relate improvements to resource use and human involvement.
6.3 Benchmarks and Evaluation Resources
Table 4 organizes existing resources into embodied and RSI-related benchmarks according to their
primary evaluation focus. The resources include task suites, benchmark protocols, and supporting
evaluation frameworks; a resource may support more than one focus.
Embodied benchmarks.Task-oriented benchmarks assess task learning, performance, and gener-
alization(Liuetal.,2023a), aswellasrobustnessandphysical-worldperformance(Zhouetal.,2025b;
Atreya et al., 2025). Alongside task-level evaluations, supporting resources examine the reliability
of success and reward judgments (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026) and world-model-based
policy assessment (Tseng et al., 2026). Evaluation also extends to the development process, assessing
robot programming and policy-training workflows (Fu et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026).
RSI-related benchmarks (primarily digital).Recent resources examine agent-driven method
development and iterative improvement in digital settings. AI4AI-Bench and RSIBench-Data assess
changes to training algorithms and data strategies through subsequent model performance (Chi
et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026a). RSI-Exam and HarnessDev evaluate executable method or harness
revisions (RSI-Exam Team, 2026; Wu et al., 2026c), while PAST-Bench examines the contribution
of accumulated experience to later agent performance (Xue et al., 2026). However, a benchmark
jointly evaluating the Physical RSI methods remains an open need.

7 Challenges and Future Directions
Learning from uncertain physical experience.Physical interaction provides data and learning
signals for robot training, but partial observability, sensor noise, and stochastic outcomes make it
difficult to distinguish informative feedback from misleading signals. In Physical RSI, when the
system uses uncertain feedback to revise its own training procedure, it may carry misguided updates
into later rounds and repeatedly reinforce them through subsequent learning. How to derive reliable
learning signals from physical experience so that inherited procedure changes improve subsequent
learning without compounding feedback errors remains an open challenge.
Causal attribution across harness components.Execution feedback does not uniquely iden-
tify the harness components responsible for failure. Dependencies among memory, skills, and work-
flows allow errors to propagate, so observed deviations may reflect upstream defects or interactions
among otherwise valid components. Concurrent updates further confound attribution, as perfor-
mance changes cannot be assigned to individual modifications without controlled comparisons. Par-
tial observability and limited physical trial budgets restrict such comparisons, leaving both the
source of failure and the effect of intervention uncertain. Effective harness adaptation therefore
depends on distinguishing causal dependencies from observed associations and isolating the effects
of modifications sufficiently to justify their targets and scope.
Non-stationarity in the improvement loop.Evidence supporting a retained update is condi-
tional on the system configuration and physical conditions under which it was obtained. Subsequent
component revisions can alter dependencies and invalidate compatibility assumptions, while envi-
ronmental changes can shift the conditions governing an update’s effectiveness. Historical outcomes
consequently provide uneven support for current adoption decisions. The same dependence ap-
plies to improvement strategies, whose measured effectiveness may change with the capabilities and
experience available to the system. Sustained improvement requires tracking these dependencies

text:
Physical RSI
and reassessing evidence as its underlying conditions change, while limiting the physical cost of
revalidation.
Reward hacking and evaluation leakage.Improvement procedures in Physical RSI rely on
success detectors, learned rewards, and model-based judgments that may not faithfully reflect
physical task outcomes. Benchmarks of robotic outcome assessment expose errors in these sig-
nals (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026), while reward hacking in digital research agents
illustrates how optimization can exploit an imperfect evaluation target (Huang et al., 2026). AsΦ
evolves, changes toTrainorVermay amplify such biases across subsequent updates. Moreover, even
when the external evaluatorEand criterionQare protected from direct access, repeated use of eval-
uation results for candidate selection can compromise their statistical independence (Dwork et al.,
2015). A central direction is therefore to combine independently checked physical outcomes with
controlled disclosure of evaluation feedback and fresh or statistically corrected final tests, so that
higher scores reflect actual capability gains rather than exploitation of the measurement process.
Safety across recursive updates.Maintaining safety becomes harder asΦevolves, particularly
when drift inVerfavors updates that pass local checks while increasing physical risk. Existing guar-
antees remain limited: the proof-preserving methods reviewed in Section 5 cover structured model
and controller revisions (Fulton and Platzer, 2019). Extending these guarantees to inherited changes
inΦremains open. Exhaustive revalidation after every update can exceed physical trial budgets
and itself incur harm. A concrete direction is selective reassessment: identifying assumptions inval-
idated by an update or environmental drift, reusing evidence that remains valid, and concentrating
new trials on unresolved safety claims. Such reassessment requires per-round risk bounds to remain
valid as verification and data collection adapt, while preserving protected requirements and effective
interruption. Comparisons of successive procedures from matched starting systems and experience,
under equal budgets, fixed safety rules, and protectedE,Q, would test whether recursive gain can
be established across tasks without relaxing constraints or concealing physical risk incurred during
rejected trials, resets, and recovery.
Benchmarking verified recursive gain.Existing robot benchmarks assess task performance,
feedback reliability, and agent-driven program or training development (Navasardyan et al., 2026;
Fu et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026), but do not directly establish whether revisions to the improvement
procedureΦmake subsequent improvement more effective. Higher successor performance may re-
sult from accumulated experience or stronger starting systems rather than a better improvement
mechanism. The central challenge is to evaluate mechanism-level recursive gain under comparable
conditions. Future benchmarks should track autonomous revisions, inheritance, and subsequent use
ofΦ, and compareΦk withΦ k−1 from the same starting generation and experience, under matched
tasks and resource budgets.
8 Conclusion
This study introduces a unified framework for Physical Recursive Self-Improvement, extending robot
autonomy from task execution to improving both capabilities and the procedures that produce
them. The L0–L5 framework classifies systems according to their update targets, task scope, and
evidence of recursive gain. Guided by this framework, we investigate existing methods around
harness adaptation and model training, alongside the safety, control, and evaluation mechanisms
that support successive updates. Our analysis highlights a key gap: improved task performance alone
does not establish that the improvement procedure itself has become more effective. Demonstrating
Physical RSI therefore requires independent comparisons of successive procedures under matched
starting conditions and resource budgets, with gains demonstrated across tasks. Future progress
depends on reliable physical feedback, clearer attribution of gains to procedure changes, and safety
assessments that remain valid as systems and environments evolve. Addressing these challenges
would pave the way for robots that autonomously improve both what they can do and how they

learn, while ensuring safety. The ultimate goal of Physical RSI is for robots to become increasingly
capable of improving themselves as they encounter new tasks and challenges in the physical world.

text:
LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness
Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
Andrea Yaoyun Cui Hanyu Wang Xinyi Wang Bangzheng Li Lin Zhang
Zhenggang Tang Shyamal Buch Dejia Xu Matthew Tancik
Luma AI
Abstract:Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment envi-
ronments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and re-
mounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads
wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot’s
hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark
spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-
arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table
height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 condi-
tions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-
action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with
rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle
severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies sub-
stantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual
perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We
release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation
parameters for each episode.
