title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models

text:
1 Introduction
A learned robot policy is expected to generalize beyond its training conditions, including varia-
tions in the robot itself. The robot executing a policy often differs from the one used to collect its
demonstrations: cameras are bumped and remounted, camera-to-arm calibration drifts, control rates
change, gripper pads wear, and the arm may be mounted on a different table. The task remains the
same; what changes is the rig, the hardware beneath the policy and the way it is set up.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3] are the dominant approach to such policies, and
LIBERO [4] is a standard benchmark in which the best open models achieve success rates of 93-
98% of episodes. Existing robustness benchmarks built on LIBERO and other simulators perturb the
task [5], visual observations [6], or scene factors such as color, lighting, and distractors [7, 8]. Their
rig perturbations are limited to the camera viewpoint, the arm’s initial configuration, and the table
position; none evaluates camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, the wrist camera,
proprioception, or the end effector. A policy can therefore appear robust across existing benchmarks
while remaining dependent on a specific rig configuration.
We propose LIBERO-RIG, which perturbs the rig along 11 axes, each at five severity levels ranging
from everyday drift to a markedly different setup, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO
suites (Fig. 1). We evaluate nine VLA models spanning four action-decoding families using 500
episodes per condition, for a total of 881,500 episodes. To our knowledge, LIBERO-RIG is the
first robustness benchmark for VLA models that targets the rig itself; it gives each model a per-axis
robustness profile rather than a single score, revealing failure patterns associated with model design.
2 The LIBERO-RIG Benchmark
Problem and rig.The rig is parameterized by the scene camera’s 1 orientation, 2 position, and
3 field of view, 4 the wrist camera’s mounting pose, 5 the camera-to-arm calibration, the con-
troller’s 6 gain and 7 rate, 8 the noise in the arm’s reported state, 9 the arm’s base pose, 10 the
table height, and 11 the end-effector pad geometry. LIBERO [4] simulates a Franka Panda arm
in MuJoCo [9] using robosuite [10]; LIBERO-RIG keeps each task’s instruction, object identities,
success predicate, and nominal initial states fixed while changing only the rig.
Axes.Table 1 lists the 11 axes, their corresponding physical changes, and the severity endpoints.
We classify each fault by its direct effect on camera images at a fixed arm and object configuration:
an observable fault changes at least one image, whereas a latent fault leaves all images unchanged
and affects the policy only through the arm’s motion or its reported state.

able, L latent, W weakly observable (visible only in close-range wrist views). Each severity ladder
runs from s1 to s5; Appendix B lists the parameters at each level.

Conditions and scoring.Every axis has five severity levels, s1 to s5, ranging from the smallest
tested magnitude to a markedly different setup; control frequency is read by rate. A condition is a
combination of suite, axis, and level. Table height applies to only two suites, yielding 210 perturbed
conditions and four nominal ones. Each condition evaluates its suite’s ten tasks from LIBERO’s
50 fixed initial states per task, for a total of 500 episodes; LingBot-V A provides a checkpoint only
for LIBERO-10. The score is the raw success rate for each axis, averaged over its conditions and
compared with the model’s unperturbed success rate. The policy receives no fault metadata.
Fairness checks.A perturbed condition provides a valid test of the policy only if the task remains
solvable and its goal visible. We verify that every condition has been solved, either a controller with
access to the fault parameters or at least one evaluated model, and we audit goal visibility for the
camera axes (Appendix H).
Models.We evaluate OpenVLA-OFT [11], OFT-Plus (the LIBERO-Plus authors’ checkpoint of
the same architecture [6]),π 0 [3],π 0.5 [12], X-VLA [13], NORA [14], MolmoAct [15], and two
world-model policies, Cosmos Policy [16] and LingBot-V A [17] (Appendix J).
3 Findings
Table 2 presents the main result; pooled results include the eight models evaluated on all four suites,
and Appendix C reports each model’s success rate at every axis and severity level.
Finding 1: Performance degradation varies across axes.At severity 3, mean success rates across
the eleven axes range from 0.448 to 0.931 (Fig. 2; permutation test,p <0.001). Moving the scene
camera to a new mount cuts success nearly in half; reorienting it in place and shifting the robot’s
base produce the next-largest drops. At the other end, noise on the reported arm pose causes no
observed degradation. The ordering is similar at severities 4 and 5 (Fig. 6).
Finding 2: Only the first severity level is free.Pooled over models and axes, success moves from
0.932 to 0.914 at level 1, the only level within a 5 percent non-inferiority margin of nominal (test in
Appendix E); level 2 reduces success by 9 percent relative to nominal (0.845), with further declines
to 0.767, 0.591, and 0.509 at levels 3, 4, and 5, respectively (Fig. 3, Table 3).
Finding 3:π 0.5 ranks first in every suite, but its lead is statistically supported in only three.
π0.5 ranks first on LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, and LIBERO-Goal, remaining first in nearly
every resample of each suite’s tasks. On LIBERO-10, its lead is narrow: it retains top rank in 65
percent of task resamples with five rivals not statistically distinguishable from it (task-resampled
ranks and sign-flip tests; Fig. 4, Table 4, Appendix E).
Finding 4: Robustness is lowest on the long-horizon suite.Every model evaluated on all four
suites has a lower success rate on LIBERO-10 than its average across the other three suites, with

model at severities 4 and 5 (paired sign-flip test,p= 0.008; Table 7, Fig. 10).
Finding 5: Motion errors reduce success, while state-reporting errors do not, suggesting re-
liance on vision.The controller executes each command using the true joint values, while the policy
receives the arm state as an input vector; proprioception noise corrupts only the latter, so the arm
still moves correctly and success remains unchanged (0.931 versus 0.932 pooled). Two controls
on OpenVLA-OFT support this interpretation: fully corrupting the reported pose leaves success on
LIBERO-Spatial at its nominal rate of 0.970, consistent with visual localization of the arm, whereas
injecting the same noise into the controller’s own state estimate, which introduces actual motion
errors, reduces success from 0.960 to 0.470 at 2 cm (Appendix G).
Finding 6: Visual robustness training does not mitigate faults the camera cannot see; an
absolute-pose interface is largely insensitive to calibration faults.OFT-Plus, which shares an
architecture with OpenVLA-OFT further trained on LIBERO-Plus’s perturbations, improves only
on the camera axes represented in its training (camera orientation 0.867 versus 0.701, camera posi-
tion 0.787 versus 0.590) and performs within 0.02 of OpenVLA-OFT on action-frame rotation and
every other axis. These results suggest that robustness learned through visual augmentation does
not transfer to faults that leave the image unchanged. X-VLA, which outputs absolute poses, shows
little degradation under the same calibration faults (0.968 versus a 0.976 nominal), consistent with
the hypothesis that an absolute goal allows repeated correction of the remaining pose error, whereas
errors in a delta policy can accumulate (Appendix D).
4 Limitations and Conclusion
Limitations.All measurements are collected in simulation, using one embodiment, with one axis
perturbed per episode. Raw success rates reflect both baseline task proficiency and robustness, and
uncertainty intervals are based on ten tasks per suite.
Conclusion.LIBERO-RIG perturbs only the robot rig and leaves every LIBERO task unchanged,
allowing us to measure sensitivity to rig changes while holding the task fixed. Nine VLA models
succeed on 93 to 98 percent of standard LIBERO episodes; across the eight evaluated on all four
suites, pooled success falls to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Cam-
era placement is the most damaging axis, calibration and timing faults are not mitigated by visual
robustness training, and sensitivity to faults varies with the action interface. The per-axis profiles
show practitioners which rig changes each model tolerates (Table 5), and we release the benchmark
together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.

This appendix gives additional figures and tables (Section A), the exact definition and fairness checks
of every axis (Section B), the full results grids and the severity 4 and 5 versions of every analysis
(Section C), the findings moved from the main text (Section D), the statistical methods (Section E),
the control-frequency decomposition (Section F), the proprioception follow-ups (Section G), the
diagnostics and the scoring decision (Section H), the cut latency axis (Section I), model setup and
parity (Section J), compute and provenance (Section L), and the rig-augmentation pilot (Section M).
B The Axes in Detail
Fig. 5 shows the ladders of the observable axes. For every axis we state what physically changes, the
exact mathematics of the perturbation, and the fairness checks: the tests that confirm the perturbation
preserves task feasibility. An axis that is too weak lets every model pass; one that is too strong breaks
the task itself, so zero success no longer indicates policy failure. Four checks apply to every axis
and are stated once. A bit-exact parity gate: before any run, the harness must reproduce a fixed
set of archived reference results exactly. Frozen manifests: all perturbation values are specified in
advance in checksummed files, 107,000 entries, so every episode’s perturbation is fixed in advance
and replayable under a pinned software configuration. Ladders that start small: levels 1 and 2 are
the smaller tested magnitudes (2 and 5 degrees of camera twist, 1 and 2 cm of base displacement),
so each ladder brackets the transition instead of starting past it; we do not claim that they represent
measured real-world drift. Same tasks, same starts: every axis runs the same 40 tasks from the same
fixed initial states as the unperturbed baseline. No check filters the score; all results are published as
diagnostics. Notation:vis the ladder value at the condition’s severity level;±marks a per-episode
signddrawn from the frozen manifest; multi-part axes draw each component’s sign independently,
so an episode’s direction is a sign pattern; magnitudes are fixed within a condition, except that

D Additional Findings from the Profiles
Control-frequency mismatch damages policies by overshoot.A 20 Hz control period realizes
about 17 percent of a requested displacement, so policies learn to ask for near the 5 cm cap; a 5 Hz
period realizes about 64 percent, the policy cannot tell, and the error compounds across the action
chunk, so a quarter of the trained rate costs 0.78 of pooled success. For OpenVLA-OFT, four times
the simulated time recovers little (0.099 to 0.206 of its nominal) while a fixed interval between
observations recovers most (0.803); Section F gives the decomposition. The two models that predict
video jointly with their actions, Cosmos Policy and LingBot-V A, sit at the bottom of this axis (0.419,
the worst four-suite rate, and 0.318 on LIBERO-10), which suggests that training on video at a fixed
frame rate ties a policy’s actions to that clock, a hypothesis resting on two rows.
The action interface is associated with sensitivity to different faults.X-VLA outputs absolute
poses, and the calibration faults that hurt every other model have little effect on it, 0.968 on action-
frame rotation and on gain error against a 0.976 nominal, since an absolute goal shrinks at every step
the gap these faults distort, whereas a delta policy’s errors accumulate. The same interface offers
no apparent protection against perturbations to the scene cameras (0.329 and 0.295) and pays on
control frequency (0.557), so X-VLA lands sixth of eight. Training data and chunk length differ too,
so this is an association rather than a controlled comparison.
Robustness training transfers only to the axes represented in training.OFT-Plus beats
OpenVLA-OFT overall, 0.796 against 0.761 from near-identical nominals, and the gains are con-
centrated on the camera axes its training mixture perturbs: camera orientation 0.867 against 0.701,
camera position 0.787 against 0.590, field of view 0.922 against 0.874. On every other axis, in-
cluding the wrist camera, which the mixture leaves unperturbed, the two differ by at most 0.02; a
benchmark of camera perturbations alone would call OFT-Plus robust.
E Statistical Methods
Two properties of the data drive every choice below. The data are clustered: a condition holds
500 episodes from 10 tasks, and the episodes within a task have correlated outcomes, so the unit
that varies independently is the task. On the same statistic, the pooled severity-3 rate over 168,000
episodes, treating episodes as independent gives a 95 percent interval of 0.765 to 0.769; with the
task as the unit it is 0.742 to 0.789, about twelve times wider. The data are paired: every model
is evaluated on the same 40 tasks, from the same initial states, under perturbations pinned in the
frozen manifests, so task-to-task difficulty cancels when models or axes are compared within a
block. Everything below follows from those two facts. One more convention: pooled rates weight
episodes equally, so a suite with a table-height axis (spatial, goal) carries 11 of 42 conditions at
a level and the other two suites 10 of 42; weighting the four suites equally instead changes every
pooled level by at most 0.001, and the leaderboard weights axes, not episodes, equally. Unless
otherwise specified, analyses use 10,000 permutations, 5,000 bootstrap draws, and a fixed seed, and
every input is a per-condition result file holding successes and trials per task, so every number can
be recomputed from episode counts.

13 cm. Speed is not what is lost: each command travels 3.7 times farther but commands arrive a
quarter as often, so achievable speed at 5 Hz is about 94 percent of nominal.
Two clocks.One action is consumed per control step, 50 ms at 20 Hz and 200 ms at 5 Hz, and
that is when the delta re-anchors on the arm’s true measured pose. The network runs far less often:
once per chunk, so every 8 control steps for OpenVLA-OFT, which is 400 ms at 20 Hz and 1.6 s
at 5 Hz. Re-anchoring is on the fast clock, but new visual information arrives on the slow clock,
so every step executes a command based on an outdated observation. This is also why V2 works
without touching the servo: it shortens only the slow clock.
Retired explanations.Two explanations were ruled out by these runs. “The task stops fitting in
the speed budget” fails because the realization fraction is not constant with rate, so achievable speed
is roughly preserved. “The world moves on during the long chunk” fails because LIBERO is quasi-
static: objects do not evolve on their own, so there is no physical deadline for an action to miss. A
secondary channel is visible but not separately quantified: closing the gripper takes about 6 steps at
20 Hz and completes inside 1 step at 5 Hz, which compresses the learned grasp-phase coordination.

I The Excluded Axis: Actuation Latency
An actuation-latency axis (commands executed 1, 2, 3, 5, or 8 control steps late, 50 to 400 ms)
was part of the pilot design. It is the most destructive fault we measured: 400 ms of delay took
the OpenVLA-OFT baseline from 97 percent to 1 percent in the pilot screen, and a compensating
replay witness solved every latency condition. It was cut from the score because a fix exists entirely
in the software around the policy: an executor that waits until the arm has settled and then re-
plans, instead of executing a stale action chunk, removes the fault without modifying the policy, and
LIBERO’s quasi-static scenes permit this intervention. An axis that a systems engineer can zero
out without touching the model measures the executor, not the policy. The data will be released as
a separate system track, and the level-5 latency condition survives as a parity-gate condition (1 of
100). Destructive is not the same as fair to ask.
J Model Setup and Parity
Table 16 lists every arm. All models except the two OpenVLA-OFT variants run as policy servers
behind a single unchanged client that speaks the openpi wire protocol; the OpenVLA-OFT variants
run in-process through the authors’ evaluation code with a perturbation hook. Before entering the
benchmark, each model ran a nominal preflight of 400 episodes under its authors’ settings (100 for
the LIBERO-10-only arm; a separate run for the arms added later, the screen tier’s nominal condi-
tions for the earlier arms), read against its published average with 0.85 as the guideline. Table 16
lists the published average beside our measured confirm nominal. The gaps (NORA 87.9 against
83.8, MolmoAct 86.6 against 84.5, LingBot-V A 98.5 against 95.0 on LIBERO-10) have not been
isolated to a cause. The documented differences are our image preprocessing (NORA), the serving
stack (MolmoAct’s published number comes from a vLLM variant), and a single seed against a
multi-seed average (Cosmos Policy); none has been ablated. NORA and MolmoAct entered below
the guideline, at 0.818 and 0.848 in their 400-episode preflight, after integration checks. The pre-
flight is a parity and integration check: it caught the X-VLA delta-mode collapse described below.

K Sources for the Benchmark Comparison
Table 18 records, for each benchmark in Table 17, the version we checked and which factors its
reported evaluation varies. The comparison is limited to these five benchmarks; it does not claim
that no other work has varied a given factor, and it separates a released benchmark’s evaluation from
a simulator capability and from training-time randomization.
L Compute and Provenance
All evaluations ran on nodes with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs, the cluster’s 80 GB variant; every
policy server fit on one GPU, so the memory capacity reflected available hardware rather than a
requirement. A node typically ran one policy server on one GPU and seven simulation workers on
the rest (four suite servers and four workers for the per-suite autoregressive models). The confirm
tier evaluates 2,140 units (condition, task) per four-suite model, 107,000 episodes each, and 881,500
episodes over the nine arms; the screen tier is 21,400 episodes per four-suite arm (5,100 for LingBot-
V A). We count a node as occupied from its first to its last logged episode, so node-hours include
idle tails and reruns, and GPU-hours are eight times node-hours;scripts/compute_hours.py
recomputes every figure below from the event logs. Measured this way, the confirm tier cost 36
node-hours each for OpenVLA-OFT and OFT-Plus, 40 for X-VLA, 63 forπ 0.5, 64 forπ 0, 167
for Cosmos Policy, 272 for NORA, 202 for LingBot-V A on its single suite, and about 5,900 for
MolmoAct: roughly 6,800 node-hours, or 54,000 GPU-hours, in all. Wall-clock cost is dominated
by inference speed. MolmoAct’s autoregressive decoding with a reasoning trace completed about
0.4 units per node-hour, its 100 Hz units took a median of 22 hours of worker time each (6.5 to
96 hours), and its confirm tier ran for 11 days over 95 node allocations; across all arms, up to 80
nodes were active at once. Every confirm episode has a video, the commanded action sequence with
its seeds and budgets, and an event log, with one exception: four MolmoAct units (200 episodes)
finished through a queue-bypass runner that recorded success counts only. A full arm’s videos are
about 107,000 files and 8 to 11 GB. Results are archived with the frozen manifests and checksums,
and the leaderboard is rebuilt from the per-condition files by a single script.

finding in the main text: augmentation improves performance on the trained camera faults, at a cost
elsewhere, and does nothing for faults that appear only in the robot’s motion.

text:
MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
Trieu Nguyen1, Frazier N. Baker1, Ruoxi Gao1, Daniel Adu-Ampratwum4, Xia Ning1,2,3,4
1Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University
2Department of Biomedical Informatics, The Ohio State University
3Translational Data Analytics Institute, The Ohio State University
4Division of Medicinal Chemistry and Pharmacognosy, The Ohio State University
Correspondence:ning.104@osu.edu
Abstract
Multi-objective molecular optimization is a crit-
ical process in drug discovery that aims to
modify a given molecule to simultaneously
improve multiple properties while maintain-
ing a similar overall structure. This process
often requires iterative modifications guided
by computational or experimental feedback.
Recent large language model (LLM)-based
methods have begun to explore this iterative
approach; however, these methods are not
explicitly trained to leverage such feedback,
while existing approaches primarily focus on
single-turn molecular optimization. To ad-
dress this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feed-
back Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a
reinforcement learning framework that trains
an LLM to progressively optimize molecules
using feedback from previous turns. MFG
introduces a feedback vector capturing both
property improvements and source molecule
similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned re-
ward function that promotes progressive im-
provement across turns. We apply MFG over
GeLLM3O, a state-of-the-art LLM model for
multi-objective molecular optimization, eval-
uate GeLLM3O-MFG on ten multi-objective
molecular optimization tasks. The results
demonstrate that GeLLM3O-MFG achieves
the highest average similarity-constrained suc-
cess rate (81.50%), outperforming the base
model GeLLM3O (70.81%).
1 Introduction
Multi-objective molecular optimization (MOMO)
(Sun et al., 2022) is a critical process in drug dis-
covery (Hughes et al., 2011) that aims to modify a
given molecule to simultaneously improve multi-
ple properties while maintaining a similar overall
structure. Such improvements are necessary be-
cause even promising molecules may suffer from
poor solubility, insufficient selectivity, or toxicity
that hinders their development into viable drugs.
Achieving these improvements often requires iter-
ative structural modifications to balance multiple,
potentially competing molecular properties. By it-
eratively reasoning on how to modify molecules,
chemists can rely on not only their expert knowl-
edge, but also computational (Nicolaou and Brown,
2013) or experimental feedback. Large language
models (LLMs) have shown promise on similar it-
erative tasks through multi-turn reasoning (Naveed
et al., 2025), providing a promising mechanism to
mimic this approach to MOMO.
Recent efforts (Ye et al., 2025; Zuo et al., 2025)
have used LLMs for MOMO. Several methods (Liu
et al., 2023; Le et al., 2024) incorporated iterative
feedback at inference-time, prompting LLMs to
modify molecules over multiple turns while incor-
porating feedback on the modified molecules of
previous turns. However, these methods are not
trained on how to leverage such feedback. Instead,
they rely only on the LLMs’ general-purpose pre-
training and basic reasoning capabilities. Other
methods have used supervised finetuning methods
(Dey et al., 2025) and reinforcement learning (RL)
(Liu et al., 2025) to train models for MOMO. How-
ever, training is limited to non-iterative, single-turn
generation, with no specialized training on multi-
turn feedback.
Here, we introduce MFG, aMulti-turnFeedback
Guided framework for MOMO. MFG formulates
MOMO as a multi-turn problem with feedback,
using RL to train an LLM to iteratively optimize
molecules by leveraging feedback from previous
turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector that cap-
tures both property improvements and similarity to
the given source molecule at each turn, providing
dynamically updated feedback to guide the LLM
policy throughout the optimization process. MFG’s
RL training is guided by a reward function that
aligns with this feedback while also encouraging
progressive improvement across turns. During in-
ference, MFG can use its trained model to generate
1
arXiv:2610.18851v1 [cs.AI] 13 Oct 2026
title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization

text:
multiple candidate molecules at each turn and se-
lect the best molecule for further turns, carefully
balancing property improvement and similarity. To-
gether, MFG serves as a powerful new framework
for MOMO with feedback.
To evaluate MFG, we instantiate
GeLLM3O-MFG, using GeLLM3O, a state-
of-the-art molecular optimization LLM, as the
base model for MFG’s RL training. We compare
GeLLM3O-MFG against GeLLM3O and other
existing molecular optimization baselines on the
MuMOInstruct dataset (Dey et al., 2025), a bench-
mark featuring diverse property combinations and
both in-distribution and out-of-distribution MOMO
tasks. Across all tasks, GeLLM3O-MFG achieves
the highest average similarity-constrained success
rate (81.50%), outperforming the best baseline
(BioMedGPT-Mol, 77.81%) and GeLLM3O
(70.81%). An ablation study shows that multi-turn
feedback and RL training each contribute a
distinct advantage to MFG. Additionally, a case
study illustrates how GeLLM3O-MFG adapts
its optimization strategy based on feedback.
GeLLM3O-MFG is publicly available at https:
//anonymous.4open.science/r/MFG-85BD/.
2 Related Work
RL for Molecular optimizationExisting molec-
ular optimization LLMs such as GeLLM3O (Dey
et al., 2025) have explored instruction tuning
of general-purpose LLMs on large-scale MOMO
tasks (see Appendix A.1 for a summary of more
related work). However, this supervised learn-
ing approach may limit model’s ability to explore
chemical space beyond the distribution of train-
ing examples. Recent works have leveraged RL to
further align molecular optimization LLMs with
desired molecule properties. For example, DrugIm-
proverGPT (Liu et al., 2025) employed reward-
based RL to explore molecule modifications for
improving multiple molecule properties. However,
the sparsity of high-reward molecules in chemical
space can make effective exploration challenging.
To address this challenge, RePO (Li et al., 2026)
leveraged reference optimized molecules to provide
LLMs with templates of successful optimization.
Despite different designs of RL methods, existing
works primarily optimize source molecules in a
single turn, treating each optimization as an inde-
pendent process. Our work considers a new setting
in which molecules are iteratively optimized over
multiple turns, and develops a novel multi-turn
training framework for this setting. To the best of
our knowledge, our work is the first to improve
molecular optimization LLMs through multi-turn
RL.
3 MFG Framework
3.1 Problem Formulation
Multi-objective molecular optimization (MOMO)
seeks to modify a source moleculeC0 into a struc-
turally similar molecule C while improving m
propertiesP = (p1,p2,···, pm). Existing LLM-
based approaches commonly formulate this task
as a single-turn problem, where an LLM directly
generatesC in a single response when prompted
withC0 andP. However, this single-turn approach
offers limited opportunity to adjust the optimiza-
tion strategy. MOMO can be very challenging, as
structural changes that improve one property may
degrade another, and improvement patterns may
not remain consistent across differentC 0.
To address this challenge, we reformulate
MOMO as a multi-turn problem with feedback,
where an LLM iteratively generates optimized
molecules for a givenC0 andP, adjusting its strate-
gies based on previous turn’s property change and
similarity toC0. Under this formulation, we con-
sider the LLM with parameters θ as a policy πθ
that decides how to generate a moleculeCt at any
turnt givenC0,P, and the sequence of previous
turns up to t−1 , denoted as τ 1:t−1. Each turn
τt is defined as τt = (Ct, ft), where ft∈R m+1
is a feedback vector measuring the quality of Ct,
with the first m entries indicating degradation or
improvement in each property objective p∈P,
and the final entry representing the similarity toC0.
This provides πθ with valuable insight into each
specific MOMO problem, allowing it to adjust its
molecular optimization strategy through trial-and-
error. An optimalπθ leverages this feedback across
all turns to maximize the average improvement on
the property setP and maintain strong similarity
toC 0.

ing optimization problem:

turns, with reward signals guiding progressive im-

MFG is illustrated in Figure 1.
3.2 MFG Training
MFG trainsπθ to leverage feedback for multi-turn
MOMO by maximizing an expected rewardR(Ct)
(Section 3.2.2). Specifically, we use group-relative
policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) to
trainπθ by sampling multiple candidate molecules
Ct at each turnt conditioned onC0,P, andτ1:t−1,
and updating πθ based on their relative rewards.
To optimize the expectation overt in Eq. 1, MFG
samples t∼Uniform(1,T) during training, en-
suring that πθ is trained to leverage feedback at
every turn in multi-turn MOMO. MFG employs
on-policy training, where the previous turnsτ1:t−1
are generated using the sameπθ that generatesCt.
However, MFG treats τ1:t−1 as fixed condition-
ing context rather than optimizing its generation
based on R(Ct). Together, these design choices
allowπθ to learn effective feedback-guided molec-
ular optimization strategies by comparing candi-
date molecules generated under the same condi-
tioning context. Asπθ is updated during training,
the conditioning of previous turns τ1:t−1, which
are generated on-policy and used as conditioning
context, also reflect the policy’s changing output
distribution.
3.2.1 Candidate Advancement Criterion
To encourage progressive improvements across
turns, MFG defines a candidate selection criterion
Advance(·) with two purposes: (1) during training,
identifying the best molecule from previous turns
as a reference for progressive improvement; and (2)
during inference, selecting a promising molecule
to carry forward, along with its feedback, to guide
subsequent optimization. Specifically, Advance(·)
is a hierarchical selection criterion that balances im-
provements across multiple target properties with
structural similarity toC0 through prioritized com-
parisons. It prioritizes molecules satisfying a pre-
defined similarity threshold δ toC0, followed by
molecules that improve all target properties. When
no candidate improves all properties, those improv-
ing more properties are preferred, preventing large
gains in one property from outweighing broader
improvements. Together, Advance(·) prioritizes
the breadth of property improvements over their
magnitude while preserving structural similarity
(see Appendix A.2 for details).

for rewarding property improvements, while

better molecules across turns. Specifically,R(Ct)

3.3 MFG Inference
At inference time, MFG performs iterative molec-
ular optimization using the trained policyπθ, con-
ditioned on the source molecule C0, target prop-
erty setP, initially empty set of previous turns
τ. At each turn t, MFG samples N candidates
and applies the selection criterion Advance(·)
introduced in Section 3.2.1 to obtain Ct =
Advance({C1

and its feedback vector ft, capturing property
changes and structural similarity relative to C0,
form the updatedτ1:t =τ 1:t−1∪{(Ct,ft)}. This
process repeats until turn T , with each selected
molecule and its feedback incorporated into the
conditioning context for the next turn. The final
optimized molecule CT is then selected from all
T×N generated candidates according to the crite-
ria described in Section 4.3.
Unlike the final output selection, Advance(·)
contributes to feedback construction during infer-
ence by determining which intermediate molecule
and its associated feedback are carried forward to
subsequent turns. This selection aims to carry for-
ward a promising intermediate molecule that pro-
vides a meaningful direction for subsequent opti-
mization, allowing future turns to build on partial
progress. Thus, Advance(·) supports feedback-
guided MOMO by limiting the propagation of unfa-
vorable candidates and retaining informative feed-
back that helps the model adapt across turns.
4 Experimental Settings
4.1 GeLLM 3O-MFG
We use MFG to train GeLLM3O-MFG, a multi-
turn MOMO model based on GeLLM3O-P(6)Llama,
a state-of-the-art single-turn MOMO model.
GeLLM3O-P(6)Llama is particularly suitable for
training with MFG because its previous training on
single-turn MOMO has allowed it to acquire sub-
stantial knowledge of structure-property relation-
ships. Implementation details of GeLLM3O-MFG
are provided in Appendix A.4.
4.2 Dataset
GeLLM3O-MFG is trained and evaluated using
the MuMOInstruct benchmark dataset following
the training/testing split established by GeLLM3O.
MuMOInstruct includes multi-property optimiza-
tion tasks on combinations of six target properties:
blood-brain barrier permeability (B), dopamine re-
ceptor D2 binding affinity ( D), human intestinal
absorption (H), mutagenicity (M), penalized logP, a
measure of lipophilicity (P), and quantitative esti-
mate of drug-likeness (Q). The optimization objec-
tive is to increase the values of B, D, H, P, and Q,
while decreasing that of M. Each task consists of
a set of source molecules, paired with their corre-
sponding reference optimized molecules that we
use for reward normalization in Eq 3. Specifically,
the property improvements achieved by the ref-
erence optimized molecule relative to the source
molecule are used to normalizeG(·), while its struc-
tural similarity to the source molecule is used to
4
title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization

text:
normalizeS(·)(details in Appendix A.3).
The evaluation set consists of five in-distribution
(IND) tasks (BDP, BDQ, BPQ, DPQ, and BDPQ) and five
out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks (MPQ, BDMQ, BHMQ,
BMPQ, and HMPQ). IND tasks evaluate the model’s
optimization capability on property combinations
seen during training, while OOD tasks assess its
zero-shot generalization to unseen property combi-
nations.
4.3 Evaluation Metrics
Following GeLLM3O, we evaluate optimization
performance using three complementary metrics:
(1) Success Rate( SRα), which is the propor-
tion of source molecules successfully optimized
to improve all property objectives while main-
taining Tanimoto similarity of at least α to the
source molecule;(2) Similarity( Sim) that is the
average Tanimoto similarity between the opti-
mized molecules and their corresponding source
molecules; and(3) Relative Improvement( RI)
measuring the average relative change across
the target properties with respect to the source
molecules (Appendix A.5). Higher SRα, Sim and
RI are desirable, indicating better overall optimiza-
tion performance. For each source molecule C0,
we select the optimized molecule C as the candi-
date with the highest RI among those that improve
all target properties and satisfy the similarity thresh-
oldα. If no such candidate exists, the optimization
is considered unsuccessful.
4.4 Baselines
We evaluate GeLLM3O-MFG against the base
model GeLLM3O-P(6)Llama, and two categories
of LLMs with different levels of chemistry-
specific training: general-purpose LLMs and
LLMs for chemistry which are trained on large-
scale chemistry instruction tasks. We use
GeLLM3O-P(6)Llama to directly assess the im-
provement introduced by MFG while keeping the
underlying model architecture fixed. In terms of
general-purpose LLMs, we select two of the largest
and most capable open-weight models available to
us at the time of evaluation, Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen
Team, 2026) and Ministral-3-8B (Liu et al., 2026).
They serve as references for molecular opti-
mization without adaptation to the chemistry do-
main. We choose LlaSMol (Yu et al., 2024) and
BioMedGPT-Mol (Zuo et al., 2025) as LLMs for
chemistry baselines due to their reported strong
performance on MOMO tasks. For fair compar-
ison, all baselines use identical inputs, inference
settings (Section 4.5), and output processing proce-
dures, with model and prompt details provided in
Appendix A.6.
4.5 Inference Settings
We evaluate all methods under both single-turn and
multi-turn settings, denoted as ST and MT, respec-
tively. For baselines originally designed for ST
optimization, we extend them to the MT setting by
applying iterative inference with the same feedback
vector and selection criterion as MFG. This allows
us to separate the contribution of MFG inference
from MFG training.
Following the evaluation protocol ofGeLLM3O,
we generate a maximum of 20 molecules through-
out the optimization process for each source
molecule. For T -turn optimization, we generate
an equal number of candidates at each turn. To en-
sure a comprehensive evaluation, we independently
evaluate each method withT∈{1,2,3,4} turns.
We report the results corresponding to the highest
SR across the evaluated values ofT for each task.
The full results for each value ofT are provided in
Appendix A.7.
5 Results
5.1 Performance on MOMO tasks
5.1.1 Overall comparison with baselines
Tables 1 and 2 present a comprehensive comparison
between GeLLM3O-MFG and all the baselines on
IND and OOD MOMO tasks, respectively. Overall,
GeLLM3O-MFG achieves the highest SR0.5 on 6
of the 10 tasks and highest RI on 9 tasks. Specif-
ically, it achieves higher average SR0.5 (81.50%
vs. 77.81%) and RI (2.63 vs. 2.08) than the
strongest baseline, BioMedGPT-Mol. Given that
the inference settings are consistent across all meth-
ods, the superior performance of GeLLM3O-MFG
can be attributed to MFG’s training design, rather
than the inference strategy alone.GeLLM3O-MFG
also maintains an average Sim of 0.60, matching
GeLLM3O (0.60) and BioMedGPT-Mol(0.60), in-
dicating that stronger property optimization does
not compromise average structural similarity. This
further indicates that the similarity-sensitive reward
assist the optimization process in preserving de-
sired molecular structures.

5.2 Ablation Study
To investigate the contribution of MT feedback-
guided training beyond single-turn RL training,
we compare GeLLM3O-MFG with GeLLM3O-RL.
Both models are initialized from GeLLM3O and
trained using GRPO under identical settings. How-
ever, GeLLM3O-RL uses ST training (T= 1 ) with-
out intermediate feedback. Because there are no
intermediate molecules in this setting, we only
maximizeRbase(·) (Eq. 3) during GeLLM3O-RL’s
training. To better study the differences between
GeLLM3O-MFG and GeLLM3O-RL in terms of
similarity-constrained optimization, we evaluate
SR under two different similarity thresholds: 0.5
and 0.6, denoted asSR 0.5 andSR 0.6, respectively.
5.2.1 Overall comparison of GeLLM3O-MFG
and GeLLM3O-RL
As shown in Table 3, ST RL training alone leads to
notable improvements in MOMO performance. Un-
der ST inference, GeLLM3O-RL achieves a higher
average SR0.5 than the base model GeLLM3O
(75.87% vs. 70.05%). Given that both models
share the same backbone and inference setting,
these results highlight the effectiveness of our re-
ward function in guiding RL training. Specifically,
as GeLLM3O-RL was trained with ST setting, it
indicates that theRbase component can provide a
strong learning signal for MOMO.
Building on this improvement,GeLLM3O-MFG
further outperforms GeLLM3O-RL under MT in-
ference, achieving higher average SR0.5 (81.50%
vs. 79.23%) and SR0.6 (64.45% vs. 61.78%).
Moreover, moving from ST to MT increases SR0.5
and SR0.6 by approximately 5.27 and 2.03% for
GeLLM3O-MFG, compared with smaller gains of
3.36 and 1.12 for GeLLM3O-RL, respectively. As
both models were trained with GRPO and follow
identical inference setting, these larger gains high-

5.2.2 Performance under different similarity
thresholds
The advantage of MFG becomes more pronounced
under a more stringent similarity thresholdα= 0.6
as demonstrated in Table 3. In the ST setting,
GeLLM3O-MFG improves overGeLLM3O-RL by
only 0.37% on average at SR0.5, but by 1.77% at

at SR0.5 to 2.67% at SR0.6. Both models use

suggest that MFG’s multi-turn training enables the
GeLLM3O-MFG to better leverage intermediate
feedback to adjust its optimization strategies. The
higher success rates also reflect GeLLM3O-MFG’s
ability to better balance property improvement and
structural similarity preservation.
5.3 Case Study
Figure 2 shows a successful two-turn optimization
by GeLLM3O-MFG on four properties: B, D, P,
and Q. In this optimization, the first turn substan-
tially improves B, P, and Q, while the second turn
focuses on improving D. The source molecule (Fig-
ure 2a) contains multiple polyphenolic esters that
contribute to low lipophilicity and high molecu-
lar weight, both of which reduce B and Q. In the
first turn, GeLLM3O-MFG reduces polarity by hy-
drolyzing one phenolic ester and replacing another
with a 1,1,1-trifluoropropyl ester. These modi-
fications also reduce the molecular weight from
718 to 461, which improves Q by aligning bet-
ter with molecular weight guidelines for drug-like
molecules, such as Lipinski’s Rule of Five (Lip-
inski et al., 2001). However, the changes intro-
duced in this turn change very little to improve
the molecule’s predicted DRD2 activity, increasing
from 0.03 to 0.05.
Based on this feedback, GeLLM3O-MFG pri-
oritizes D in the second turn, replacing the free
dihydrobenzofuran carboxylic acid with a 4,4-
difluoropiperidinyl group and hydrolyzing the
1,1,1-trifluoropropyl ester. This produces a sub-
stantial improvement on D, while also further im-
proving B, P, and Q. The improvement on D may be
driven in part by the introduction of a cyclic amine,
which helps the molecule better resemble patterns
in established drugs targeting DRD2. Taken to-
gether, this multi-turn optimization example illus-
trates how GeLLM3O-MFG shifts priorities across
turns based on feedback, resulting in higher-quality
candidate molecules after multiple turns.
6 Conclusion
In this work, we introduce MFG for molecu-
lar optimization, a multi-turn RL framework that
trains LLMs to iteratively optimize molecules us-
ing previously generated candidates and their prop-
erty feedback. By training a SOTA molecular
optimization LLM, GeLLM3O, with MFG, we
develop GeLLM3O-MFG. Across 10 MOMO
tasks, GeLLM3O-MFG outperforms GeLLM3O
and achieves competitive performance against ex-
isting baselines, improving molecular properties
while preserving structural similarity. Extensive
analyses demonstrate MFG’s effectiveness in lever-
aging multi-turn feedback for progressive molecu-
lar optimization. Together, these findings highlight
the advantages of MFG in training LLMs to adapt
their molecular optimization strategies across turns.

Limitations
Despite the strong performance of MFG in multi-
objective molecular optimization, several limi-
tations remain. (1) Our experiments are con-
ducted on MuMOInstruct, which includes MOMO
tasks involving six target properties. Although
GeLLM3O-MFG demonstrates strong generaliza-
tion to out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks with unseen
property combinations, its effectiveness on addi-
tional property objectives remains unexplored. (2)
MFG relies on property oracles to provide inter-
mediate property feedback and compute rewards
for generated molecules. The reliability of this
feedback depends on the accuracy of the property
oracles, and the improvements observed in our eval-
uations have not been experimentally validated. (3)
During training, the reward function uses the target
molecule provided by MuMOInstruct to normalize
property improvements and structural similarity.
This requirement may limit the applicability of the
current training framework to datasets without cor-
responding target molecules. (4) We apply MFG to
GeLLM3O to develop GeLLM3O-MFG. Although
the results demonstrate the effectiveness of MFG
on this model, further evaluations on other molecu-
lar optimization LLMs are needed to establish the
generalizability of our framework.
Ethical considerations
MFG for molecular optimization aims to improve
multiple property objectives through iterative gen-
eration guided by intermediate property feedback.
Although our framework is developed for molecu-
lar optimization rather than harmful applications,
its ability to generate and optimize candidate
molecules may also be used to produce potentially
unsafe compounds. Moreover, improvements in
target property objectives and structural similarity
to the source molecule do not necessarily indicate
that the generated molecules are safe for practi-
cal use. We therefore emphasize that molecules
generated by MFG should undergo careful safety
evaluation by expert chemists before being con-
sidered for synthesis or experimental testing. Any
practical application of the framework and its gen-
erated molecules should also adhere to relevant
safety regulations, ethical guidelines, and estab-
lished professional practices.

A Appendix
A.1 Related Work
Molecular optimizationComputational meth-
ods for molecular optimization has been ex-
plored through a variety of paradigms, including
molecule string translation and graph-based gener-
ation. Chemformer (Irwin et al., 2022) and Prompt-
MolOpt (Wu et al., 2024) used transformer models
to translate input molecule strings into optimized
molecules. Modof (Chen et al., 2021) and MI-
MOSA (Fu et al., 2021) instead formulated molec-
ular optimization as a graph modification problem
and designed graph neural network-based meth-
ods to edit substructures. However, these methods
are developed for specific objectives and may have
limited generalizability across diverse optimization
tasks. More recently, LLMs have shown the poten-
tial for molecular optimization by treating molecule
string as a chemical language. For example, Chat-
Drug (Liu et al., 2023) and Re2DF (Le et al., 2024)
designed inference-time methods to iteratively re-
fine molecules based on LLM dialogue with ex-
ternal domain feedback. DrugAssist (Ye et al.,
2025) and GeLLM 3O (Dey et al., 2025) further
instruction-tuned general-purpose LLMs specifi-
cally for molecular optimization. BioMedGPT-Mol
(Zuo et al., 2025) incorporated molecular optimiza-
tion as one of multiple chemical tasks in a founda-
tion chemical language model. Building on these
ideas, our work finetunes a molecular optimization
LLM via reinforcement learning (RL) so that it can
be applied multiple times to generate progressively
improved molecules.

A.4 Implementation Details
TrainingWe use a group size of four for GRPO
per prompt. For groups with uninformative re-
wards, we apply dynamic resampling with up to
three attempts. We set the upper clipping parame-
ter to 0.28, the KL coefficient to 0.1, and the max-
imum completion length to 96 tokens. Training
uses fused AdamW withβ1 = 0.9,β2 = 0.95,ϵ=
10−8, weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at
1.0. For the training data, we sample 100 source
molecules for each tasks in MuMOInstruct, exclud-
ing the 5 OOD tasks. Training GeLLM 3O-MFG
took approximately 36 hours using two NVIDIA
A100 GPUs.
For parameter-efficient training, we use LoRA
with rank 16, scaling parameter 32, and dropout
0.05. We apply LoRA to the attention and
Feed-Forward Network (FFN) projection layers
in every Transformer block, while keeping all
pretrained model parameters frozen. Training
of GeLLM3O-RL follows the same setup as
GeLLM3O-MFG, but excludes generated context,
feedback, and the reward bonus (Eq. 4). In terms
of hyperparameters in reward function,κ in Eq. 5
is set to 1.25,δh in Eq. 7 is 0.6 andδ in Eq. 2 is
0.4.
InferenceAs we discussed in Section 4.5, N is
set to 20/T . Candidate selection criterion uses the

A.6 Prompt and Feedback Templates
All models receive the same initial prompt specify-

Your task is to modify the given molecule

In the MT setting, each valid generation is fol-
lowed by feedback on its structural similarity to the
source molecule and improvements in each target
property, as described in Section 3.1. The feedback
is structured as follows:
- Similarity to input molecule: [value]
([band])
- [property]: [source] -> [candidate]
([change], [status]; [direction])
Here, we categorize structural similarity into four
bands: very high for similarity at least 0.6, high
for [0.5,0.6) , moderate for [0.4,0.5) , and low be-
low 0.4.
The feedback is also tailored based on whether
a best molecule has been identified in previous

model to further improve uponC∗

For invalid generations, we provide corrective
feedback specifying the reason for failure. This
allows the model to identify generation errors and
refine its molecular generation strategy in subse-
quent turns.

text:
Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on
Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
Yuante Li1*, Junwei Quan 2*, Kai Qiu 1, Kate Zhang 1, Yicheng Tao 1
1 Carnegie Mellon University, 2 University of Toronto
✉yuantel@cs.cmu.edu, junwei.quan@mail.utoronto.ca
Abstract
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
(RLVR) relies on costly model-generated re-
sponses, motivating larger rollout batches and
square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to
approximately preserve progress per sample
with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is
less understood in practical multi-step training.
We develop a two-clock framework that sepa-
rates the samples needed to make progress from
those consumed before collapse. Under a local
quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves
first-order drift per sample but not progress:
larger batches take fewer, longer updates and
lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-
dependent critical batch beyond which sam-
ple efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hy-
pothesis predicts a complementary failure clock
whose sample count remains approximately in-
variant along the square-root rule. Controlled
GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
across a 16× batch range support both predic-
tions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially
for larger batches, but the progress gap persists
without it. Widening the clip trades stability
for a transient speed gain. The progress gap
reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose
checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the
two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-
step RLVR schedule: start below the critical
batch and switch to a larger batch before failure.
Our code is available at: two-clocks-rlvr.
1 Introduction
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
(RLVR) (Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025)
has become a widely used post-training approach
for language models, spanning mathematical rea-
soning (Hubert et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025),
code (Wei et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025a), and
broader domains scored against reference an-
swers (Su et al., 2025). Its appeal is that large

Progress slows with the batch, while failure stays on the

amounts of policy-generated data can be scored
without human preference labels, but training re-
mains expensive because this data must be regen-
erated as the policy changes:every policy update
requires fresh rollouts, and generation domi-
nates the cost.Practitioners therefore enlarge the
rollout batch, the number of responses generated
by one policy before it is updated, and rely on the
square-root ruleto transfer the learning rate across
batch sizes, scaling it with the square root of the
batch (Malladi et al., 2022; Hilton et al., 2022). For
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao
et al., 2024) with one optimizer step per rollout, the
rule approximately works: rollout batches from
512 to 8K responses follow learning curves within
about one accuracy point of each other when plot-
ted against the number of samples consumed (Li
et al., 2026).
However, practical RLVR training rarely oper-
ates in this one-step regime. To amortize genera-
tion, practical RLVR recipes split each rollout into
mini-batches and take one optimizer step on each.

text:
DAPO, for example, uses 16 optimizer steps per
rollout (Yu et al., 2025). From the second step on-
ward, the current policy has moved away from the
policy that generated the data, so the token-level im-
portance ratios depart from one and the PPO-style
ratio clip begins to suppress gradient contributions
from tokens whose ratios move beyond the clipping
range.
In our multi-step GRPO experiments, three phe-
nomena appear together under the square-root rule:
➀ Progress slows with batch size.Larger rollout
batches learn more slowly per sample. ➁ Failure
keeps time in samples.Without the clip, larger
batches collapse after the same number of sam-
ples as smaller ones, despite taking far fewer op-
timizer steps. ➂ Clipping helps larger batches
most.Although clipping is often viewed as a bot-
tleneck on learning (Qi et al., 2026; Yang et al.,
2026a), its stabilizing effect is strongest for the
larger batches. Figure 1 visualizes this split into
two clocks: progress becomes increasingly sample-
inefficient with larger rollout batches, while failure
stays locked to the number of samples consumed.
Prior work studies these effects separately: batch-
size invariance (Hilton et al., 2022; Li et al., 2026),
critical-batch behavior with the learning rate tuned
at every batch (McCandlish et al., 2018), and clip-
ping at a fixed batch size. None explains why
all three emerge together under the same batch-
dependent learning-rate rule.
We explain these phenomena with atwo-clock
frameworkof batch scaling. Its central observa-
tion is thatthe square-root rule preserves the pol-
icy’s drift per sample, the persistent displacement
it accumulates, but not the progress that drift pro-
duces.A larger rollout batch takes fewer optimizer
steps on the same samples, and the square-root rule
makes each step longer. Under a local quadratic
model, these fewer, longer steps accumulate the
same drift per sample but lose more progress to cur-
vature. This gives a progress clock, which counts
samples to a target accuracy and slows beyond a
learning-rate-dependent critical batch. If collapse
occurs when accumulated drift reaches a threshold,
the same scaling rule gives a failure clock that is
invariant in samples. The progress clock follows
from the local quadratic model, and the failure
clock rests on a drift-threshold hypothesis that we
test.
We test the two-clock model with controlled
GRPO experiments that vary rollout batch size,
learning rate, and clipping over a sixteenfold range
of rollout batches. The progress clock departs
from sample invariance beyond a critical batch:
with eight steps per rollout, as the learning rate
rises tenfold, the sample-cost exponent climbs from
0.15 to 0.44. Unlike the tuned-learning-rate pic-
ture (McCandlish et al., 2018), the critical batch
therefore shrinks with the learning rate assigned
by the square-root rule and lies well below the gra-
dient noise scale. The failure clock, in contrast,
does not move along the rule: without the clip,
a 4,096 batch fails after 56 to 80 optimizer steps
and a 512 batch after 648, yet both fail after 30 to
50k samples. Restoring the clip delays collapse
twofold for the small batch and fourfold for the
large one, and the progress gap is present with or
without it. The progress gap reappears on a second
dataset, a second checkpoint, and a 7B model. The
separation between the two clocks further yields
a simple batch schedule:start below the critical
batch for sample-efficient progress, then switch
to a larger batch when throughput or stability
makes it preferable.The ramp approaches the
best fixed batch while generating three quarters of
its samples at the large batch.
To summarize, our contributions are as follows.
➀ We introduce a two-clock framework for multi-
step GRPO, in which a local model derives
a learning-rate-dependent critical batch for
progress, while a drift-threshold hypothesis pre-
dicts failure at a fixed number of samples along
the square-root rule.
➁ We test these predictions across batch size, learn-
ing rate, clipping, model scale, and dataset, with
failure-law fits that favor drift scaling over noise-
driven alternatives and clip and replay controls
showing that the clip delays failure while the
progress gap persists without it.
➂ We derive a practical batch schedule for multi-
step RLVR from the two clocks: start below
the critical batch and switch to a larger batch
before failure. In our experiments, this schedule
approaches the best fixed-batch performance.

Predictions.The model gives three testable pre-
dictions, corresponding to the three phenomena of
the introduction.
P1. Progress slows beyond a critical batch.Sam-
ple efficiency degrades with the batch as the
curvature term becomes important, more so at
higher learning rates, and even where the clip
cannot act.
P2. Failure keeps time in samples.Without the
clip, the square-root rule preserves the failure
point in samples, and lowering the learning
rate delays failure linearly, as the drift law
predicts, not quadratically, as a noise-driven
1/η2 law would.
P3. The clip buys stability rather than sustained
speed.Larger batches are clipped more, so
the clip should delay their failure most without
removing the progress gap, and widening it
should give this protection up.

test gradient-norm clipping separately. Each run

The penalty appears beyond a critical batch.
Across four rollout batches, increasing the batch

5.2 Failure keeps time in samples (P2)
P2 predicts that without clipping, failure is gov-
erned by consumed samples rather than optimizer
steps and does not move along the square-root rule.
Failure aligns in samples, not steps.Removing
the clip exposes this clock (Fig. 4). At the gradient-
norm onset, the 4,096 batch fails after only 7–10
rollouts, or 56–80 optimizer steps, while the 512
batch lasts 81 rollouts, or 648 steps. Yet both fail
after 30–50k responses.
The square-root rule preserves the failure point.
Across 21 unclipped runs, we vary the optimizer
batch by 32× and the learning rate by nearly 6×
and fitN fail∝b βη−γ (Table 4). Along the square-
root rule the failure point does not move with the
batch:β−γ/2 =−0.08 over the failed runs and
0.11 with the censored runs included, and both 90%
intervals contain zero, which rules out the batch-
blind prediction of −1/2. The fitted γ= 0.64 –
0.72 rules out the random-walk prediction of 2,
and of the three candidate forms only the drift form
survives a likelihood-ratio test against the free fit
(p≈0.3 , against p <10−4 for the other two).
Fig. 5 plots each run against the law, and fourteen
of the eighteen failing runs lie within a factor of
1.5 of it.
The failure pattern favors accumulated drift.
Failure depends on the learning rate far more
weakly than the quadratic law of a noise-driven
random walk, and at the highest learning rates it
coincides with a jump of about four orders of mag-
nitude in the KL divergence between the updated
and rollout policies. The failure point is also not an
artifact of disabling gradient-norm clipping: with
a norm cap of 1.0, the small batch fails after 36k
samples, within the 31–46k range of its seeds.
Robustness.Failure also keeps time in samples
on the 7B model, with a model-specific constant.
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, the two batches fail 6×
apart in rollouts but only 1.3× apart in samples.
Along the square-root rule, larger batches thus fail
after the same number of consumed samples de-
spite taking far fewer optimizer steps.
5.3 The clip buys stability rather than
sustained speed (P3)
P3 predicts that the clip, acting on the drift, delays
failure, more for the large batch, and that widen-

The two clocks give a simple batch-selection rule.
Its one free choice, the switch point, is forgiving
over a broad range.
Below the critical batch, use the largest efficient
batch.Since progress changes little below B∗
while larger batches are no less stable, the model
favors the largest batch that remains below the crit-

When a larger batch is needed for throughput, train
first with a small batch and switch, before its pre-
dicted failure point, to a larger and more stable
batch. We reset the optimizer state and repeat the
one-rollout warm-up at the switch. The resulting
ramps lie well above the fixed large-batch curves
and track the best fixed batch, while generating
three quarters of their samples with the large batch
(Fig. 7). App. G finds that switches between 25k
and 74k samples perform similarly, and the failure
law bounds how late the switch can come.
7 Related Work
Batch-size scaling and invariance.Batch size is
a basic scaling variable in optimization, affecting
both computational efficiency and training dynam-
ics. The linear rule for SGD (Smith et al., 2018),
which also motivates growing the batch during
training, and the square-root rule for Adam (Mal-
ladi et al., 2022) keep training trajectories compa-
rable across batch sizes. Hilton et al. (2022) make
PPO batch-size invariant by decoupling the clip’s
proximal policy from the behavior policy, given a
sufficiently small optimizer batch, while Li et al.
(2026) show that square-root scaling keeps GRPO
learning curves aligned with one optimizer step per
rollout over a bounded range of batch sizes. In
contrast, we study the multi-step regime, where
this batch-size invariance no longer holds and drift
preservation does not imply progress preservation.
Critical batch.Beyond a critical batch, larger
batches stop saving optimizer steps and start cost-
ing samples. With the learning rate re-tuned at
every batch, the critical batch of McCandlish et al.
(2018) equals the gradient noise scale and does not
depend on the learning rate. Under square-root
scaling, by contrast, the learning rate is coupled to
batch size, leading to a different critical batch that
depends on the learning-rate scale. In LLM RL,
larger batches have been found to reach higher final
accuracy (Yang et al., 2026b; Khatri et al., 2026)
while learning more slowly (Khatri et al., 2026).
Our two-clock view connects these observations by
separating the batch scale governing progress from
the sample scale governing failure.
Training collapse.Batch scaling also affects
training stability. Suk and Duan (2025) derive a
step-size threshold above which RLVR collapses,
while Song et al. (2026) find that collapse time in
asynchronous GRPO scales roughly as 1/η, the
fixed-batch case of Eq. (7), and attribute it to direc-
tional drift. We add the batch dimension: along the
square-root rule, failure is approximately invariant
in consumed samples.
Ratio clipping.Training stability in GRPO is
closely tied to ratio clipping. Trust-region meth-
ods replace or soften the hard clip (Qi et al., 2026;
Dwyer et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Jia et al.,
2026), while Tian et al. (2026) relax it to enable
stale-rollout reuse and Khatri et al. (2026) show
that the clip threshold changes RL scaling behavior.
In contrast to work that treats clipping as a bottle-
neck (Qi et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a), we find
that it mainly buys stability, at a transient cost in
speed.
8 Conclusion
Scaling rules are often interpreted as promises
of invariance. For multi-step GRPO, the square-
root rule instead preserves first-order drift per sam-
ple, not progress per sample, yielding two clocks:
progress slows beyond a learning-rate-dependent
critical batch, while a drift-threshold hypothesis
predicts an approximately sample-invariant failure
point. Our experiments support these predictions
and show that ratio clipping buys stability, espe-
cially for larger batches, while the progress gap per-
sists without it. Together, the two clocks suggest a
simple strategy for multi-step RLVR: train below
the critical batch for efficient progress, then switch
to a larger batch before failure when throughput
demands it.

text:
Limitations
We broaden our evaluation across multiple check-
points, two datasets, and a 7B model, but compute
and resource constraints still limit our coverage to
one model family and one task domain. Our theory
is intentionally local, and direct measurement of
the curvature term is computationally expensive
at this scale, so we evaluate it through its testable
predictions. Failure points also exhibit intrinsic
variation across seeds. Finally, we measure sam-
ple efficiency in responses, while token, compute,
and wall-clock efficiency additionally depend on
generation lengths, hardware, and system imple-
mentation.
Ethical Considerations
This work analyzes the training dynamics of RLVR
on public math datasets with open-weight models
and releases no new model or dataset. Its main soci-
etal relevance is environmental: our batch schedule
aims to reduce the number of generated samples
a large batch needs to reach a given accuracy, al-
though our own study required many training runs
(App. B reports the hardware). We see no addi-
tional risks beyond those of LLM post-training in
general.

AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with
Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
Xin Gao2,∗ Yifan Yang1,† Xin Li3 Pan Wang4 Yan Li5 Muzhao Tian6
Mingxi Cheng1 Bei Liu1 Kai Qiu1 Qi Dai1 Dong Chen1 Yue Dong1
Leandros Tassiulas2,† Rex Ying2,† Ji Li1 Chong Luo1
1 Microsoft 2 Yale University 3 Nanyang Technological University
4 University of Pittsburgh 5 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 6 Fudan University
Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code
is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models
cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting
spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can
misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction.
We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt
while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do
so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and
makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal
rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while
a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric
(VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through
reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning,
aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark
that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly
consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve
the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode
benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to
same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references,AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B
improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to
those of closed-source frontier models such asGPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
Project Page:https://microsoft.github.io/AesCode/
Correspondence:yifanyang@microsoft.com, {leandros.tassiulas, rex.ying}@yale.edu
† Corresponding authors. ∗ Work was done during an internship at Microsoft Research Asia.
1 Introduction
Information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards pack dense content into a
single canvas [1, 2]. Generating them as code is highly desirable because the output remains structured,
editable, and verifiable. However, code models suffer from a fundamental limitation: they cannot “see”
the canvas. Spatial layout, hierarchy, and color are declared line by line, resulting in outputs that
satisfy content constraints but often appear visually dated. In contrast, image generators excel at

text:
INPUTS Prompts (abridged) + refs Create a landscape hospital analytics dashboard infographic ... "Admission by Department" ... "Admission vs Cost Over Time" ... Create a portrait 1024x1536 HTML/CSS event poster ... "Future Workspace Summit" ... "Harbor Convention Center, Singapore" ... Generated code (excerpt) ...
... Render 1 2 1 2 Figure 1Information-rich infographics generated as code.Prompts specify content, while image-generator references offer visual design guidance. The examples show a landscape dashboard and portrait poster rendered from generated HTML/CSS. composing visually striking pages [3, 4], yet frequently misrender text, numbers, and logical relations, producing raster outputs that cannot be edited or verified [5, 6]. These complementary strengths motivate a novel setting where an image generator provides anaesthetic guidancefor the code model. Specifically, a reference image generated from the same prompt serves as a conditional input to supply layout and style inspiration. While existing image-to-code methods [7–9] also use images as input, they treat them as absolute ground truth for pixel-level reconstruction. This rigid replication and its associated image-level metrics [10–12] fail in our setting because they force the code model to mimic the hallucinated content of the generated prior and penalize valid design variations. Our fundamental setting therefore challenges the code model to strictly satisfy the prompt’s content while flexibly extracting layout and style from a noisy reference image. Simply providing the reference image as an input is insufficient. Off-the-shelf vision-language models (VLMs) naturally entangle visual features with text semantics. When given a noisy reference, they tend to either reproduce its hallucinated content or ignore its layout entirely. The model therefore requires explicit training to extract the aesthetic prior while adhering to the text prompt. To facilitate this, we propose AesCode, which conceptualizes the generated target as a Design Graph. This structured intermediate representation explicitly separates semantic information from visual cues. Within this graph, nodes represent distinct functional elements such as text blocks, tables, and charts. Each node possesses decoupled attributes for its required content (e.g., specific strings or data series) and its visual properties (e.g., bounding boxes and colors). Edges explicitly define structural relationships, including hierarchical containment and spatial alignment. Because the graph structure makes individual properties explicitly attributable, it naturally enables decoupled reward channels tailored to distinct objectives. Blending mixed outcomes into a single score (e.g., rendering correct text but a chaotic layout) often misaligns training gradients. To preserve specific learning signals, we derive synergic cross-modal rewards directly from the graph: deterministic verifiers provide fast, absolute checks for properties readable from code and DOM rendering, while a VLM judge assesses aesthetics through aVisual Graph Rubric(VGR), avoiding unstable holistic scoring by answering node-specific binary questions. We then balance these channels using Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) [13], preventing dense verification signals from overwhelming sparse aesthetic feedback. We also release an infographic benchmark evaluating verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with automated visual scores closely matching human judgments. Ablations confirm that reference images consistently improve visual quality as an aesthetic prior across all tested models. Given the same references, our AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B gain 31.1 and 22.4 Visual points over their Qwen3-VL backbones, achieving visual quality comparable to frontier models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 while making noticeably fewer content errors. 2
title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards

text:
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We introduce a novel paradigm for aesthetic code generation that utilizes image generators as an
aesthetic prior. A reference image generated from the same prompt conditions the code model as
input and provides visual signals during training.
• We propose AesCode, which introduces decoupled cross-modal rewards driven by a design graph.
It pairs deterministic verifiers for structural correctness with a sample-specific, graph-based VLM
judge for aesthetic quality.
• We release an infographic benchmark that evaluates correctness and visual quality separately,
with human-aligned visual scores. References help every model we test, and AesCode matches
leading proprietary models visually while following the prompt more closely.
2 Related Work
Visual Design and Code Generation.Posters, slides, and infographics can be generated as images
or code. Image generators such as PosterMaker [4] and BizGen [14] compose appealing pages, but
still misrender text and data on dense content [6], and their raster outputs cannot be edited. Code is
editable and verifiable. When written from text alone, as in LIDA [15] and PPTAgent [2], it is composed
without seeing the page and often looks plain. When written from an image, as in Design2Code [8] and
ChartMimic [16], it copies the input as ground truth. Closest to ours, DesignAsCode [17] and Editable
Visual Design [18] let a coding agent consult a generated image, but only at inference time; the code
model is never trained to use it. We instead train the code model to follow a prompt-generated image
as anaesthetic priorfor layout and style.
Reward Design for Visual Generation.RL training requires a reward for the rendered page. In
image-to-code, this reward is usually similarity to the input image, measured with visual metrics
[19, 20] or MLLM critics [11, 12]. For a generated reference, however, this would penalize valid
alternatives and reward copied errors. Without a target image, rule-based rewards are precise but
limited to what a program can check, such as element overlap in AeSlides [21], while holistic MLLM
judges [22, 23] give scores that shift with prompt phrasing. A more stable alternative breaks one
judgment into many yes/no questions, first for text-to-image evaluation [24] and more recently as
rubric rewards for RL [25, 26]. These questions, however, are derived from text alone and cannot check
the design a reference proposes. We therefore build adesign graphfrom the prompt and the reference,
verify code-level properties with rules, and turn the remaining visual properties into aVisual Graph
Rubric(VGR) tied to graph elements.
Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning.Critic-free methods such as GRPO [27] normalize rewards
within a sampled group and, following DeepSeek-R1 [28], have become a standard recipe for post-
training LLMs and VLMs [29]. They assume a single reward, however: when several rewards are
summed before normalization, a dense, near-saturated rule reward can drown out a sparse aesthetic
one. MO-GRPO [30] reweights rewards by their variance, while GDPO [13] normalizes each reward
separately. We adopt GDPO to balance our rule-based and VGR rewards.
Section A extends this review with a fuller discussion of each of the three threads above.
3 Method
AesCode learns visual design through graph-structured supervision. We first construct a target design
graph that combines prompt-required content with non-authoritative reference cues (Section 3.1). We
then route its properties to deterministic and perceptual reward channels (Section 3.2) and optimize
them with SFT and GDPO [13] (Section 3.3). Finally, we define a separate evaluation protocol for

3.1 Design Graph as a Supervision Target
The promptp specifies required information, while visual design admits many valid solutions. Learning
needs a concrete signal, so an image generator supplies one compelling possibilityIref, which may be
factually or structurally wrong. We therefore organize supervision as a design graph rather than a
monolithic target, scoring prompt-derived requirements independently of the reference.
We define the supervision target as

nodes come from a closed vocabulary of atomic elements, such as text, images, charts, tables, and
badges, and of containers, such as regions, cards, panels, lists, and groups, which hold other nodes
instead of rendering content; three or more interchangeable siblings collapse into one group node with
a count attribute. AttributesXV record content, geometry, and appearance, including structured
chart and table data, and each edge(u,τ,v )∈E carries a relation typeτ covering containment,
alignment, order, adjacency, and semantic connection. This decomposition lets prompt requirements
and reference cues constrain complementary properties independently, making supervision attributable
across semantic dimensions, and since it assumes only elements and their two-dimensional structure,

measurable evidence in the rendering are programmatically verifiable, while appearance and higher-
order relations vary by sample and require visual judgment. We therefore use deterministic verifiers
and a sample-specific VLM-as-judge channel, detailed in Section D.

3.4 Final Evaluation Protocol
Training requires a concrete reference, but evaluation must accept multiple valid designs. We therefore
assess the artifact itself throughRule,Visual, and their meanOverall.
Rule.Rule averages Text, Boundary, and Table/Chart (Section 3.2), which verify exact content,
canvas containment, and structured data from code and rendering.
Visual.Visual converts open-ended, sample-specific quality into a checklistQp derived from prompt
requirements.Contentchecks required-element presence and completeness;Layoutcovers organization,
relations, and collisions; andStylejudges hierarchy, typography, color, and component finish against
a production-ready standard. Each checklist averages 35.8 questions. A VLM answers fixed yes/no
questions from the candidate rendering, and Visual averages the three dimensions. These are absolute
criteria for the artifact rather than pairwise comparisons. We develop the pipeline on a separate
