then revises wording and coverage. Annotators review questions and rank output pairs; ranking
disagreements guide each revision. Once consistency exceeds90%and no issues remain, we freeze the
pipeline and apply it unchanged to the disjoint 300-instance benchmark, giving every system the same
sample-specific criteria. Section E details the pipeline, while Section E.3 confirms strong agreement
with human aesthetic judgments and pairwise choices.
4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
Training data.We curate a candidate pool of approximately 18,000 human-designed slides, posters,
dashboards, and webpages, clustered by their CLIP image features. For each sampled image, GPT-
5.4-mini infers a generation prompt that specifies required contents (e.g., text and charts) without
prescribing visual layout or styles. For SFT, we construct 3,000 demonstrations using GPT-5.5 paired
with the original human designs. We generate three rollouts per prompt–image pair and keep the
highest-scoring candidate if its reward exceeds0.85, otherwise resampling from the same cluster.
Retaining original designs for SFT teaches the prompt-and-reference-to-code format without image-
generation overhead. For RL, we score eight rollouts from the cold-start policy on every remaining
prompt, keep the prompts whosepass@1and pass@8rates leave usable learning signal, rebalance
them across clusters, and replace the original images with synthetic references from GPT-Image-2,
yielding roughly 8,000 prompts. See details in Section B.1.
Benchmark and baselines.Our test set for benchmarking contains 300 prompts, with GPT-Image-2
references (Section B.3). We compare proprietary and open-source models under prompt-only and
reference-conditioned settings. Final evaluation follows the protocol in Section 3.4 (detailed checklist
construction and a complete example checklist appear in Section E.1). We additionally evaluate
Design2Code [8], SlidesBench [31], and GDB/lica [32] using their respective protocols (Section E.2).
Implementation details.AesCode uses Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B, with SFT at a learning
rate of10−5 followed by GDPO using AdamW at5× 10−6. Each RL step samples128prompts
with8rollouts each; the 8B and 32B models train for400and520steps, respectively. Remaining
optimization, decoding, and rendering settings appear in Section C.1.
4.2 Main Results
Main observations.Table 1 reveals three main observations. First, reference images improve visual
presentation for all closed and open models by providing explicit layout and aesthetic anchors. Yet,
Style remains a shared bottleneck below60%: this metric gives credit only when a design requires no
further visual revision before production delivery. Second, models leverage visual guidance differently.
Claude Opus 4.8 excels in content fidelity and uses references to elevate layout and style, whereas
GPT-5.5 starts with stronger style and benefits most in content and layout. Most open models
are highly imbalanced: some satisfy code-level constraints but remain weak visually, while others
struggle on both. Qwen3.8 and Qwen3.5 stand out for more balanced visual planning, with Qwen3.8
showing the best balance between Rule and Visual among the open models evaluated. Its relatively
high prompt-only Visual score leaves limited room for further gains from an additional reference
(73.15→ 75.72). Third, our training substantially improves both base backbones, raising Overall
from51 .93to82 .94at 8B and from61.10to85 .89at 32B. The 32B model also leads Table/Chart at
90.37. We require tables to use HTML table structures and charts to use ECharts, which constrains
the solution space to executable, directly verifiable implementations and provides clear rewards for
optimization. Overall, AesCode leads in verifiable correctness while matching frontier models such as

Failure analysis.Lower-performing samples show three recurring failure modes (Figure 5). First,
canvas overflow persists, though it is rare after training: code generation cannot reliably anticipate
final pixel geometry, leaving visually grounded refinement to future work. Second, relational structure
is harder than individual elements, since the model must understand content relations and render
them as spatial connections, yet relation-level rewards stay sparse and do not localize the failed edge.
Third, semantic elements often degrade into generic marks, since such icons require fine-grained SVG
drawing grounded in meaning.
5 Conclusion
This work asks how code models can generate information-rich visual artifacts that are both verifiable
and visually compelling. We address this challenge by representing each target as a design graph that
captures element content, visual attributes, and relations. Prompt requirements define what must be
conveyed, while image-generated references guide how it should look; together, they yield targeted
rewards that help compact code models internalize cross-modal understanding, organization, and
visual judgment. AesCode matches frontier systems in human-aligned visual quality and surpasses
them in verifiable correctness, with much of this capability retained even without reference input
at inference. More broadly, our results show that image generators can serve not only as content
generators, but also as scalable teachers of visual design for structured generative models. Remaining
challenges in pixel-level geometry, complex relations, and semantic visual elements call for visually
grounded iterative refinement and more precise structural feedback.

A Extended Related Work
Visual design and code generation.Image generators now produce product posters [4] and article-level
infographics [14], and COLE [33] assembles multi-layered designs from a pipeline of specialized models
rather than general-purpose code. On dense infographics, however, they still distort data encodings and
misspell strings [6], and even a correct output is a raster that cannot be edited or checked element by
element. Generating code avoids this. Text-to-code methods write visualization code [15], layouts [34], or
slides [2, 31], but compose the page without seeing it. Image-to-code methods recover the code behind a
rendered webpage [7, 8, 35], chart [16, 36], or SVG [37]. Because the input is the rendering of an existing
program, a closer copy is always a better answer.
The closest work combines an image model with code at inference time. PosterVerse renders HTML
typography over a generated background [38], DesignAsCode uses an image-editing model to propose an
improved render during reflection [17], and, concurrently, Editable Visual Design lets a coding agent use
a generated visual as a global reference for composition and color [18]. In each case, the image steers a
prompted pipeline, and the code model is never trained to use it. AesCode instead trains the code model
to follow a prompt-generated reference as an aesthetic prior while ignoring its content errors, and turns the
same reference into a training signal.
Reward design for visual generation.Image-to-code RL rewards a rollout by how closely its render matches
the input image, using visual similarity [19, 20] or MLLM critics [10–12]. This is valid only when the
input is an exact target. A generated reference is not: many programs realize the same prompt, and the
generator may alter requested content. Without a target image, rule-based rewards such as layout metrics
for slides [21] are stable but cover only what a program can decide. Preference-trained reward models
[39, 40] capture subjective quality but inherit labeler noise. Holistic MLLM judges [22, 23] need no training,
but their scores vary with prompt phrasing, and when used as an aesthetic reward, as in WebGen-R1 [41],
they reflect general quality rather than what suits a particular prompt.
Judgments become more reliable when split into narrow yes/no questions. TIFA [42] and DSG [24] do so
for text-to-image evaluation, ArtifactsBench uses per-task checklists to evaluate rendered artifacts [43], and
instruction-derived rubrics now serve as RL rewards for language models [25, 44] and, concurrently, for
SVG [26]. All of these derive their questions from text alone. Our Visual Graph Rubric derives them from
a design graph of both the prompt and the reference, so it can check the layout and style the reference
proposes, and each failure points to a specific element. Properties a program can decide are left to rule-based
verifiers.
Multi-objective reinforcement learning.Post-training RL has moved from PPO [45, 46] to critic-free,
group-normalized methods such as GRPO [27], and we follow the R1-style recipe of a supervised cold start
followed by such RL [28, 29]. With seven reward channels, summing them before group normalization lets
their different scales and firing rates interfere, so a dense, near-saturated channel can suppress a sparse
but informative one. MO-GRPO reweights rewards by their variance [30], while GDPO normalizes each
channel separately [13]. We adopt GDPO because our channels differ widely in how often they fire and
how much they vary.
B Data and Benchmark Construction
B.1 Source Designs and Stratified Sampling
Every split is built from human-designed graphics, because content is what they supply best: the text has
a reason to be there, the sections stand in a sensible relation to one another, and the reading order reflects
an actual communicative intent. Prompts and verifiable requirements are therefore inferred from human
designs for the SFT, RL, and benchmark splits alike. Visual style is a separate matter. Designs that are
modern and polished in every respect are a small and unevenly distributed minority of the collected pool,
so the style of a given source image is largely an accident of where it was sampled from.
This separation decides which image the policy sees as its reference. Cold-start SFT shows the original
human design, since that stage only establishes the prompt-and-image-to-code format. RL and the
16
title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards

text:
benchmark instead show a reference that an image generator produces from the inferred prompt. This
is the input the method is built for: at deployment, an image generator turns a design intent into one
concrete visual proposal, and a code model implements that proposal as markup. A generated reference
supplies a uniform contemporary register, but it is one sample from a generator and need not agree with its
prompt in every string or ordering. Training and evaluating on human designs would tune the policy to an
input it never receives at deployment.
We collect approximately 18,000 human-designed slides, posters, dashboards, and webpages, extract CLIP
image features, and cluster the pool. Distances from each cluster center are divided into equal-width
intervals, and each sampling round draws equal numbers of samples from these intervals without replacement,
so that peripheral designs are covered as well as those near the centers. Strata too sparse to support the
allocation are excluded. Because sources are drawn without replacement, the SFT, RL, and benchmark
splits are disjoint; Section B.4 checks this directly on the released files.
Most of the pool comes from public design collections released under the MIT and Apache-2.0 licenses; the
remainder is internal data used for training only. We do not release the source images. We release the
artifacts our pipeline produces: the inferred prompts, the verifiable requirements, the generated reference
images, and the generated markup and renderings of every evaluated arm. Since the references are generated
from text prompts rather than copied from the source designs, the release contains everything needed to
reproduce the RL setup and the benchmark without redistributing the underlying collections.
B.2 Prompt Inference and SFT Demonstrations
GPT-5.4-mini infers a generation prompt from each sampled image. The prompt specifies the artifact
type and its content, including required text, charts, and data, and names the major layout zones and
the reading flow, since a request that lists content without saying how it is organized does not describe a
deliverable. It may carry one coarse register cue, such as a warm or cool palette, but prescribes none of
the appearance choices the visual channels supervise: no specific colors, component shapes, spacing, or
typography. The image supplies that guidance. The requirement record extracted alongside the prompt is
stricter and admits only exact strings, chart data, and table data. We call such a promptcontent-only.
To build SFT data, GPT-5.5 receives the prompt together with the original human design and writes
three HTML candidates. We render and score them with our reward system and keep the highest-scoring
candidate if its reward exceeds0.85; clusters left below their allocation are resampled. This yields 3,000
demonstrations, each storing the prompt, the original image, the selected code, and the requirements. No
image generator is called at this stage.
Figure B1 shows one demonstration. Because the supervision target is markup, a demonstration is a triple
rather than a pair: the source design the prompt was inferred from, the markup the loss is computed on,
and the render the reward system scored during filtering. The excerpt also shows the properties the rule
checks depend on. The page is a fixed artboard at the requested canvas size, every visible string lives in its
own text node, and icons are built from styled elements rather than fetched as assets, so a render can be
read back and checked against the item’s requirements.
B.3 RL and Benchmark References
For the pool remaining after SFT construction, we infer content-only prompts and select the RL set by
difficulty. The cold-start policy generates eight rollouts per prompt, and the reward system of Section D
scores each one, giving a pass@1 and a pass@8 rate per prompt without additional annotation. Prompts
solved on nearly every rollout carry little gradient signal under a group-normalized objective, and prompts
failed on every rollout carry none, so we keep the band in which pass@1 and pass@8 separate. The retained
prompts are then rebalanced across CLIP clusters so that the difficulty filter does not concentrate the RL
set in whichever artifact type the SFT policy found hardest. This yields7,408RL prompts, shared by both
backbones. GPT-Image-2 generates a new reference from each prompt, and the original human design is
never shown to the policy.
The held-out benchmark contains 300 items drawn across the four artifact types and the CLIP clusters,
with no source design shared with SFT or RL. Prompts and references are constructed exactly as for RL,

B.5 Prompts Used for Data Construction
Two model calls stand between a source design and a usable training item. The first reads the source image
and returns the generation prompt together with its verifiable requirements; the second turns that prompt
into a reference image. We print the first template in full, since it carries the contract the reward depends
on, and describe the second in prose.
The first call produces the prompt and the requirements in a single JSON object rather than extracting
requirements from the prompt afterwards, and it forbids anytext_exact requirement whose string does
not appear exactly in the generation prompt. A requirement is thus a marked verification point inside the
prompt, not an independent claim about the source image, and a model that follows the prompt cannot
be penalized for a string it was never asked to produce. The template keeps style at the level of one
coarse category cue, which leaves palette, typography, and decoration to the reference image. Two further
rules exist because the target is code: charts must be requested as ECharts with literal data arrays, since
otherwise a static picture of a chart would be an acceptable reading of the prompt, and content HTML
cannot draw, such as photographs and brand logos, must be requested as a sizedplacehold.coslot.

The second call generates the reference image with GPT-Image-2. The prompt cannot be passed through
unchanged, because it was written for a code generator: aplacehold.co slot tells the model to leave a
region empty, and constraints such as CSS-only icons or no photographs exist only because HTML cannot
draw them. Passing these through would make the reference inherit the limitations of the code target. A
deterministic rewrite therefore turns each placeholder request into a description of the illustration it stands
for and drops the code-only constraints and pixel sizing, while leaving layout structure, text, and chart and
table values untouched, so that the reference and the requirements still describe the same artifact. A fixed
prefix then asks for a contemporary editorial register and fully drawn illustrations. This instruction applies
to the reference only: the code prompt still requests placeholder slots, and the judge counts a placeholder
as the image being present. The canvas follows the aspect ratio of the source design, rounded to a multiple
of16.
C Implementation and Additional Results
This section gives the settings needed to reproduce a run and the results that support the main text. All
scores use the Rule and Visual columns of Table 1.
C.1 Implementation Details
Training configuration.AesCode uses Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B backbones. Cold-start SFT
uses the 3,000 demonstrations above with a learning rate of10−5, followed by GDPO on the same7,408
RL prompts for both scales, so that the two backbones differ only in capacity. We use verl’s FSDP–vLLM
hybrid engine without a critic or a separately trained reward model. RL uses AdamW with a constant
21
title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards

text:
learning rate of5× 10−6, no warmup, and weight decay0.01. Each step samples 128 prompts with eight
rollouts each and runs one optimization epoch; the 8B and 32B models are trained for 400 and 520 steps.
KL regularization is applied in the loss rather than the reward, with KL and entropy coefficients both
0.001. Rollouts use temperature1.0and top-p 1.0, with prompt and response each capped at 8,192 tokens.
Inference and decoding.Benchmark generation uses three rollouts per prompt with temperature0.8,
top-p 0.95, at most 12,000 output tokens, and a model context of 24,576 tokens. Closed-source baselines
are queried through their hosted APIs with the same prompt and rollout count. Reasoning-mode endpoints
do not accept sampling parameters and run at provider defaults; the other hosted arms use0.8and0 .95.
No arm is tuned on our benchmark. All generations were collected between 28 August and 18 September
2026, and we release the generated markup and renderings of every arm.
Rendering sandbox.Candidate HTML is rendered from a local file in a sandboxed Playwright browser.
The canvas size comes from the reference metadata, with1280× 720used only when it is absent; the
viewport is enlarged when necessary and the screenshot is clipped to the canvas. ECharts and placeholder
assets are served locally, and other external requests are blocked. The renderer exports the DOM, computed
styles, bounding boxes, console status, and the screenshot, and a 120-second safeguard recycles stalled
workers.

C.4 Additional Qualitative Results
Figures C2 and C3 show a random sample of AesCode-32B outputs, complementing the side-by-side
comparison in Figure 3 at a size where the pages can be read. Each panel is a single rollout on a randomly
drawn held-out benchmark prompt, rendered in the evaluation sandbox and shown unedited. The sample

D Reward System
This section specifies each training reward of Section 3.2. Reference-side evidence comes from the prompt,
its requirements, andIref; element correspondences use text, type, semantic role, and relative geometry,
and no verifier requires pixel-perfect reconstruction. Figure D1 summarizes the seven channels. These
rewards supply the learning signal only; the reported scores are defined separately in Section E.
D.1 Per-Rollout Reward Record
Every rollout produces a structured record rather than a single scalar. For each channelv the record
holds an applicability maskmv∈{ 0, 1}, a raw scoresv∈ [0, 1], and a diagnostic payloadev (Table D1).
Results markednot applicableare excluded from aggregation, whereas explicit zero-score failures are
included. Infrastructure failures are recorded separately from semantic ones, so a judge timeout is never
read as negative design feedback, and the same record serves training curves, benchmark aggregation, and
qualitative diagnosis.
D.2 Verifiable Requirements
Verifiable requirements are extracted from the prompt before generation and do not depend on any candidate
output. The schema has three types:text_exact retains the exact required string, andchart_data and
table_data retain the expected object type, labels, series, and values. Canvas metadata supplies the target
dimensions used by Boundary. Pairwise and group relations are not part of this schema; graph-bound VGR
predicates supervise them during training, and the prompt-derived Visual checklist evaluates them at test

Each stored predicate keeps its type, binding, question, pass-answer polarity, model answer, and pass flag,
so we can see which criterion changes between two rollouts even when their aggregate scores are similar.
Three rules of the templates carry most of the behavior we rely on. First, the layout class (free form,
symmetric grid, timeline sequence, hub and spoke, or hierarchical) is committed before any question is
written and sets the subgraph quota, because a forced subgraph question on a flat grid is only a row-
alignment question under a graph label. Second, repeated identical elements are folded into one group
node with a count, so four KPI cards produce one layout predicate rather than four existence checks.
Third, opaque image and icon slots are addressed only by their geometry and position, never by their
depicted content, because the reference generator may draw a different picture in the same slot and a
content question would penalize a difference the prompt never specified. A programmatic linter checks
every rubric for missing bindings, inconsistent polarity, and questions about text or image content; over the
7,408training rubrics it flags20(0 .3%), and99.6%of questions bind to an element of their own graph.
The template asks for10to20questions, and realized rubrics average14.1(range12–19).

an edge, a background fill, or an unambiguous gap. Do not invent nodes for

E Evaluation Protocol and Human Study
The final benchmark does not reuse the reference-conditioned SemanticLayout, Whitespace, or VGR rewards
of Section D; every reported score is computed from the prompt and the candidate rendering alone. Rule
averages the prompt-derived Text, Boundary, and Table/Chart scores, and89of the300prompts carry at
least one table or chart requirement. Visual is produced by the checklist pipeline below. Because both
Visual and the training rubric rest on model judgments, the section closes with a blinded human study
that audits them.
E.1 Visual Checklist
Checklist questions are authored from the prompt and its parsed requirements, and proposals that are
ambiguous, not decidable from a rendering, or that prescribe a particular implementation are discarded.
The pipeline was developed on a separate 50-instance set that does not overlap the benchmark, then frozen
and applied unchanged to the300benchmark items. The frozen checklists contain10,727questions, of
which1 ,925are Content,4 ,565Layout, and4 ,237Style, with26–50questions per prompt (mean35 .8).
Each question is answered from the candidate rendering, a dimension score is the pass rate of its questions,
and Visual is the mean of the available dimensions; the two prompts with no Content question have that
dimension excluded rather than scored zero.
Every question names the element it is about, is decidable from a single rendering, and carries a kind label
that maps to one dimension. Content collects kinds that ask whether a required element is present and
intact, such as located presence, element count, and element integrity. Layout collects kinds about how
elements sit relative to one another or to the canvas, such as collision, containment, structure, and page
balance. Style collects kinds about the quality of rendering, such as element quality, icon quality, concrete
attribute, and page density. Per-kind quotas keep a page from being scored almost entirely on whether its

Checklist question contract, abridged
Each question must:
- be answerable YES or NO from a single rendered image, with no reference
image and no access to the markup;
- name the element it is about, so that the answer can be attributed;
- state any threshold it depends on, such as a fraction of the canvas or a
ratio between margins;
- carry an explicit pass_answer, since some questions state a property the
page should have and others ask whether a defect is present;
- declare its kind, which fixes the dimension it is reported under.
Reject a proposed question if it:
- asks about the content of a placeholder image slot;
- prescribes a particular implementation rather than a visible outcome;
- restates a browser default that any page satisfies;
- bundles several claims that could not fail independently.
A small number of whole-page Style questions are written as disqualifier lists, in which any one of several
defects fails the page; the delivery-gate questions in Section E.1 are of this form. They ask whether the
page clears a publication bar at all, so splitting them would report one verdict several times. They bind to
the canvas, and all element-level questions follow the atomicity rule.
At scoring time the frozen checklist is answered one category at a time over the same image, so the judge
has a single decision criterion per call. We reproduce the judging template in full. Three of its provisions
matter for reading the numbers. The canvas is fixed, so an element that runs past the edge counts as lost
content, while full-bleed bands that merely touch the edge are not defects. Placeholder boxes are required
by our prompts and count as the image being present, the evaluation-side counterpart of the opaque-slot
rule in Section D.4. Every answer must cite the region it was read from, and an answer that cannot is
recorded asunclearand scored as a failure, so a property the judge cannot verify does not silently pass.
Checklist judging template
SYSTEM: You are a strict but fair judge of a generated web page.
You see ONE GENERATED PAGE IMAGE and a numbered list of yes/no questions about
it. There is no reference or target image; you are never asked whether the page
resembles anything.
{brief} <- the brief for this call, printed in the next box
Rules:
- Answer ONLY from what is visible in the image.
- The image is a FIXED-SIZE CANVAS, like a slide or a poster. It is not a
scrolling page and it was not extended to fit the content: anything the page
laid out beyond this canvas is gone and you are seeing all there is. So an
element that runs into the canvas edge and stops mid-way -- a severed word, a
card with no bottom, a row of tiles whose last tile is sliced -- is content
that was genuinely lost, and it is a real defect. Judge the composition as a
design that had to fit this canvas.
- Full-bleed design is legitimate, not a defect: background bands, headers,
footers and images may deliberately extend to the page edge. The test is
whether something is CUT THROUGH, not whether it touches the edge.
- Read each question's polarity carefully. Some ask whether a DEFECT is present
or whether a requirement was broken; for those, "yes" means the problem IS
there.
- Grey placeholder boxes, often labelled with their pixel size, are REQUIRED by
the brief: the models are told to stand images in with https://placehold.co
rather than draw them. Treat a placeholder as the image being present and
correctly placed. Never call it missing, unfinished, low-contrast or a design
defect.
- Questions quote exact text. Match it by its distinctive words; differences in
case or punctuation do not matter, but missing or different content does.

text:
- A page carrying more content is not thereby worse, and a page carrying less is
not thereby better. Do not report a defect unless you can point to the
specific elements involved; adjacent or tightly spaced is not the same as
overlapping.
- Do not be lenient and do not be charitable. If a property is only partly true,
answer what the visible evidence shows.
How to decide each answer. This is a procedure, not advice, and it is the same
for every question and every category:
1. Before you answer, find the evidence in the image and put it in`where`: the
region you looked at and what you saw there.`where`is REQUIRED on EVERY
answer. "yes" and "no" are equally claims about the image and both must be
shown. Neither one is the safe default.
2. If you cannot write that`where`from the image, you do not have the
evidence, and "unclear" is your only remaining answer. You may not fall back
on "yes", and you may not fall back on "no" either.
3. Answer "unclear" whenever the evidence is missing, ambiguous, too small to
resolve, or you would answer differently on a second look. Say in`where`
what you looked for and could not resolve.
Both answers need evidence because the questions do not share a polarity. Some
state a property the page should have, where "yes" is the good outcome. Others
ask whether a defect is present, where "no" is the good outcome. You are not
told which kind you are looking at, and you must not try to infer it: decide
only what the image shows.
What does NOT count as evidence, in either direction:
- Not seeing something. Failing to find a defect does not establish that a
stated property holds, and failing to find an element does not establish that
it is absent. A region you did not resolve is "unclear", not "no".
- The page looking clean, orderly, professional or complete overall.
- What a region probably contains, judged from the rest of the page.
- The brief, the question's own wording, or what a page like this usually does.
- A guess you would not repeat if you looked again.

E.2 External Benchmark Protocols
We evaluate Design2Code, SlidesBench, and GDB/lica under their official protocols. Design2Code measures
block matching, text similarity, position, color, and CLIP similarity against the target webpage, and
generations that fail to render receive zero. SlidesBench scores content, layout, and color on a 0–5 scale.
For GDB/lica we report NIMA, CLIP, PickScore, FID, color harmony, and OCR fidelity, where OCR is the
fraction of ground-truth tokens recovered by Tesseract (page segmentation mode 6) after the benchmark’s
normalization; on the same 100 renders it gives 0.719, 0.561, and 0.685 for GPT-5.5, Qwen3-VL-32B, and
AesCode-32B. All rows of Table 2 are run by us with one decoding, rendering, and scoring pipeline per
benchmark, so scores are comparable across systems within a benchmark but not across benchmarks.
E.3 Human Study on Our Benchmark
We recruited 52 participants and retained 150 completed questionnaires after quality control; questionnaires
completed by the same participant contain disjoint items, and all participants gave informed consent. Each
questionnaire has 35–36 formal items, namely six judge-reliability, 10–11 Content, three or four aesthetic,
and 16 consistency items, plus an instruction check and an obvious visual sentinel. Every formal item is
judged by three different participants. Block and item order are counterbalanced, and system identity,
automatic scores, machine answers, and reference images are hidden. Incomplete sessions, failed checks,
and image-loading failures are excluded independently of response direction, and uncertainty estimates
account for repeated observations within sessions and briefs.

text:
Judge reliability.This study asks whether people reproduce the local decisions of the automatic judges.
We sample 150 predicates each from the training VGR and the Visual checklist, stratified by dimension.
Each page shows one candidate image and one predicate, answered Yes, No, or Unclear, and the automatic
answer is compared with the three-person majority. For the automatic judge, Unclear is a failure because
every answer must cite evidence; for people, Unclear is missing, since abstaining is not asserting that a
property is absent. Agreement is therefore computed over predicates whose human majority is Yes or No.
Content and aesthetic quality.This study tests whether AesCode-32B satisfies more explicit Content
requirements than GPT-5.5 while matching its aesthetic quality. The Content task covers all 267 eligible
briefs with one frozen image per system: of the 300 briefs, 30 are reserved for the pilot that fixed the
protocol, two have no Content question, and one lacks a complete set of GPT-5.5 renders. Participants see
the brief, one image, and its Content questions; the two systems appear on separate pages, and no session
contains both versions of a brief. Responses are averaged within question and then within image, with
Unclear treated as missing. The aesthetic task shows one image from each system for 80 briefs, without the
brief or checklist, and asks for a 1–7 rating. Equivalence requires the entire 95% confidence interval of the
difference to lie within the pre-specified[−0.5,+0.5]margin.
Score–preference consistency.This study asks whether Visual scores predict human preference. Five
images for each of 80 briefs form ten within-brief pairs. Participants see one anonymized pair without the
brief and choose A better, B better, Tie, or Unclear; each pair receives three judgments with balanced
left–right order. For pairs with unequal scores, choosing the higher-scoring image counts 1, Tie 0.5, and the
lower-scoring image 0, with Unclear missing. Equal-score pairs are reported separately, and agreement is
broken down by score gap.
E.4 Human Study on External Benchmarks
We additionally collect 50 completed questionnaires of 16 or 17 pairwise items for Design2Code, SlidesBench,
and GDB/lica. For each benchmark, the eight evaluated systems form 28 model pairs, from each of which
we freeze two score-blind, same-task comparisons, giving 56 image pairs per benchmark and 168 overall;
every pair is judged five times, for 840 judgments. Each page shows two anonymized outputs and asks
which is more aesthetically polished, with the task, reference, system identity, and scores hidden.
Each benchmark is summarized by a per-sample composite. Design2Code averages Block, Text, Position,
Color, and CLIP; SlidesBench averages Content, Layout, and Color; GDB/lica averages normalized NIMA,
CLIP, PickScore, Color Harmony, OCR, and a reversed paired feature distance, since FID is defined only
over a set of images. Agreement is scored as above and averaged first within and then across pairs. To
compare gaps across scales we use100|sA−sB|/R, whereR is the metric range, grouped into< 5,5–15,
and≥15; confidence intervals use a source-task cluster bootstrap (Table E5).

text:
binds relation- and subgraph-type predicates to these edges (Section D.4). The mode persists because it is
the hardest objective to optimize, for two reasons.
First, credit for a relation is implicit. A relation predicate is one of about fourteen rubric questions whose
pass rate forms a single channel, and GDPO normalizes per channel rather than per question, so the
advantage of a violated relation is shared with every other criterion on the page. Subgraph-level supervision
is also sparse and coarse: only46of the10,727checklist predicates are subgraph-level, and a failed one
marks the page rather than the responsible edge.
Second, the objective is intrinsically demanding. On the46relational prompts, pairwise relation predicates
pass at95.3%and local structure predicates at95.8%, while the whole-subgraph predicate passes at75.4%.
Drawing nodes and local arrangements is local and readily learned; holding a timeline, hierarchy, or branch
set together as one connected object requires knowledge of the content, reasoning over it, and planning the
global layout around it. GPT-5.5 shows the same ordering, so the difficulty lies in the predicate type rather
than in our pipeline. The five-link example in Figure 5 illustrates this: every link element exists, and one
shared geometry rule removes every vertical stroke at once.
Semantic elements fail at a similar level of abstraction. In Figure 5, the controls sit in plausible slots with
a consistent treatment, yet a phone, camera, gear, beaker, atom, or monitor becomes hard to tell apart.
Rendering a recognizable icon means mapping a meaning to a drawn form in fine-grained SVG, which
draws on the visual knowledge of the backbone. Our rewards supervise the slot’s presence, geometry, and
treatment, and by design leave its depicted content unscored, because the reference generator may draw a
different picture in the same slot (Section D.4).

Hybrid Reasoning Agents
Jiaru Zou1,2*†, Yunzhe Qi3,4†, Sirui Chen3†, Federico Bianchi2, Shang Zhu2, Pan Lu1, Jingrui He3, James Zou1,2
1Stanford University 2Together AI 3UIUC 4Meta
*Project Lead †Core Contributor
A B S T R A C T
How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external
environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers
an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these
two directions withHybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between
latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a
lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent’s
continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve
tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this
architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning:HybridSFT
stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then
HybridRLscales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We
evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine,
search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning
both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while
delivering 35.5%–54.7% token reduction, 1.8×–2.6×faster inference, and 2.7×–3.7×cost savings.

title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents

text:
Hybrid Reasoning Agents
1. Introduction
Frontier intelligence no longer scales through the model’s reasoning alone, but depends increasingly
on its ability to interact with the external world (Kwa et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Team, 2026).
To solve a hard problem, an LLM agent must reach beyond the model itself by continually invoking
specialized tools, observing feedback from the environment, and adapting its next move (Feng et al.,
2026; Qu et al., 2025; Silver and Sutton, 2025). Beneath this expanding repertoire of agent harnesses
lies a single lingua franca:text, the common medium of both the agent’s autoregressive generation
and its environment interaction (Sumers et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b). All intermediate reasoning
trajectories are generated token by token as text before the agent can act on the environment.
A separate line of work on latent reasoning points in a different direction (Chen et al., 2025; Zhu et al.,
2025b). By unfolding computation directly in continuous hidden space, latent models bypass the need
to decode and verbalize every intermediate step, providing more efficient internal reasoning within
the model’s “own language" (Hao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). However, today’s
latent reasoners remain largely sealed behind the model boundary. Unlike decoded text, continuous
latent vectors (i) lack native pathways for tool invocation across multi-turn agentic reasoning (Chang
et al., 2026), and (ii) do not readily expose human-interpretable semantics, leaving them difficult to
supervise during training (Chen et al., 2026) and to audit or debug at inference (Korbak et al., 2025).
These constraints keep latent reasoning models from operating as capable agents in their own right.
Taken together, agentic interaction and efficient inner reasoning have so far required a different
medium each, leaving the two lines of work apart in the development of next-generation agents. We
believe this division can be closed by building a new type of agent that combines both strengths
tothink beyond text while still acting through it. We call this unified designHybridAgent, one that
dynamically navigates between latent reasoning and text-based interaction within a single generation.
Building such an agent is hard, since it needs to handle both dense continuous vectors and sparse
discrete tokens as hybrid inputs, and determine when to transition between text and latent modes to
balance agentic actions and reasoning efficiency. To offset the hardness, we first revisit the model
architecture and extend its autoregressive generation interface to support hybrid inputs. At the heart
of this design isHybridLink, a lightweight residual adapter that bridges latent thoughts from the last-
layer hidden space back into the input embedding space and enables sequence-wise recurrence within
latent mode. Then, we realize multi-turn hybrid generation through the agent’s own working memory,
carrying complete hybrid trajectories of text, latent thoughts, and tool observations across turns.
Surprisingly, we find that HybridAgent can render its thoughts in latent mode as human-readable
pseudo-text, making latent reasoning transparent and directly inspectable rather than opaque.
To further unlock the potential of hybrid reasoning, we equip HybridAgent with dedicated post-
training algorithms.HybridSFTfirst stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation through activation
and self-conditioned training, which adapts the backbone to reason over latent thoughts produced by
its own HybridLink, enabling reliable coordination between the two components and closing the train-
inference mismatch. Then,HybridRLscales agentic reasoning capabilities by training HybridAgent
to adaptively balance latent reasoning and text-based interaction. To realize this, we enable policy
optimization over hybrid trajectories through hybrid policy factorization and exact rollout replay.
We provide theoretical grounding for HybridAgent through complementary analyses of multi-turn
context continuation and hybrid policy optimization. From an architectural standpoint, we show that
continuous working memory losslessly preserves the entire hybrid context across different turns. From
a learning perspective, the hybrid policy factorization and exact latent-context replay in HybridRL
provide a well-founded basis for policy updates over complete hybrid trajectories.

with Qwen3-Base models (Yang et al., 2025a) across 4B, 8B, and 14B scales. Compared with frontier
LLM agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent reasoning, HybridAgent
achieves an average performance improvement of 10.4% and exhibits strong test-time scalability. In
terms of efficiency, HybridAgent reduces token usage by 35.5%–54.7%, delivers 1.8×–2.6× inference
speedup, and lowers computational cost by 2.7×–3.7×. Additional in-depth analyses of training
dynamics, reasoning auditability, and agentic tool-use reliability reveal a clear division of labor
between the two reasoning modes: HybridAgent shifts more internal reasoning into semantically rich
and interpretable latent thoughts, while reserving text for external inspection and tool interaction.

3. Building a Hybrid Reasoning Agent
We introduce HybridAgent, a hybrid framework that dynamically navigates between explicit text and
continuous latent reasoning within a single unified generation process. As illustrated in Figure 1, the
architecture preserves an LLM agent’s autoregressive generation and tool-calling interfaces while
accommodating both text and latent inputs. Below, we first present the hybrid interface for seamless
text-latent mode transition (Section 3.1), followed by multi-turn hybrid generation (Section 3.2).

3.1. Hybrid Mode Interface
Existing latent reasoning models typically feed the last-layer hidden stateℎ𝑡 directly back as the
next-step input𝑒𝑡+1. This design is not well suited to hybrid generation, as substitutingℎ𝑡 for a token
embedding creates a representation mismatch with the pretrained input space, making transitions
between continuous latent states and discrete tokens difficult. To support both latent and text modes
in a shared input interface, we add a lightweight adapterHybridLinkto work alongside the backbone.
HybridLink as a Bridge.An LLM agent’s last-layer hidden states naturally encode the semantics of
its current generation, so the HybridLinkR is designed to carry this information from the hidden
representation space back into the input embedding space. Formally, given any last-layer hidden
stateℎ 𝑡, HybridLink simulates its corresponding next-step input embedding as:

where𝑊1,𝑊 2 are standard linear projections,𝜎 is an activation function (e.g., GELU). As the residual

Dynamic Text-Latent Mode Transition.Next, we describe how HybridAgent transitions between
text and latent modes during generation, together with the entry and exit decisions for each mode.
In text mode, HybridAgent behaves exactly as a standard LLM, sampling the next token from the
vocabulary at each step. The process continues until the agent generates one special token<latent>,
which serves as the entry anchor for the latent mode. For the next forward pass, the agent uses
HybridLink for latent reasoning in place of the LM head and token embedding layer.
In latent mode, each step’s last-layer hidden state is passed through HybridLink via Eq. 4, allowing
HybridAgent to continue its generation flow entirely in latent space without token decoding and
re-embedding. Thissequence-wiserecurrentcomputationovercontinuousrepresentationsextendsthe
agent’s effective reasoning depth, enabling more expressive internal reasoning. The latent reasoning
span terminates when the semantics of the last-layer hidden stateℎ𝑡 align with the exit anchor

4. Learning to Perform Hybrid Reasoning
With the overall framework in place, we now turn to training. As HybridAgent leaves the backbone
architecture intact, no pre-training from scratch is required. Instead, we adapt the standard agentic
post-training pipeline of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to the hybrid setting. The
two training stages serve complementary roles: SFT teaches the agent to coordinate with HybridLink
and instantiate reliable tool use for stable hybrid generation (Section 4.1), while RL further scales
reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text (Section 4.2).
4.1. Stabilize Generation via Hybrid Supervised Fine-tuning
As a first step toward stabilizing hybrid reasoning in HybridAgent, we design the entire HybridSFT
stage through a hybrid data curation pipeline and a staged training procedure.
Hybrid Data Recipe.To curate high-quality training data, we filter existing text-based agentic
SFT datasets from multiple sources and convert them into hybrid trajectories through automatic
annotation. We assign reasoning steps to latent mode based on both LLM Experts’ judgments and
target models’ own prediction entropy, while retaining a small set of key steps for tool interactions
and external debugging/auditing in text mode (see Appendix E for data curation details).
Format and HybridLink Activation.As a warm start, we adapt the backbone to the hybrid data
format and initialize the HybridLink. For format activation, we perform standard text SFT to teach
the backbone when to enter and exit latent mode by emitting the two special anchor tokens. We then

Policy Update via Exact Rollout Replay.Policy optimization generally involves rebuilding a differen-
tiable computation graph for the rollouts. Applying this to HybridAgent further requires recomputing
sampled text-token likelihoods conditioned on the same preceding latent thoughts used during rollout.
We satisfy this requirement viaexact latent-context replay. During hybrid rollout, we record latent
thoughts alongside sampled text tokens and tool observations. During policy updates, we replay
the full hybrid trajectory in embedding space with a single differentiable forward pass, keeping the
recorded latent inputs unchanged while recomputing the sampled likelihoods in Eq. 10.
Algorithm 1 outlines the full HybridRL training procedure. We keep the HybridLink fixed to preserve
deterministic latent transitions. For the reward design, we simply formulate it as:
𝑟(𝜏)=𝑟 correct+𝑟 format+𝑟 tool,(11)
where𝑟correct measures answer correctness,𝑟format penalizes invalid formatting, and𝑟tool encourages
multi-tool use. We impose no explicit reward for mode usage, allowing HybridAgent to adaptively
balance text and latent generation and discover effective hybrid reasoning strategies during RL.
5. Empirical Evaluations
Tasks and Datasets.We conduct comprehensive evaluations of HybridAgent on 11 benchmarks
across various domains: (i)Mathematical Reasoning, including AIME 25 (math ai, 2025), AIME
26 (MathArena, 2026), and MATH500 (HuggingFaceH4, 2023); (ii)Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning,
including GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023), MedQA (Yang et al., 2024), and MuSiQue (Trivedi
et al., 2022); and (iii)Agentic Reasoning, including General AI Assistants (GAIA) (Mialon et al., 2024),
Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) (Center for AI Safety et al., 2026), WebWalker (Wu et al., 2025),
SealQA (Pham et al., 2026), and DeepSearchQA (DSQA) (Gupta et al., 2026). We adopt the standard
evaluation metric for each dataset. Additional benchmark details are in Appendix H.1.
Baselines.For baseline comparisons, we evaluate HybridAgent against (i)Text-based Agentic Methods,
coveringstandardtextSFT(withtools)andmulti-turntool-integratedRLmethodssuchasGRPO(Shao
et al., 2024) and ARPO (Dong et al., 2025b); (ii)Latent Reasoning Methods, including SoftThinking
(Zhang et al., 2025), Coconut (Hao et al., 2024), and SoftCoT (Xu et al., 2025b); (iii)Frontier LLM
Agents, including GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026), Kimi-K3 (Team, 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (GLM-5-Team
et al., 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), QwQ-32B (Team, 2025); and (iv)Agentic
Frameworks, including ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025a), and WebThinker (Li
et al., 2025b). Additional baseline details are provided in Appendix H.2.
Models and Training Setups.We instantiate HybridAgent with Qwen3-Base backbones (Yang et al.,
2025a) at three scales of 4B, 8B, and 14B. We then apply HybridSFT with 54K hybrid trajectories
curated through our automatic annotation pipeline, followed by HybridRL with 12K deep reasoning
examples (Yu et al., 2025) and 1K agentic search examples (Dong et al., 2025b). During RL, we set
rollout batches of 512 trajectories (64×8), followed by one optimization pass over 8 minibatches.
Implementation Details.HybridAgent interacts with external environments primarily through two
typesoftools: aPythoninterpreterwithinsandboxenvironmentsandalivesearchengine(e.g., Tavily).
We cap tool usage at 10 calls per trajectory and retrieve the top 10 snippets for each search query.
As current serving engines do not support multi-turn hybrid generation, we extend the training and
inference infrastructure to enable text, latent, and tool-calling transitions and persistent KV working-
memory transfer. RL rollouts use a sampling temperature of 1.0, and evaluation uses temperature
0.6, top-p 0.95, and top-k 20. We conduct experiments on H100 GPUs using five independent seeds.
Additional training/inference details and hyperparameter setups are provided in Appendix H.3.

reasoning is whether shifting computation into latent mode might potentially compromise the external
auditability provided by text. To examine this, we evaluate HybridAgent against matched text agents
on MATH500 and AIME25/26, covering 560 problems under identical setups. For each question,
an external observer sees only the exposed text steps, tool calls, and tool outputs, while latent
spans remain hidden behind their boundary markers. We evaluate four complementary dimensions
following commonly adopted evaluation protocols.
• Monitoring: Measure whether a blind external monitor can predict rollout correctness from the
input problem and visible trace generated by each agent, following Baker et al. (2025). We report
AUROC using GPT-4o-mini (Hurst et al., 2024) as a weak monitor, which relies primarily on the
visible trace rather than solving the problem independently, and GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026) as
a strong monitor with more powerful task-solving capability.
• Debugging: Following first-error localization (Zheng et al., 2025a), a judge model (GPT-5.6-Luna)
is deployed to identify the first erroneous visible step from a failed rollout and produces a corrective
hint, with the diagnosis verified against the reference ground-truth solution.
• Correction: Each failed problem is re-attempted using the corrective hint generated during debug-
ging, and compared against a generic correctness-only feedback baseline (Huang et al., 2024) that
simply tells the agent its previous answer was incorrect and asks it to retry.
• Rationale Sufficiency: Following sufficiency evaluation in DeYoung et al. (2020), a weak reader
(GPT-4o-mini) predicts the agent’s own answer from the exposed text steps alone after removing the
final answer, measuring whether the visible trace retains sufficient decision-relevant information.
As shown in Table 7, HybridAgent exposes 43%-49% fewer text-mode tokens while performing
170-183 reasoning steps in latent mode, yet the visible trace contains 26%-28% more key reasoning
steps per 100 tokens. This reduction preserves external monitorability, with AUROC remaining within
0.022 of matched text agents across both weak and strong monitors. The exposed text also remains
debuggable, localizing the first error in 98%-99% of failed rollouts and yielding reference-consistent
diagnoses in 97%-98% of cases with below 1% answer leakage. Moreover, text-derived corrective
hints produce significant fix-rate gains of 5.4 and 9.1 points at 14B and 8B, while rationale sufficiency
remains comparable to or higher than text agents. As shown by the analyses above, HybridAgent
uses its text mode to maintain a compact yet informative textual interface for external monitoring,
debugging, and correction. This provides an important safeguard for agent generation, facilitating
human auditing and intervention while preserving efficient internal reasoning.

7. Related Work
Latent Reasoning Beyond Text.Recent works have explored applying intermediate reasoning
beyond discrete language tokens into continuous hidden spaces (Hao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026;
Zhu et al., 2025a), allowing models to perform internal computation without explicitly verbalizing
every reasoning step (Geiping et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025b). Existing approaches
broadly realize this idea by inputting last-layer hidden states (Saunshi et al., 2025; Tack et al., 2026),
compressing textual chains of thought into latent representations (Cheng and Van Durme, 2024;
Zhang et al., 2026a), or directly optimizing continuous reasoning trajectories (Chen et al., 2024; Tan
et al., 2026). These methods improve reasoning efficiency and depth but make direct inspection and
external interaction difficult (Chen et al., 2026; Korbak et al., 2025). HybridAgent builds on this
direction by integrating directly inspectable latent reasoning as a native built-in mode within the
agentic generation process, while preserving direct text-based auditing and tool interaction.
AgenticReasoningandToolUse.FrontierLLMagents(DeepSeek-AI,2026;GLM-5-Teametal.,2026;
Team, 2026) extend reasoning beyond static generation by interacting with external environments
through tools (Qu et al., 2025; Shen, 2024), such as search engines (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al.,
2025b), code interpreters (Bianchi et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026), and APIs (Patil et al., 2025; Qin
et al., 2024). A growing line of work further improves these capabilities through post-training over
multi-turn tool-use trajectories (Dong et al., 2025a; Qian et al., 2025), enabling agents to plan,
act, observe, and revise their reasoning (Li et al., 2025c; Su et al., 2025). Despite this progress,
existing agentic frameworks remain text-centric for both model-side reasoning and environment-side
interaction, incurring large generation overhead from verbalizing every intermediate step (Cuadron
et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025a). HybridAgent decouples these roles by interleaving continuous thoughts
for internal reasoning and retaining text only where explicit interaction and monitoring are required.
We discuss additional related work and its relation to HybridAgent in Appendix D.
8. Discussion and Future Directions
Implications for Frontier Agent Safety and Secure Deployment.Frontier labs (e.g., OpenAI,
Anthropic) provide API-based access to reasoning models while hiding the chain-of-thought from
customers to protect intellectual property and limit information leakage, yet Panfilov et al. (2026)
show that the encrypted traces returned to clients can be replayed into a sibling model and transcribed
verbatim. HybridAgent places proprietary reasoning on a different footing. Latent thoughts exist
only as backbone hidden states that are readable solely through the provider-owned HybridLink
(Section 3), so no text exists to leak. The same property aids monitoring. Because the latent trace is
held by the provider rather than the client, providers can assess the safety of reasoning and actions
over the full readout, including the portion users never see, while the agent benefits from faster inner
thinking. Text mode is then reserved for what users legitimately need, such as tool calls, key decisions,
and the final answer, preserving an auditable trace without exposing the full reasoning.
Future Directions on Hybrid Agent Harness and Efficient Post-Training.Future work can build
a new type of agent harness around HybridAgent, where latent working memory is a first-class
component. Context management can then operate on KV entries directly, workflows can schedule
steps by mode, keeping tool calls and human-facing checkpoints in text while routine computation
stays latent, and one agent’s hybrid trajectory can serve as its message to another. Hybrid generation
canalsomakepost-trainingmoreefficient. Becauselatentthoughtsremainauditableduringrollout, an
external critic can assign step-level credit to latent spans, branch promising trajectories, or terminate
ones whose latent reasoning has already gone wrong, before any text or tool call is produced.

9. Conclusion
We introduce HybridAgent, a unified hybrid reasoning framework that combines efficient latent
reasoning with text-based inspection and tool interaction. HybridAgent enables multi-turn hybrid
generation through both architectural designs and dedicated post-training algorithms on SFT and RL
stages. Across 11 benchmarks and 3 model scales, HybridAgent achieves strong performance against
advanced LLM agents and agentic frameworks spanning text-based and latent reasoning methods,
while substantially reducing inference time, token usage, and computational cost. Overall, HybridA-
gent provides a scalable and efficient framework for next-generation agents that can reason beyond
human language while retaining agentic interaction in environments and external inspectability.

The format and HybridLink activation provide a well-aligned initialization, but both are teacher-forced
(Figure 11, left). At every latent position, the backbone consumes the ground-truth embedding
Emb(𝑦) , and HybridLink is trained only to match its outputR(ℎ) to that target; the prediction itself
is never fed back as an input. At inference, the agent instead runs free (Figure 11, right). Once
it enters latent mode, every subsequent input is its ownR(ℎ), which neither the backbone nor
HybridLink has been conditioned on. This train-inference mismatch is akin toexposure bias(Bengio
et al., 2015; Ranzato et al., 2015), a standard issue in autoregressive sequence models that are trained
on ground-truth prefixes but consume their own predictions at inference.
It is worth noting that exposure bias is present in both text and latent modes, since both feed the
model’s own outputs back as inputs. In text mode (as in standard LLM SFT), each fed-back input
is sampled and re-embedded, and thus always corresponds to a token in the discrete vocabulary. A
prediction error, where the sampled token differs from the ground-truth target, only changes which
token is fed back; the input representation itself never leaves the set seen in training, so errors cannot
compound in the input space. Latent mode, in contrast, has no such projection.R(ℎ) is continuous
and fed back unquantized, so even a small deviation from the target embedding becomes an input the
backbone has never seen in training. This deviation propagates to the next hidden state and hence
the next latent input, compounding over the tens to hundreds of steps in a latent span and gradually
eroding the semantic coherence of the latent trace.
Self-conditioned HybridSFTcloses this gap by training both components on the model’s own generated
latent inputs. As in Figure 4, the teacher-forced first pass applies HybridLink to the last-layer hidden
state at each latent position, yielding the model’s own prediction of the next latent input. The second
pass then replaces the ground-truth latent embeddings with these predictions and trains the backbone

and HybridLink jointly, so both parts learn under the same latent inputs they encounter at inference.
Under this training scheme, the backbone learns to read, and HybridLink learns to produce, latent
inputs under the same conditions they encounter at inference. Thus, HybridAgent is trained as an
integrated whole rather than two separately activated components.
B.2. Learning When to Enter and Exit Latent Mode
As stated in Section 3, HybridAgent transitions between modes through two special tokens, the entry
anchor <latent> and the exit anchor</latent>. Within a latent span, these anchors are the only
positions supervised byLBackbone, while every other latent position is supervised byLHybridLink alone.
The two transitions are not symmetric, however. Entering latent mode is decided in text mode, where
the backbone samples the next token from the vocabulary as usual, whereas exiting must be decided
from a continuous latent state through the readout in Eq. 5. HybridSFT therefore treats the entry
anchor as an ordinary token and gives the exit anchor dedicated supervision.
Entry as a Text-Mode Decision.Since entering is a text mode decision,<latent> is simply a
cross-entropy target, and the backbone learns from the preceding context when to switch. The anchor
position then serves as the first latent step, with its last-layer hidden state passed through HybridLink
to produce the next latent input, so the span begins without any additional mechanism.
Exit as a Latent-Mode Decision.Exiting takes place in latent mode, where no token is sampled. By
Eq. 5, a span closes when the HybridLink’s outputR(ℎ) is nearest toEmb(</latent>), a decision
depending on both components, where the backbone produces a hidden state that encodes the exit
and HybridLink maps it onto the anchor embedding. HybridSFT therefore supervises the last latent
step of each span from both sides. On the HybridLink side, the regression target at this step is
Emb(</latent>), given slightly more weight than the span interior so that the single exit signal is
not diluted. On the backbone side,</latent> is also a cross-entropy target predicted from the same
hidden state, so the backbone itself learns to signal the exit.

text:
Hybrid Reasoning Agents
D. Extended Related Work
Adaptive Reasoning on Text and Latent Space.Beyond fixed-length chains of thought, recent
work lets LLMs adapt how long and in which medium they reason (Bigverdi et al., 2024; Lv et al.,
2026; Yang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026), for example by learning when to stop latent reasoning or
deciding whether explicit deliberation is needed (Ning et al., 2025). Several methods interleave
latent reasoning with text decoding (Yue et al., 2025), using confidence or entropy signals (Xu et al.,
2026) to shift into continuous representations at uncertain steps and explore alternative reasoning
paths (Fu and Luo, 2026; Shi et al., 2026). However, existing methods largely operate within one
reasoning pass or switch modes only at single-turn granularity, and their latent states remain largely
opaque to inspect directly. Orthogonal to this line, HybridAgent uses latent mode for efficient deeper
reasoning, carries latent context across multiple turns through continuous working memory, keeps
latent thoughts directly readable, and preserves the agentic tool-use abilities for long-horizon tasks.
Hybrid Communication among Agents.A recent line of work in multi-agent systems (MAS) parallel
to HybridAgent studieshybrid-protocol communication, in which each inter-agent message combines
two media. A latent channel carries dense intermediate signals such as hidden states or KV entries,
while a text channel carries concise commitments that remain inspectable. Early instances augment
each natural-language message with the sender’s internal state trajectory (Tang et al., 2025), and later
work formalizes the dual-channel design by routing elaborate reasoning through latent vectors while
keeping answers and decisions in text (Dai et al., 2026; Mou et al., 2026). More recent works take
the same view from the deployment side, pairing every latent payload with a visible text commitment
wherever oversight is required (Liu, 2026) and evaluating the security of latent transfer alongside
visible text (Brito and Baquero, 2026). Complementary to these inter-agent protocols in the MAS
setting, HybridAgent decides the medium at the level of each generation step within a single agent,
switching between latent reasoning and text-based tool interaction over multi-turn trajectories.
KV-Cache Reuse.Reusing key–value (KV) entries across generation steps is standard practice for
efficient serving (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), and recent work extends it across requests,
caching shared prefixes and prompt modules (Gim et al., 2024; Juravsky et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024)
and composing independently encoded caches so that repeated context need not be prefilled again
(Hu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b). These methods treat the KV cache as an
optimization over a context that could in principle be re-encoded from text. HybridAgent likewise
builds on the backbone’s own KV entries, using them as a unified working memory that stores and
propagates both latent and text information across multi-turn hybrid generation.

Figure 12| Hybrid Data Curation Pipeline.We convert text-based demonstrations into multi-turn
hybrid trajectories using complementary signals from LLM judgments and model entropy to assign
reasoning modes, followed by a visibility audit that preserves decision-critical steps in text mode.
We curate the hybrid training data by converting existing multi-turn agentic demonstrations (Dong
et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2025) into 54k hybrid trajectories for text and latent supervision. Specifically,
an automatic annotation pipeline is designed to assign each source CoT step to either text or latent
mode, based on complementary signals from external LLM judges and the target model’s entropy-
based confidence, with no human labeling needed. Accordingly, high-confidence reasoning steps
that the model can handle reliably are assigned as latent targets, while audit-critical reasoning and
tool-interaction steps are retained as text targets. We describe the detailed curation pipeline below.

deterministic procedure, recording their exact character offsets. These offsets allow subsequent
annotations to identify and group steps while preserving the original content and ordering.

each reasoning step to text or latent mode, with tool interactions and key steps needed for external

external selection with the target model’s prediction entropy. We teacher-force the original textual

H. Experiment Setups
H.1. Benchmark and Evaluation Details
WeevaluateHybridAgenton11benchmarksspanningmathematical,knowledge-intensive,andagentic
reasoning. Together, these benchmarks assess complementary capabilities in multi-step problem
solving,specializedknowledgeapplication,evidenceintegration,andtool-assistedinformationseeking.
We follow the setup of Dong et al. (2025b) and describe each benchmark in detail below.
(i) Mathematical Reasoning Tasks
AIME 25(math ai, 2025): AIME 25 comprises 30 problems from the 2025 American Invitational
Mathematics Examination, covering algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Its integer-
answer problems evaluate competition-level mathematical reasoning, requiring models to combine
mathematical insights with precise multi-step calculations.
AIME 26(MathArena, 2026): AIME 26 contains 30 problems from the 2026 American Invitational
Mathematics Examination, following the same competition format as AIME 25. It provides a comple-
mentary assessment of mathematical problem solving across a separate annual problem set, testing
sustained reasoning and accurate numerical derivation.
MATH500(HuggingFaceH4, 2023): MATH500 is a 500-problem subset of the MATH test set, spanning
7 mathematical subjects and 5 difficulty levels. It evaluates math reasoning across diverse problem
types, including symbolic manipulation, geometric deduction, and numerical computation.
(ii) Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning Tasks
GPQA-Diamond(Rein et al., 2023): GPQA-Diamond is a curated subset of 198 expert-written multiple-
choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry. Selected through expert and non-expert validation,
these questions assess advanced scientific knowledge and reasoning that remain challenging for
non-experts even with web access.
MedQA(Yang et al., 2024): MedQA is a multiple-choice question-answering benchmark derived from
professional medical licensing examinations. The dataset contains 300 questions in total. Its questions
assess medical knowledge and clinical reasoning, requiring models to interpret patient information
and identify appropriate diagnoses, investigations, or treatments.
MuSiQue(Trivedi et al., 2022): MuSiQue is a multi-hop question-answering benchmark constructed
by composing single-hop questions into connected reasoning chains of two to four hops. It evaluates
the ability to combine evidence across multiple passages, with question construction designed to
reduce shortcuts that bypass intermediate reasoning steps. Following Dong et al. (2025b), we use
200 test-set questions for downstream evaluation across all methods.

(iii) Agentic Reasoning Tasks
General AI Assistants (GAIA)(Mialon et al., 2024): GAIA evaluates general-purpose assistants on
real-world questions involving reasoning, web browsing, information processing, and external tool
use. Its three difficulty levels reflect increasingly demanding combinations of reasoning steps and
tool interactions, assessing the ability to coordinate these capabilities toward a verifiable answer.
Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)(Center for AI Safety et al., 2026): HLE comprises expert-authored
questions across a broad range of academic disciplines, including mathematics, natural sciences, and
the humanities. Its multiple-choice and short-answer problems assess advanced subject knowledge
and reasoning on questions designed to resist quick answers through direct web retrieval.
WebWalker(Wu et al., 2025): WebWalkerQA, referred to as WebWalker in our evaluations, is an
agentic search benchmark requiring exploration of website subpages and integration of information
from one or multiple sources. Its easy, medium, and hard categories reflect increasing traversal depth,
testing the ability to locate and synthesize evidence beyond surface-level search results.
SealQA(Pham et al., 2026): SealQA evaluates search-augmented question answering on factual
questions for which retrieved information may be noisy, conflicting, or unhelpful. We evaluate on Seal-
0 and Seal-Hard, which test factual accuracy and reasoning under challenging retrieval conditions.
Seal-0 targets questions selected for near-zero accuracy among the non-reasoning models used during
benchmark construction; Seal-Hard includes a broader collection of difficult questions.
DeepSearchQA (DSQA)(Gupta et al., 2026): DeepSearchQA evaluates multi-step web research through
tasks that require assembling complete answer sets from information distributed across sources. It
tests search planning, evidence aggregation, entity disambiguation, and the ability to determine
when sufficient information has been collected. We report both full-correct rate and F1 score to assess
complete task success and the balance between answer precision and coverage.
H.2. Baseline Details
To evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of HybridAgent, we compare with 4 categories of methods,
including (i) Text-based Agentic Methods, (ii) Latent Reasoning Methods, (iii) Frontier LLM Agents,
and (iv) Agentic Frameworks. We describe the implementation details of each baseline below.
(i) Text-based Agentic Methods
Standard Text SFT: We apply standard SFT using the same training data and backbone models
as HybridAgent. During evaluation, the models can invoke tools and incorporate the returned
observations into subsequent reasoning. We use this baseline mostly to compare with the HybridSFT.
Agentic RL (GRPO/ARPO): We apply commonly adopted agentic RL methods after standard text
SFT to further train the text agent baselines. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) optimizes the policy using
group-normalized rewards from sampled responses without requiring a separate critic. ARPO (Dong
et al., 2025b): ARPO combines entropy-guided adaptive rollouts with step-level advantage attribution
to improve multi-turn tool use. We train these methods using the same RL training data and backbone
models as HybridAgent, primarily to evaluate the effectiveness of HybridRL.
(ii) Latent Reasoning Methods
Coconut(Hao et al., 2024): Coconut performs continuous latent reasoning by directly feeding the
model’s last hidden state back as the next input embedding. A staged training curriculum progressively
replaces textual reasoning steps with latent thoughts, teaching the model to reason in continuous
space before generating a textual answer.
37

text:
Hybrid Reasoning Agents
SoftCoT(Xu et al., 2025b): SoftCoT uses a lightweight frozen assistant model to generate question-
dependent soft thought representations, which a trainable projection maps into the target LLM’s
representation space. These representations guide subsequent generation, enabling latent reasoning
while keeping the assistant and target LLM frozen.
SoftThinking(Zhang et al., 2025): SoftThinking is a context-based method that represents interme-
diate reasoning as probability-weighted mixtures of vocabulary embeddings. Feeding these hidden
continuous representations back into the model preserves alternatives from the next-token distribution.
We implement all latent reasoning baselines using the same backbone models and, where applicable,
training settings and budgets as HybridAgent to ensure a fair comparison.
(iii) Frontier LLM Agents
To evaluate HybridAgent in a broader context, we compare it with current leading closed-source and
open-source LLM agents, including GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026), Kimi-K3 (Team, 2026), GLM-5.3-
Flash (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and QwQ-32B (Team,
2025), to assess both performance and inference efficiency of HybridAgent.
(iv) Agentic Frameworks
We further compare HybridAgent with established agentic frameworks that integrate multi-step
reasoning with external tool calling and environmental interactions. We apply Qwen3-14B as the
backbone for all these frameworks, with the same tool access and usage budgets as HybridAgent.
ReAct(Yao et al., 2023): ReAct interleaves natural-language reasoning with actions and observations
from an external environment. This interaction loop allows an agent to gather information, revise its
reasoning, and determine subsequent actions based on tool feedback.
Search-o1(Li et al., 2025a): Search-o1 augments large reasoning models with adaptive search to
address knowledge gaps encountered during reasoning. Its Reason-in-Documents module analyzes
retrieved documents and extracts relevant evidence before incorporating it into ongoing reasoning.
WebThinker(Li et al., 2025b): WebThinker equips LLMs with a Deep Web Explorer that supports
iterative search, webpage navigation, and information extraction. Its Think-Search-and-Draft strategy
interleaves reasoning, evidence collection, and report generation to support complex research tasks.
Overall, thesebaselinemethodsprovidecomplementarycomparisonsacrosstrainingstages, text-based
and latent-space reasoning, and tool-integrated agentic settings.
H.3. Implementation Details
Models and Training Details.We instantiate HybridAgent with Qwen3-Base backbones (Yang
et al., 2025a) at three scales of 4B, 8B, and 14B. For HybridLink, we use the same two-layer design
across all three backbones. The HybridSFT training data is constructed by converting 54K text-only
sources (Dong et al., 2025a,b) into hybrid trajectories. We apply format and HybridLink activation
for one epoch each, followed by one additional epoch of self-conditioned training. HybridRL training
utilizes 12K deep reasoning examples (Yu et al., 2025) for math and 1K agentic reasoning and search
examples (Dong et al., 2025b) for deep search. We train HybridAgent with the GRPO objective and
set rollout batches of 512 trajectories (64× 8), followed by one optimization pass over 8 minibatches.
Training Hyperparameters.Table 10, 11, and 12 provide detailed parameter setups on HybridSFT
and HybridRL. Following Dong et al. (2025b); Yu et al. (2025), we use HybridAgent checkpoints from
deep reasoning training for mathematical evaluations and the checkpoint from agentic search training
for knowledge-intensive search and agentic reasoning evaluations, as detailed in Appendix H.1.
