Infrastructure and Configurations.As existing training and inference frameworks such as verl
(Shengetal.,2025)andvLLM(Kwonetal.,2023)donotdirectlysupportmulti-turnhybridgeneration,
we extend their infrastructure to enable hybrid training and generation in HybridAgent. A shared
generation loop coordinates text mode, latent mode, and tool interaction while maintaining each
trajectory’s persistent KV cache as continuous working memory across turns. The agent enters latent
mode through the special entry anchor<latent>, feeds HybridLink-generated latent inputs back
into the backbone, and returns to text mode when the nearest-token readout matches the exit anchor
</latent>, as in Eq. 5. Tool observations are tokenized and processed against the existing working
memory, appending new KV entries without reconstructing or re-prefilling earlier context.
The engine also supports batched rollouts with per-sequence state tracking, allowing trajectories to
occupy different generation states within the same batch. Pending tool calls execute concurrently,
with waiting and completed sequences masked from further generation. Per-sequence attention masks
and position tracking preserve each trajectory’s causal context as generation proceeds. For HybridRL,
exact latent-context replay recomputes sampled text-token likelihoods in a single differentiable
forward pass while keeping recorded latent inputs unchanged. We check rollout–replay agreement of
log-probabilities at unchanged policy parameters. Multi-node data parallelism, sharded optimizer
states, mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, and resumable checkpoints support full-parameter
backbone optimization. Overall, the same engine supports RL rollouts, training-time validation, and
downstream evaluation, ensuring consistent mode transitions and working-memory handling across
configurable sampling settings, generation budgets, and tool-call setups.

I have one gallon of honey and one gallon of mayonnaise at 25◦C. If I remove one cup of honey at a time, how

TEXT I need the smallest number of one-cup removals that makes the remaining honey lighter than one gallon
of mayonnaise.

of honey and mayonnaise at 25◦C from the speciﬁed chemistry reference.

densities at 25◦C.

search
density of honey and mayonnaise in g/mL

Substance | Density at 25°C (g/cm3) | --- | | blood | 1.035 | | body fat | 0.918 [. . . ]

TEXT For the calculation, I use 1.42 g/mL for honey and 0.91 g/mL for mayonnaise. I’ll convert the volumes
to milliliters to calculate their masses.

mhoney = 1.42 × 3785.41 = 5375 .2822 g.

I now need the mass removed per cup to determine when the honey falls below this value.

After removing n cups, the required inequality is
5375.2822 − 335.95496n < 3444.7231,
n > 5375.2822 − 3444.7231
335.95496 ≈ 5.74648.
The smallest valid integer is n = 6. I’ll verify this with Python.
TEXT Each cup removes 335.95496 g. The condition 5375.2822 − 335.95496n < 3444.7231 requires

python
from math import floor
rho_h, rho_m = 1.42, 0.91

DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
Minghao Luo
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
luominghao@link.cuhk.edu.hk
Liang Chen*
EPFL
l.chen@epfl.ch
Abstract
Reasoning models achieve strong performance
through long chains of thought (CoT), but of-
ten spend more tokens than needed to solve a
problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT re-
quire additional training for each model, add
a fixed steering vector to the model’s hid-
den states, or use decoding heuristics such
as stopping early or banning words likewait,
which can reduce accuracy. We propose Doubt-
Less, a training-free decoding method in which
a much smaller reasoning model steers the
large one towards brevity. The small model
reads the large model’s CoT so far twice, once
prompted to be brief (thebrief thinker) and
once prompted to be verbose (theverbose
thinker), and the difference between its two
logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added
to the large model’s logits at every step of
the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition
mathematics, graduate-level science and com-
petitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the
CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged
accuracy, outperforming five inference-time
baselines. We also show that DoubtLess re-
duces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a
self-debugging coding agent with unchanged
task performance. It also generalizes to two
other model families with unchanged accuracy.
When combined with training-based compres-
sion, it further shortens the CoT of a model
already trained for brevity. Ablations and be-
havioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces
repeated checking, with most token savings
coming after the correct answer first appears
in the CoT. Our code is available at https:
//github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
1 Introduction
Reasoning models such as Qwen3 and DeepSeek-
R1 write a chain of thought (CoT) between the
tokens <think> and </think> before they answer.

and under DoubtLess. Of the tokens DoubtLess re-

On a hard problem the CoT holds most of the out-
put, and a large part of it re-derives and re-verifies
a result the model has already reached (Chen et al.,
2024; Sui et al., 2025). Under plain decoding, that
is, sampling from the model as released, a correct
run of Qwen3-32B writes 32–69% of its CoT after
the correct answer first appears (Figure 1). Not all
of this checking is redundant. A check made while
the model works, or a first check of its answer,
can catch an error, but repeating a check that has
already been made adds tokens without adding in-
formation. A method that shortens the CoT should
remove the redundant checks and keep the neces-
sary ones.
Existing methods for shortening the CoT fall
into two groups. Training-based methods add
a length penalty or a token limit to reinforce-
ment learning (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Hou
et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) or fine-tune on short
traces (Chen et al., 2024). Both change the weights,
so every new model needs another round of train-
ing. Inference-time methods ask for brevity in the
1

title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning

text:
prompt (Renze and Guven, 2024; Han et al., 2025;
Xu et al., 2025), block words such aswaitthat open
another round of checking (Wang et al., 2025), end
the CoT once an answer looks ready or a token
budget is spent (Yang et al., 2025b; Song et al.,
2026; Muennighoff et al., 2025), or add a fixed
steering vector to the model’s hidden states (Azizi
et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025).
Prompting depends on how closely the model fol-
lows the instruction. Keyword bans suppress the
same words across contexts, activation steering
adds the same vector to the hidden states at ev-
ery step, and early stopping ends the CoT once its
criterion is met. These controls can shorten useful
reasoning as well as redundant checks.
In this paper we propose DoubtLess, a training-
free decoding method that steers a reasoning model
with a much smaller reasoning model that shares
its tokenizer (Figure 2). At every step of the CoT,
the small model reads the text the large model has
written so far twice: once after an instruction to
go straight to the answer, as thebrief thinker, and
once after an instruction to double-check every step,
as theverbose thinker. The difference between
the two logit vectors, multiplied by a strength α,
is added to the large model’s logits. The small
model only suggests a direction, towards what the
brief thinker would write next and away from what
the verbose thinker would. The large model still
decides which tokens are possible, and the CoT
can end only where the large model itself would
consider ending it (Section 2). Inspired by DEx-
perts (Liu et al., 2021), DoubtLess steers the large
model through the vocabulary it shares with a small
model, but needs no trained expert, since both sides
of the contrast come from one off-the-shelf small
model under two instructions.
Two properties set DoubtLess apart from prompt-
ing, keyword bans, activation steering and early
stopping. First, the contrast is dynamic. It is re-
computed from the current context at every step,
so a word such asButis pushed down after an an-
swer and left almost untouched before it, whereas
a keyword ban blocks it everywhere and activation
steering applies one fixed vector at every step. Sec-
ond, the brief and verbose thinkers disagree most
after the correct answer first appears in the CoT,
where the brief thinker would wrap up and the ver-
bose one would check again (Section 5.1). Most of
the removed tokens come from this later checking.

With Qwen3-32B steered by Qwen3-0.6B, Doubt-
Less removes 31% of the thinking tokens with un-
changed accuracy, more than any baseline. It keeps
accuracy where the baselines lose it. On AIME
2025, for example, blocking the words that open
another round of checking costs 14 points, while
DoubtLess costs none. DoubtLess also extends to
an agent, a model trained for brevity and two other
model families. It reduces thinking per turn by
20% in a self-debugging coding agent and further
shortens the CoT of a model trained for brevity
with LACONIC (Liu et al., 2026). On AIME 2025
and AMC 2023, it removes 25% and 40% of the
thinking of EXAONE-4.0 and Granite-4.2, each
steered by a small model of its own family, where
a concise prompt removes 8% and 14%. Finally,
our ablations show that the strength sets how much
is removed, that a negative strength lengthens the
CoT instead, and that the shortening depends on
which tokens the small model pushes down.
Our main contributions are as follows:
• DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in
which an off-the-shelf small model, run under a
brief and a verbose instruction, supplies a logit
direction that shortens a reasoning model’s CoT.
• An evaluation in which DoubtLess removes
more thinking than five inference-time baselines
on seven benchmarks with unchanged accuracy,
and shortens the CoT of a self-debugging coding
agent and of two other model families.

When it acts.The two thinkers read the same text
and differ only in the instruction, so they disagree
only where the instruction matters (one CoT in
Figure 3; the analysis in Section 5.1). While the
model is still working towards an answer, both
expect the derivation to continue, and the CoT is
left almost unchanged: in the upper box of Figure 3
only two tokens are shaded, and theWaitthat opens
a check inside the derivation is not one of them.
Once an answer has been stated, the verbose thinker
expects another round of checking and the brief
thinker expects the CoT to end, so the words that
start a new check, such asBut,Letandmaybein
the lower box, are down-weighted by a factor of
five or more. Unlike NoWait, DoubtLess therefore
bans no word. It makes another round of checking
less likely to begin once an answer is in place, and
what the CoT loses is those rounds. Whether the
next sentence starts another check or continues the
derivation is largely a matter of form, which a small
model can judge even on a problem it could not
solve.
Where the contrast applies.The contrast acts
only on the CoT. The answer after </think> is
decoded by the large model alone. Within the CoT,
the large model keeps its own logits for </think>
and the end-of-sequence token and its own top-p
candidates, so the small model can only reorder
tokens the large model was already willing to write
(Algorithm 1, Appendices A and C).

Baselines.We compare DoubtLess with plain de-
coding and with five training-free methods of the
kinds in Section 1: a prompt, a ban on words, two
rules that end the CoT early and a steering vec-
tor.Concise promptasks the large model itself to
be brief: the brief thinker’s sentence, which tells
the model to go straight to the answer and not to
re-derive or re-verify anything, is appended to the
large model’s own instruction. How much it re-
moves depends on how closely the large model fol-
lows the instruction.NoWait(Wang et al., 2025)
blocks 17 words that open another round of check-
ing (wait,alternatively,hmm,but,howeverand
others) throughout the generation, by adding a bias
of−100 to the logits of their single-token forms
(89 token ids).DEER(Yang et al., 2025b) ends
the CoT early. At each of the first ten occurrences
ofWaitit induces a trial answer, ends the CoT if
the geometric mean of the trial’s token probabili-
ties exceeds 0.95, and otherwise discards the trial
and lets the CoT continue. It also ends the CoT
once it reaches 0.8 of the budget. A DEER run
is a prefix of the plain-decoding run followed by
</think> and a freshly sampled answer, so we
evaluate it on the stored plain-decoding runs with
the same engine, sampler and seeds (Appendix D).
ThinkBrake(Song et al., 2026) ends the CoT at a
sentence boundary once </think> comes within a
logit margin of 0.1 of the most likely token, read
after a single newline as in the authors’ code, and
is evaluated like DEER (Appendix D).ASC(Az-
izi et al., 2026) adds a fixed steering vector to the
large model’s hidden states after one layer, at ev-
ery decoding step. We use the training-free ver-
sion in the authors’ released code, in which the
vector is the mean difference between the hidden
states at the last token of a verbose and of a concise
CoT, here Qwen3-32B’s own CoTs on 100 MATH-
500 problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman
et al., 2024) under its plain instruction and un-
der the brief thinker’s sentence. It is added after
layer 57 of 64, the layer the authors use for the

4 Results
4.1 Main results
DoubtLess shortens the CoT more than any
baseline.Across the seven benchmarks, Doubt-
Less removes 31% of the thinking tokens with un-
changed accuracy (Table 1, overall column; inter-
vals in Table 7). This is the largest reduction among
the six methods (Figure 4a). The concise prompt
comes closest, but DoubtLess removes more than
it on six of the seven benchmarks. The other base-
lines remove less, and ThinkBrake and NoWait lose
more accuracy than DoubtLess.
The reduction holds on harder problems.
DoubtLess shortens the CoT significantly on ev-
ery benchmark (Table 7). The baselines are uneven.
On mathematics, the concise prompt removes less
on harder benchmarks, from 31% on AMC 2023 to
13% on HMMT 2025, the easiest and the hardest
for plain decoding, while DoubtLess still removes
31% on HMMT 2025. ThinkBrake cuts the CoT
on science and code but barely on mathematics.
DoubtLess keeps accuracy on every benchmark.
In contrast, NoWait, DEER and ThinkBrake
each lose accuracy significantly on at least one
benchmark (Table 7): NoWait on AIME 2025
and LiveCodeBench, DEER on LiveCodeBench,
and ThinkBrake on OlympiadBench and Live-
CodeBench. DoubtLess also lowers the share of
runs that reach the budget, from 2.4% under plain
decoding to 0.4%.
4.2 Other model families
DoubtLess carries over to EXAONE-4.0 and
Granite-4.2, each steered by a small model of its
own family, and shortens their CoT without los-
ing accuracy (Figure 4b, Table 8 in Appendix H).
The concise prompt, however, varies from model
to model. It comes close to DoubtLess on Qwen3-
32B, but on the other two DoubtLess removes about
three times as much. This depends on whether the
model complies. A prompt can only ask the large
model to be brief, and models differ in how far they
follow such a request, whereas DoubtLess asks the
large model for nothing and changes its next-token
distribution directly.
4.3 Coding agent
We extend DoubtLess to a self-debugging cod-
ing agent on HumanEval+ (Chen et al., 2021; Liu
et al., 2023), which writes a program, runs the
tests and gets one repair turn on failure. Doubt-
Less is applied inside the CoT of every turn (Ap-
pendix J). Over the 164 problems, the agent thinks
20% less per turn and improves its pass rate by
2.0 points over plain decoding (Table 1, Agent col-
umn). DEER removes 41% and improves the pass
rate by 4.5 points. It ends the CoT once 80% of the
turn’s thinking budget is spent, which leaves room
for a program in every turn, whereas under plain
decoding 16–20% of the turns use the whole budget
for thinking and write no program (Appendix J).
NoWait and ThinkBrake remove more but lower
the pass rate, ThinkBrake by 6.9 points.

5 Analysis and discussion
5.1 What DoubtLess removes
Most removed tokens follow the first appear-
ance of the answer.We split each run at the point
where the correct answer first appears in the CoT
(Appendix I). DoubtLess cuts the thinking after
this point by half and the thinking before it by a
fifth (Figure 5a), so most of the removed tokens
lie after it on each of the six benchmarks on which
the answer can be located (Table 11). In Figure 6,
both methods reach the answer after about a thou-

same check again and again. Useful checks remain.
On AIME 2025 problem 11, an algebraic check
restores a wrongly excluded root, which is then
included in the final answer (Appendix I).
The two thinkers disagree after the answer.
Read by the small model under both instructions,
correct plain-decoding runs on AIME 2025 show a
mean divergence between the two next-token dis-
tributions seven times larger after the answer than
before it (Figure 7a), and the same holds under
human-annotated answer boundaries (Appendix I).

5.2 DoubtLess complements training-based
compression
Training-based methods shorten the CoT by chang-
ing the weights, while DoubtLess acts only at de-
coding time, so the two can be combined. We
test this on a Qwen3-32B checkpoint fine-tuned
with LACONIC (Liu et al., 2026), which adds an
adaptive length penalty to the task reward during
reinforcement learning, and steer it with Qwen3-
0.6B at α=5. Across mathematics, science and
coding-agent benchmarks, DoubtLess further re-
duces thinking tokens by 29–52% with unchanged
task performance (Table 2). DoubtLess thus com-
plements training-based compression and applies
to an already compressed model without further
training.

5.3 Inference cost
We measure end-to-end inference latency on a sin-
gle B200 GPU, decoding one problem at a time
on 14 problems, two from each of the seven bench-
marks. DoubtLess takes 119.4 seconds per problem
on average, compared with 156.2 seconds for plain
decoding and 137.5 seconds for the concise prompt,
reducing latency by 24% and 13%, respectively.
The small model’s two forward passes of 0.6B pa-
rameters per step add about 4% to the FLOPs of
the 32B model.
6 Ablation study
We vary the direction and the strength of the con-
trast and the size of the small model.
6.1 Effect of the contrast direction
Therandom-targetcontrol tests whether the short-
ening comes from which tokens the small model
pushes down or from perturbing the logits at
all. At every step it keeps the adjustment values
α(zbrief−z verbose) but assigns them to randomly
chosen tokens of the top-p set, so the size and scope
of the change stay the same and only its direction is
lost. With random targets, the thinking length stays
within 8% of plain decoding on every benchmark
and changes by 1% overall, against 31% for Doubt-
Less (Table 7, Figure 10). The shortening therefore
comes from the direction the small model supplies.
6.2 Effect of the strength
On AIME 2025, DoubtLess removes more as the
strength grows, with unchanged accuracy up to
the default α=5, and at α=10 it loses 7.8 points
(Figure 8). A negative strength,α=−5, lengthens
the CoT by 26% instead, so the strength also sets
the direction of the change.
6.3 Effect of the small-model size
We show that a larger small model at the same α
acts as a stronger contrast. With Qwen3-1.7B or
Qwen3-4B in place of Qwen3-0.6B, DoubtLess
removes close to 60% of the thinking tokens on
AIME 2025 and, likeα=10 with the 0.6B model,
goes past the point where accuracy holds (Table 5).
With Qwen3-32B itself as the small model (at
α=1), DoubtLess removes 26%, against 29% for
the 0.6B model, so the smallest and cheapest model
of the family, our default, gives up nothing.
7 Related work
Overthinking.Reasoning models spend a large
share of their tokens re-deriving and re-verifying
results they have already reached, even on simple
problems (Chen et al., 2024; Sui et al., 2025), and
their token spend tracks the difficulty of a problem
only loosely (Pu et al., 2025). Section 5.1 shows
that the tokens DoubtLess removes come mainly
from the checking after the answer.
Shortening the CoT at inference time.Methods
that leave the model unchanged end the CoT once a
budget is spent or the answer appears settled (Muen-
nighoff et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Song et al.,
2026; Fu et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2025), skip it (Ma
et al., 2025), block the words that open another
round of checking (Wang et al., 2025), or ask for
brevity in the prompt (Renze and Guven, 2024; Han
et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), which works only as
far as the model follows the request (Han et al.,
2025; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025). Activation
steering adds a fixed vector to the hidden states,
taken from concise and verbose CoTs (Azizi et al.,
2026; Huang et al., 2025) or from execution and
reflection steps (Chen et al., 2025), with a strength
that can follow a signal read from the model (Lin
et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b). Budget Guidance (Li
et al., 2026a) reweights the next-token distribution
with a trained length predictor. DoubtLess also
reweights the next-token distribution, but its di-
rection comes from an off-the-shelf small model,
is recomputed from the context at every step and
leaves the large model’s own logit for </think>
untouched.
Training-based compression.Training-based
methods add a length term or a token limit to rein-
forcement learning (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025;
Hou et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026)
or fine-tune on short traces (Chen et al., 2024).

Each model needs its own training run, and the
trade-off between length and accuracy is fixed once
training ends. DoubtLess leaves the model un-
changed, sets the trade-off with one strength at
decoding time and can be added to a model trained
this way (Section 5.2).
Contrastive decoding.Contrastive decoding
scores the next token by the difference between
an expert and a weaker amateur model (Li et al.,
2023; O’Brien and Lewis, 2023), and DExperts
and proxy-tuning steer a large model with small
models that share only its vocabulary (Liu et al.,
2021, 2024). ThinkLogit (Zhang et al., 2026) and
ProxyThinker (Xiao et al., 2025) add the differ-
ence between a small reasoning model and its
base to make a large model reason more, Think-
ing by Subtraction (Tang et al., 2026) contrasts
a model with a masked copy of its own context,
and PromptCD (Bi et al., 2026) and Dong et al.
(2026) contrast two prompts on the steered model
itself. DoubtLess draws the contrast from an off-
the-shelf small model under two instructions and
uses it to shorten the CoT. Small models also work
beside large ones as drafters in speculative decod-
ing (Leviathan et al., 2023), as token suggesters
in Nudging (Fei et al., 2025) and as sentence com-
pleters in FoReaL decoding (Li et al., 2025).
8 Conclusion
DoubtLess adds the difference between a small
reasoning model’s brief and verbose thinkers to a
large reasoning model’s logits while it writes its
CoT. On seven benchmarks it removes 31% of the
thinking tokens of Qwen3-32B with unchanged
accuracy, more than five inference-time baselines.
It also shortens the CoT of a coding agent, and on
two other model families it removes about three
times as much as a concise prompt. Combined with
training-based compression, it further shortens the
CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Our
analyses support the explanation that DoubtLess
reduces redundant checking while retaining useful
verification.

11
title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning

text:
restores the large model’s own logits for </think>
and the end-of-sequence token, so the CoT ends
only where the large model itself would consider
ending it. At such a point the contrast changes the
competition. By lowering the tokens that open an-
other round of checking, it lets the large model’s
own </think> win more often. The mask is ap-
plied last, so the candidates are the top-p set of the
large model’s distribution at temperature one and
the contrast never brings in a token outside it. The
method has one hyperparameter, the strengthα.
Random-target control.The control differs
from Algorithm 1 in one step. After g is formed,
it draws a uniformly random permutation of the
positions in the top-p setS and assigns the entries
ofg at those positions to the permuted positions.
Entries outsideSare masked anyway. The permu-
tation is seeded by the run’s seed and the step index.
Everything else, includingα, the restoration of the
two logits and the mask, is identical to DoubtLess.
B Prompts
Every stream receives the problem followed by
one instruction line. On GPQA-Diamond the an-
swer is the letter of the chosen option, and on Live-
CodeBench the instruction asks for a program in
a code block. The brief and the verbose thinker
append one sentence each, and the large model’s
own stream carries neither. The concise-prompt
setting gives the large model the brief sentence.
Instruction (all streams)
Please reason step by step, and put your final answer
within\boxed{}.
Brief thinker (appended)
Be concise: go straight to the answer with the fewest
steps. Once you have a result, do NOT re-derive,
re-verify, or repeat any calculation, and do not
second-guess it.
Verbose thinker (appended)
Be extremely thorough: double-check every step,
re-verify each calculation in more than one way, and
exhaustively consider alternative cases before you
commit to a final answer.
NoWait: blocked words
wait, alternatively, hmm, but, however, alternative,
another, check, double-check, oh, maybe, verify, other,
again, now, ah, any. Each word is blocked in every
single-token surface form (capitalized, with a leading
space, after a full stop, in capitals), 89 token ids in total,
with a logit bias of−100 throughout the generation. The
seventeen words are those of Wang et al. (2025).

D Implementation details
The large model runs in vLLM 0.29 (Kwon et al.,
2023) with tensor parallelism. We load the small
model into the same vLLM model as the large one,
12
title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning

text:
so that a single request drives all three streams of
Figure 2. The small model keeps one copy of its
linear weights but two copies of its attention layers,
one for the brief thinker and one for the verbose
thinker. The two thinkers go through the linear
layers together, as a doubled batch, and through
attention separately. Under tensor parallelism the
small model is split across the GPUs by attention
head, like the large model. The three streams dif-
fer only in the instruction sentence, which sits be-
tween the problem and the last few tokens of the
chat template (Appendix B). Everything else, the
prompt, those template tokens and the generated
tokens, uses the same slot mapping in the three
streams’ paged KV caches, and we keep it in one
paged key–value cache. The request’s block table
is allocated for the large model’s sequence, and
the small model’s attention layers, which have the
same cache layout (eight key–value heads of di-
mension 128 in bfloat16, split across the GPUs),
write their keys and values into the same blocks.
vLLM then allocates, accounts for and frees the
three streams as one, with no padding and no dupli-
cated copies. The keys and values of the instruction
sentence itself, at most 64 tokens per thinker, live in
a small buffer per request that is allocated together
with the model. The position IDs are those of each
stream’s own sequence, so the thinkers see the tem-
plate tokens and the generated tokens shifted by
the length of their sentence. A key stores its own
position, so the order of the blocks does not have to
match the order of the positions. A thinker’s atten-
tion is computed in two parts, paged attention over
the request’s blocks and dense attention over the
instruction buffer, which are merged by their log-
sum-exp (vLLM’s cascade-attention kernel does
exactly this). The result is the attention over the full
sequence. In the first step all three streams prefill
the problem. The small model then reads its two in-
struction sentences against the cached problem and
fills the buffer, after which decoding proceeds with
every sampled token fed to all three streams. The
forward pass returns the three hidden states. At the
logits step we apply the three output heads, form
zbase +α(z brief−z verbose) for the requests that are
still inside their CoT, restore the</think> and end-
of-sequence logits, mask to the large model’s top-p
set (the random-target control permutes the differ-
ence within that set here) and pass z to vLLM’s
sampler, which draws with the request’s tempera-
ture, top-p, top-k and seed. Whether a request has
left its CoT is tracked on the GPU from the tokens
fed to the model, so asynchronous scheduling and
CUDA graphs work as usual. After </think> the
contrast is no longer applied. The small model runs
on a second CUDA stream and overlaps the large
model’s forward pass, and one CUDA graph per de-
coding step covers both models. With one problem
in flight, a decoding step is bound by reading the
large model’s weights (65.5 GB in bfloat16), and
the small model’s kernels run on the second stream
while those weights stream, with vLLM’s fused
kernels for its normalization and rotary embedding
and a single call of its output head for both thinkers.
We time each tokenized request from submission
to the engine until the complete response text is
returned, including prefill and decoding. Before a
run we check that the two vocabularies have the
same size (151,936 for Qwen3) and that the instruc-
tion, <think> and </think> encode to the same
ids with both tokenizers.
NoWait.The blocked words are the seventeen
of Wang et al. (2025), listed in Appendix B. The
paper expands each word to every vocabulary to-
ken that contains it as a substring and then removes
unreasonable matches by hand (its example isOhio
foroh). On the Qwen3 vocabulary the substring
rule matches 918 tokens, most of them unrelated
words such asknow,many,companyandbutton,
and the filtered list is not published. We block the
89 single-token forms of the words: the word it-
self, with a leading space, capitalized, in upper case
and after a period, which are the forms the paper
gives as its example forwait. The bias is−100, the
most negative value vLLM accepts, applied to the
whole generation, with a 32,768-token budget as
in the paper (24,576 on GPQA-Diamond) and the
sampling settings of Appendix E. For Qwen3-32B
over five seeds, the paper reports chains 13–16%
shorter on AMC 2023, AIME 2024 and AIME
2025 with accuracy changes of −0.8, +2.0 and
−2.7 points, and on GPQA-Diamond chains 15%
shorter at−6.1 points. Our plain-decoding chains
have the same lengths as the paper’s on the three
mathematics benchmarks (within 5%). NoWait
removes more in our runs (21–24%), and its accu-
racy cost falls on AIME 2025 and HMMT, while
GPQA-Diamond loses 0.3 points (Table 7). An
independent run of NoWait on Qwen3-32B in the
ThinkBrake paper (Song et al., 2026) loses 9 points
on AIME 2024 and 12 on AIME 2025 at 11–12%
fewer tokens. Our runs show the same direction,
with the largest loss on AIME 2025.
13

text:
DEER.DEER only decides when the CoT ends.
A DEER run is therefore the plain-decoding run
of the same problem and seed, cut at the first
point where the rule fires, followed by </think>
and an answer sampled with the budget that re-
mains. A run in which the rule never fires is
the plain run itself. We evaluate it on the stored
plain-decoding runs of Table 1, in the same en-
gine and with the same sampler and seeds. For
DEER we follow the authors’ released vLLM im-
plementation with its default settings. The tran-
sition point is the stringWait. At each of the
first ten, the text before it is extended with the in-
ducer \n**Final Answer**\n\boxed (on GPQA-
Diamond, the released variant . . . I believe
the final answer, rather than the option,
is \boxed ) and a trial answer of at most 20 to-
kens is decoded greedily and stopped at </think>.
Its confidence is the geometric mean of the token
probabilities from the second trial token on, and
is zero unless the trial reached </think>. The
block is closed with \n</think>\n\n when the
confidence exceeds 0.95, and in any case once
the thinking reaches 0.8× the budget (the released
think_ratio), at the segment boundary that pre-
cedes it by at most 50 tokens. After the tenth trial
no further trial is made, and the chain runs to its
own end or to the0.8× cap. The released code cov-
ers mathematics and GPQA. On LiveCodeBench
the inducer opens a python code block and the trial
may run to 1,024 tokens, with the same </think>
requirement. The DEER paper also reports Qwen3-
32B under the same sampler (temperature 0.6, top-
p0.95 , budget 32,768; its Table 8): thinking tokens
fall by 10% on AIME 2024, 9% on AIME 2025,
22% on AMC 2023 and 11% on OlympiadBench,
with accuracy within one point of plain decoding.
Our runs give 8%, 10%, 20% and 12%, with accu-
racy within 2.2 points (Table 7).
ThinkBrake.ThinkBrake (Song et al., 2026)
ends the CoT at a sentence boundary when the
margin between the most likely next token other
than </think> and </think>, on the temperature-
scaled logits, is at most τ. Its paper uses τ=0.1
for every Qwen3 model. The paper does not say
in which state the margin is read. Its only released
code (for its tool-use benchmark) appends a pe-
riod and a single newline to each prefix and reads
</think> there, which is the state in which Qwen3
closes its CoT on its own. In our runs every natural
close follows a single-newline token, whereas a
sentence inside the CoT mostly ends in a blank-
line token, after which </think> is never near the
top. Read in the state the model actually wrote,
the rule therefore does not fire. We therefore fol-
low the released code. At every sentence boundary,
a token that ends a sentence and is followed by
whitespace, or a token that ends with a newline,
the sentence’s last token is replaced by its single-
newline form (.\n\n becomes .\n) and the margin
is read there. Where the rule fires, the run keeps
its CoT up to that sentence, followed by the single
newline, </think> and a freshly sampled answer.
Like DEER, ThinkBrake is evaluated on the stored
plain-decoding runs. It removes 21% of the think-
ing tokens over the seven benchmarks at a cost of
2.3 points: 37% on GPQA-Diamond and 44% on
LiveCodeBench, where it costs 2.0 and 4.7 points,
and 3–4% on the five others (Table 7). The pa-
per reports 4–6% fewer thinking tokens on AIME
2024 and 2025 and 20% on GPQA-Diamond for
Qwen3-32B with a 16k budget.
ASC.The published version of ASC learns the
steering vector by gradient descent, which requires
an additional training run. We follow the training-
free version in the authors’ released code, which
adds the mean of the last-token differences between
verbose and concise CoTs, scaled by a strength, to
the output of one decoder layer at every forward
pass, so at every generated token and at the last
prompt token. The calibration set is the first 100
problems of MATH-500 in an order that cycles
through its subjects. For each, Qwen3-32B writes
one CoT under its plain instruction and one under
the brief thinker’s sentence, with the sampling set-
tings of Appendix E and a 16,384-token budget,
and both are read back after the plain instruction.
The authors write the concise CoTs with GPT-4o,
and we use the large model’s own. The vector is
added after layer 57. Its strength ρ is the norm of
the added vector relative to the mean norm of the
hidden state at that layer, andρ=0.2 is chosen on
AIME 2026 (Table 6).

are used for evaluation only, as in the work we
compare with. GPQA-Diamond is released under

Scoring.The visible answer after </think> is
scored, never the CoT. Integer answers (AIME,

where the problem asks for the sum of its digits.

an answer that spells out an option’s text or value,
also in LATEX, is mapped back to its letter first. Live-

cases. A run that reaches its budget without ending
its CoT scores zero.

seeds the sampler of each run with it. Intervals
are percentile bootstraps with 4,000 resamples over
problems.
Compute.All runs use vLLM 0.29, with the
small model’s two passes beside the large model

ABSTRACT
Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work
autonomously—from hours to days—on economically valuable tasks, a capa-
bility essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet
open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both
training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks
are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both.
First, we introduce TEV-GYM, thefirstlong-horizon agent training dataset with
verifiable, dense, progressive rewards—1,170 verified task environments across 7
domains. It is built on alatent-world-firstapproach that first constructs alatent
world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow,
and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from
this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complex-
ity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe:

1 INTRODUCTION
Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has shifted attention toward long-horizon
agents (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; Moonshot AI, 2026), which can work autonomously
for hours to days on complex, economically valuable tasks (Sun et al., 2026; Styles et al., 2024;
Zhu et al., 2026a). Long-horizon tasks, such as solving open problems in mathematics and science,
conducting automated machine learning research, and advancing coding and security systems, are
fundamental to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI).
Despite these promising breakthroughs, coding-agent progress in the open-source community has
focused on shorter- and mid-horizon tasks, scaled via large agentic training corpora such as SWE-
Smith (Yang et al., 2025a), TMAX (Ivison et al., 2026), Endless Terminals (Gandhi et al., 2026),
CLI-Gym (Lin et al., 2026), SETA (Shen et al., 2026), and Terminal-Universe (Wu et al., 2026).
These datasets contain thousands to tens of thousands of environments, but each involves only a
pull-request-sized fix or a short terminal session, and their unit-test-based evaluation provides only a
terminal pass/fail signal or the fraction of tests passed. By contrast, genuinely long-horizon tasks
are available only in human-authored benchmarks (Merrill et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). These
benchmarks contain only tens to a few hundred instances, each requiring weeks of expert effort. They
provide partial credit only through hand-written checkpoints and exist only as evaluation sets. Thus,
no training corpus of long-horizon tasks exists: agentic training corpora are large but short-horizon,
while long-horizon tasks exist only as small, human-authored evaluation sets.
Curating long-horizon tasks requires balancing two competing goals: tasks must be sufficiently long
and structurally complex to provide meaningful training while remaining exactly verifiable (Zeng
et al., 2026a). Scaling long-horizon environments for training is even more difficult because rewards
are sparse and available only upon task completion, depriving long-tail tasks of useful training signals.
To address both limitations, we introduce alatent-world-firstsynthesis approach that begins by
constructing alatent world, a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain. We
first represent the underlying workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) within a latent world
and then progressively render the input files from that world. This procedure allows us to control
task complexity while retaining every correct intermediate state, which provides a natural metric for
measuring progress and therefore a verifiable dense reward for our training. Unlike pipelines that ask
a language model to generate the task, inputs, and checker without a true answer, our latent world
serves as an exact answer key for reliable verification.
Long-horizon tasks come with sparse rewards, arriving only at task completion and submission,
which notoriously starves training on long-tail samples (Yu et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026; Zeng
et al., 2026a). Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024) normalizes rewards
within a group ofG rollouts of the same task, so under terminal-only reward, a group in which all
G rollouts fail has zero advantage everywhere and contributes nothing to the gradient. Mid-horizon
pipelines can afford to discard such groups (Ivison et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025) because they are
rare there; on long-horizon tasks they are most common at the start of training, when the policy is
weakest and signal is needed most. We therefore introduce progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS)
into reinforcement learning (RL), which makes training efficient and makes otherwise-intractable

Figure 1 summarizes our approach and TEV’s results, and Figure 2 ranks all models on the Terminal-
Bench (TB) 4.0 “CM” subset by Pass@1. Using our latent-world-first synthesis approach, we
introduce TEV-GYM, composed of 1,170 verified long-horizon task environments across 7 domains
(software engineering, data engineering, AI/CS research, mathematics and operations research,
security and forensics, infrastructure administration, and quantum computing). As illustrated in
Table 1, TEV-GYM’s tasks take a frontier agent a median of 12.4 minutes per rollout, about 6 times
longer than the most time-intensive prior corpus (Yang et al., 2025a), and have the lowest pass rate,
demonstrating our training data’s complexity and quality. Moreover, TEV-GYMcan be scaled beyond
a fixed collection by coding agents writing generators that produce new verified environments across
seeds and scale tiers without further model calls.
We introduce TEV-9B and TEV-27B, trained with PPRS on the unit tier and the full corpus of
TEV-GYM, respectively. On ALE-CM, the computing-and-math split of Agents’ Last Exam (Sun
et al., 2026), TEV-9B improves Pass@5 by 83% over Qwen3.5-9B, while TEV-27B improves it by
65% over Qwen3.8-27B to 0.28, matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5. Despite training only on
ALE-related data, TEV-27B generalizes to the TB 3.0 and 4.0 subsets (Merrill et al., 2026; Marten
et al., 2026; Marten, 2026), improving Pass@1 by 56% and 150%, respectively, and outperforming
GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash. On the mid-horizon TB 2.1, TEV-9B improves zero-shot Pass@1
by 28%, while TEV-27B reaches 0.794 Pass@1, matching Claude Opus 4.8-level performance. The
recipe also transfers to a larger base: applying it to GLM-5.3-Flash yields TEV-320B, which raises
Pass@1 on the TB 3.0 and 4.0 subsets by 35% and 28% and, on TB 4.0, trails only Claude Opus 5,
Claude Fable 5, and GPT-5.6 (sol).
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
• We proposelatent-world-first synthesis, a pipeline that constructs long-horizon agentic tasks
backward from a known-correct world, giving exact verification, a controllable difficulty ladder,
and a progressive reward in the middle.
• We introduceTEV-GYM, thefirstlong-horizon agent training dataset with progressive rewards,
composed of 1,170 verified long-horizon task environments across 7 domains.
• We presentTEV-27B, trained on TEV-GYMusing PPRS, and demonstrate its superior performance
on ALE-CM, the TB 3.0 and TB 4.0 subsets, and TB 2.1; the same recipe applied to GLM-5.3-Flash
givesTEV-320B, which improves further.

major domains. Within each domain, we randomly sample specifications and author our own
generator around each one. For details, please refer to Appendix A.1.

Stage 1: world construction.Each generator is a seeded program. Given a seed and a scale tier, it
procedurally generates the latent worldW , the complete, correct state of the domain (e.g., a retail
warehouse’s customers, products, and transactions, or a distributed checkpoint’s tensor shards and
topology), and we validate W against the environment’s invariants (unique identities, valid joins,
finite measures). The same step draws a seed-deriveddefect plan: exactly which records, shards, or
fields ofWwill later be corrupted, and by which declared operator.
Stage 2: workflow graph.We compile the environment’s workflow into a directed acyclic graph
(DAG) of stages with explicit dependencies, permitted parallelism, and per-stage semantic-work
estimates (e.g., profile-sources→reconcile-facts / normalize-dimensions→
load-facts→aggregate-validate→package-sidecars ). The DAG is built by
code from the scale ofW , with no model in the loop. Its critical path, the longest chain of dependent
stages, defines the task’s horizon, and its stages form the skeleton of the progress potential in §3.
Stage 3: artifact rendering.Weproject W onto the environment’s declared public interface,
materializing the clean input files in their target wire formats: CSV and TSV partitions, JSON records,
SQLite databases, safetensors shards, stripped binaries, or infrastructure manifests. Rendering
is a pure function ofW , and before proceeding we assert that it round-trips, i.e., thatW is recovered
exactly from the rendered files. Together with the invertible corruption of Stage 4, this makes the
agent’s workspaces0 fully determineW , so the correct answer is computable from what the agent
actually sees, and the ground truth is correct by construction.
Stage 4: controlled corruption.We apply the Stage-1 defect plan to the rendered files, injecting
schema drift, duplicate and missing records, categorical drift, scrambled shard indices, stale caches,
and the like (Figure 3 shows the three operators of one environment). The corrupted trees0 isthe task
the agent receives, and the untouched worldW isthe ground truth. Because rendering round-trips and
corruption is declared and invertible,s0 fully determinesW : the correct solution is computable from
what the agent sees and is known exactly without running a solver. More generally, every component

Generalization of latent-world-first synthesis.We focus on the ALE-CM domains due to resource
constraints, but the approach applies to other ALE domains. Appendix A.10 walks through three
environments built by the pipeline: a multimodal AWS cost-optimization task with its billing-

2.2 COVERAGE, CALIBRATION,ANDQUALIFICATION
Diversity.Every environment is labeled on 19 coverage axes (Appendix A.3), including subdomain,
scale, the four horizon axes, workflow stage, tool capability, artifact role, relation type, and corruption
class. The axes that matter for training are behavioral: changing their value changes what the agent
must repair (corruption class), how (workflow stage, tool capability), and through which files (artifact
role, relation type). For more details, please see our Appendix A.3.
Controllable difficulty.Two controls change a task’s difficulty. The scale tier (by defaultunit,small,
orfull) grows W (Appendix A.4) and lengthens the operational horizon: how much must be read,
joined, and written. The workflow DAG of Stage 2, together with the number of corruption classes
in the defect plan, fixes the dependency depth: how many stages must be completed, and in which
order, before any output can be right. Appendix A.5 states how we measure horizon and difficulty
and reports base-model and frontier solve rates.
Qualification gates and cleanliness.A synthesized environment is admitted only if it passes all
eight benchmark-independent gates, checked automatically at generation time and each matched to
a named failure class (Table 7). Three of them back the progress potential of §3.2: all 14 gaming
probes must score 0 (exploit resistance), the potential must lie strictly between 0 and 1 on partially
correct states and increase monotonically to 1 along the reference trajectory (progress validity),
and the progress scorer, strict verifier, and reference solvers must have disjoint code closures (role
independence). Appendix A.6 states every gate formally, together with the verifier-independent solver
audit, and Appendix A.9 describes the structural decontamination check.

4 EXPERIMENTS
Our main experiments ask three questions. Does RL on TEV-GYMimprove open models on the
long-horizon tasks it was built for, do the gains generalize to tasks of even longer horizon, and does
the model keep its general coding competence on a standard mid-horizon benchmark (§4.2)? Finally,
§4.3 ablates our latent-world-first data and the dense reward approaches, separately.
4.1 SETUP
Training.We train Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B using DPPO (Qi et al., 2026) with the reward
in our Eq. (4), scaling the training data together with the model: the 9B model trains on a 264-task
subset of TEV-GYMfrom theunitdifficulty tier, which is better suited for learning at this model
scale, while the 27B model trains on the full corpus. We chooseG=24 rollouts for each of 8 tasks
per step, a response budget of 65,536 tokens per rollout (16,384 per turn), and at most 64 tool calls,
in a sandbox that exposes a single bash tool. Our 27B model is trained on 4 nodes of B200 GPUs or
8 nodes of A100 GPUs for about 4 days. For more details, refer to Appendix C. To test whether the
recipe transfers to a larger base model, we also train GLM-5.3-Flash with the same recipe, obtaining
TEV-320B, which we evaluate on the TB 3.0 and 4.0 subsets.
Evaluation.Long-horizon agent evaluation tasks are scarce and costly, with each requiring up to
eight hours to evaluate. Our in-domain suite, ALE-CM, is the computing-and-math split of Agents’
Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026), listed in Appendix C.2 (Table 12). On TB 3.0 and 4.0 (Merrill et al.,
2026; Marten et al., 2026; Marten, 2026) we evaluate the “CM” subsets (22 and 18 tasks). To form
them we asked Claude to judge, for every TB 3.0 task, whether it belongs to the computing-and-math
domain, even if only slightly; the selection and the full task lists are given in Appendix C.2 (Table 13).
We compare leaderboard model performance on the full ALE, TB 3.0, and TB 4.0 benchmarks with
performance on our corresponding subsets. The results show that our splits are representative of
full-set performance, with Pearson correlations ofr= 0.96 for TB 3.0 P@1 andr= 0.97 for TB 4.0
P@1 (Appendix C.2; Tables 14, 15, and 16).
Train/eval decontamination.We measure lexical leakage per evaluation set: no environment of
TEV-GYMshares a 13-gram or an 8-gram with any task of ALE-CM, TB 3.0, TB 4.0 or TB 2.1,
and the median nearest-neighbor prompt Jaccard of the evaluation tasks to the dataset is 0.13 on
TB 3.0/4.0 and 0.22 on ALE-CM, against 0.24–0.25 and 0.28 for tasks of the same benchmark
compared with one another. For more details, refer to Appendix A.9, Table 10.

Qualitative results.Figure 5 traces the key decision points of four rollouts on the
k8s_payment_api_root_cause_analysis task: every agent finds the same root causes,
but TEV-27B and Claude Fable 5 ground the liveness-probe cause in the measurement that explains it
and judge rollback safe, whereas the base model and GPT-6 Astra cite only the symptoms and decline
rollback, forfeiting the decisive grader component. For more qualitative examples, see Appendix C.3.
4.3 ABLATIONSTUDY
Due to resource constraints, we conduct the ablation study in the 9B setting of §4.1.
Ablation on data curation methods.Our pipeline differs from standard LLM-synthesized corpora
in two key ways: tasks are derived from a preexisting latent world and its code-compiled workflow
DAG, and verifiers evaluate against this hidden ground truth rather than only agent-visible files.
Table 5 shows which components each ablation retains, with GPT-5.6 (sol, xhigh) replacing the
others.Public-view verifierablates only access to hidden ground truth by asking the model to write
a verifier from the agent’s view.Prompt-first, a standard self-instruct baseline, instead replaces the
entire construction pipeline by generating each prompt before its inputs, verifier, and solution, leaving
no latent world or DAG. The public-view variant causes 88% of sampled groups to be discarded
during training. Because both variants use terminal rewards, we compare them with theSparserow:
neither improves over the base model in S@1 (0.24 and 0.23 vs. 0.25), whereas our full method leads
them by0.05–0.06in S@1 and0.05in P@5.
Ablation on dense reward.Holding TEV-GYMfixed, we compare our PPRS, which uses return-
to-goGt withγ= 1 and normalizes advantages by turn index, against terminal-only sparse reward,
PPRS with per-rollout normalization (pooled norm.), and direct additive reward using Φ(st) with
γ= 0 (Yuan et al., 2026). Our method provides the best balance of performance and training
efficiency, improving S@1 by0.04 over sparse reward. Turn-index normalization preserves credit
for later turns by avoiding comparison of their smaller returns against the whole-rollout mean, while
γ= 1 propagates progress back to earlier actions. In contrast, direct additive reward repeatedly
rewards high-potential states without propagating credit, leading to more rollouts exhausting the
context window before submission and producing longer trajectories. The advantage over sparse
reward widens further at 27B, where shaped reward trains to completion but terminal-only reward
produces almost entirely zero-advantage groups and fails to complete a single optimizer step.
5 RELATEDWORK
Synthetic corpora for coding and terminal agents.Recent corpora typically mine repositories
for issues and tests or use language models to generate tasks such as bug-injected repositories and
reconstructed terminal sessions (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025a; Ivison et al., 2026; Lin et al.,
2026). Other work scales executable tool-use environments and their success conditions (Cai et al.,
2025; Fang et al., 2025), although scaling helps only when difficulty is controlled (Zhu et al., 2026b).
In contrast, our environments contain long, multi-stage workflows across mathematics and science,
machine learning, coding, and systems; are instantiated by seeded generator code rather than directly
authored by a language model; and provide a dense progress signal for every task.

Backward construction.Deriving a task from a known solution is an established family: denoising,
controlled error injection, code mutation, environment rewinding, instruction back-translation, and
procedural puzzle generation all corrupt or invert a single artifact whose ground truth is already
known (Lewis et al., 2020; Arocena et al., 2015; Tran et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2025a; Hariharan et al.,
2025; Lin et al., 2026; Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024; Stojanovski et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a;
Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). We instead corrupt a rendering of an entire latent world, so the task,
verifier, and progress signal are all functions of that one world rather than separately generated factors
that can drift apart (Zeng et al., 2026a; Ivanov & Rana, 2026).
Sparse reward and dense signal in agentic RL.Existing methods avoid uninformative rollout
groups by filtering identical rewards, selecting tasks near the policy’s current ability, or adding expert
prefixes (Yu et al., 2025; Florensa et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2025c). Other approaches provide denser
feedback through learned judges (Cui et al., 2025; Choudhury, 2025) or proxy signals such as test-pass
rates (Du et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026), but these require additional models or
capture only terminal outcomes. Our potential Φ instead measures exact progress and regression
against the latent world at every workflow stage, without requiring a critic or language-model judge.
For full related work, please refer to Appendix D.
6 CONCLUSION
We introduce a latent-world-first approach for scaling verifiable long-horizon agent training. Each
task is built backward from a known-correct latent world, which is rendered into interrelated files,
modified through controlled corruptions, and reused for exact verification and dense progress rewards.
We instantiate this approach in TEV-GYM, a collection of 1,170 verified environments across seven
domains, and show that training improves both 9B and 27B open models on ALE-CM, with gains
transferring to Terminal-Bench tasks of different horizons and to a 320B base model. One limitation
of our current study is its focus on synthetic terminal environments, and the hardest benchmarks
still show a gap between our models and leading frontier agents. Supporting new workflows also
requires authoring and validating additional environment components. Future work could simplify
this process, expand domain coverage, and combine the resulting data with stronger open models,
making more professional workflows available for reproducible RL without human step labels or
language-model judges.

AIUSE STATEMENT
We used generative AI tools for the following tasks that require disclosure.Generating synthetic
data and implementing methods:coding agents helped author the generators of TEV-GYM, that
is, the environment specifications and their reference solvers, strict verifiers, and progress scorers
(§2; Appendix A.2). Once authored, a generator is a deterministic seeded program, so no language
model participates when an environment is generated, verified, or rewarded; every generator passed
the qualification gates of Appendix A.6, and the authors reviewed each specification.Qualitative
data analysis:Claude helped judge which TB 3.0 and 4.0 tasks relate to the computing-and-math
domain of our training data, which defines our “CM” evaluation subsets; Appendix C.2 gives the
procedure and the resulting task lists, and Appendix C.2 checks that the subsets track full-benchmark
performance. Coding assistants also helped write evaluation and analysis scripts. Separately, language
models appear in our experiments as objects of study rather than as aids to the authors: GPT-5.6 (sol)
builds the two data-ablation baselines (§4.3), Gemini 3.6 Flash is the fixed evaluator of the corpus
difficulty comparison (Appendix A.8), and frontier models are evaluated as baselines. No generative
model grades any task or produces any training reward. Among tasks with recommended disclosure,
we used generative AI tools to search and summarize related literature and to draft and edit parts of
the text. Translation, surveys, interviews, and transcription are not applicable to this work. We have
reviewed all AI-assisted work, and all claims, numbers, and citations were checked by the authors.
We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced
with the aid of generative AI.
ETHICS STATEMENT
TEV-GYMis fully synthetic: every environment is generated procedurally from a seed, contains
no data collected from people, and involves no human subjects, so the corpus encodes no private
records or proprietary code. Task specifications are drawn from public benchmarks and reference
material (Appendix A.1), but every artifact an agent sees is generated by the environment itself,
and third-party benchmarks and corpora used for evaluation and comparison are used under their
published licenses (Appendix A.8). The environments simulate professional workflows such as
data reconciliation, checkpoint consolidation, systems administration, and the analysis of synthetic
binaries and packet captures in the style of capture-the-flag exercises. Each declares its toolchain in
its public contract, the agent’s workspace is seeded only with its public tree, and no task targets real
software, systems, or people. Improving open-weight agents on long-horizon terminal tasks carries
the general dual-use considerations of more capable coding agents; our security-flavored tasks are
analysis and forensics exercises over synthetic artifacts, the same class of task already present in
public terminal-agent benchmarks. Because part of the training mix is built against the interfaces
of ALE-CM, we measure train/evaluation overlap for every evaluation set and report it with its
calibration (§4.1; Appendix A.9). Frontier baselines run in their native agent harnesses, the setting
most favorable to them (Appendix C.2), and we discuss the limitations of our results in §6.
REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
We have written the paper and appendix so that every result can be reproduced from them.Data.
Every environment of TEV-GYMis a deterministic, model-free function of its generator, seed, and
scale tier (§2.1; Appendix A.2), so the corpus can be regenerated exactly, at a median of 30 s of CPU
time per environment and with no model calls. The generation stages are specified in §2.1; task
sources and the domain taxonomy in Appendix A.1 (Table 6); the coverage policy in Appendix A.3;
the scale ladder and the measurement of horizon and difficulty in Appendices A.4 and A.5; the
qualification gates in Appendix A.6 (Table 7); and per-domain statistics in Appendix A.7 (Table 8).
Appendix A.10 walks through three complete training environments, each with its public view and the
ground truth sealed behind it, so the construction can be followed end to end (the listings are excerpts
of the package files).Reward and training.The progress potential and the shaped reward are fully
specified by Eqs. (3) and (4). All three base models are publicly available and DPPO is a published
objective; §4.1 states the corpus each model is trained on, and Table 11 lists the hyperparameters
shared by every run. Each ablation changes a single component of this recipe.Evaluation.All
evaluation benchmarks are public. Appendix C.2 gives the harnesses, turn and token budgets, number
of rollouts, and metric definitions; Appendix C.2 lists every task in ALE-CM and in the TB 3.0/4.0
“CM” subsets (Tables 12 and 13); and Appendix C.2 shows that the subsets track full-benchmark
performance. The difficulty comparison of Table 1 follows Appendix A.8, which fixes the evaluator,

A DATACONSTRUCTIONDETAILS
This appendix expands the condensed description in §2.
A.1 TASKSOURCES ANDDOMAINTAXONOMY
TEV-GYM’s generators target the seven computing-and-math subdomains of Agents’ Last Exam (Sun
et al., 2026), which constitute ALE-CM and which we refer to throughout as TEV-GYM’s seven do-
mains: software engineering (9.1), data and analytics engineering (9.2), AI engineering, safety and CS
research (9.3), mathematical and operations research (9.4), cybersecurity and digital forensics (9.5),
infrastructure engineering and cloud operations (9.6), and quantum computing (9.7). Table 6 gives the
scope of each and the deterministic signals it is verified by; subdomain ids and names are taken from
the ALE taxonomy and the scope summaries follow it, reconstructed from O*NET/SOC 2018 and the
released ALE task specifications. The coverage policy of Appendix A.3 requires every domain to be
populated by at least two generators.
Sourcing.For every domain we assemble a pool of real task specifications: specifications mined from
the internet, MLE-bench (82 Kaggle competitions), or, for domain 9.7 (quantum computing), which
no benchmark suite covers, public reference material (MQT Bench’s circuit suite, Qiskit Experiments
manuals, TeNPy’s DMRG examples). From this pool we randomly sample specifications and author
our own generator around each selection: every generator is a fresh procedural design of our own,
drawing on the sampled specification for structure and difficulty only, and never reproducing its
prompt, input, answer, or grader text. A feasibility filter first restricts candidates to specifications
whose ground truth is knowable by construction and executable batch/CPU-only, excluding live-
service, vision/audio, heavy-toolchain, GPU-kernel, and open-ended “improve this” tasks; a similarity
gate then compares every new generator’s code, specification, and generated data with all already-
registered generators and rejects near-duplicates; and an adversarial review pass attacks each accepted
generator’s specification for hidden shortcuts, too short a horizon, or a disguised source before
implementation.
A.2 DETERMINISM, REPRODUCIBILITY,ANDGENERATIONCOST
Every stage of §2.1 is a pure, seeded function, and no language model participates in generation.
Each generator’s code is authored once by coding agents and reviewed by the authors (see AI use
statement); running it is model-free. An environment is therefore fully reproducible from its generator,
seed, and scale tier, and two seeds of the same generator yield provably distinct worlds (the six-seed
diversity gate of Appendix A.6). The cost of an environment therefore splits in two. A one-time
authoring cost per generator is amortized over every seed and scale tier at which it is instantiated. The
marginal cost is seconds of compute: producing one environment, including running both reference
solvers, sealing the hidden suite, and previewing the progress potential ΦW , takes a median of 30 s of
CPU time (90th percentile 82 s) and no model calls, against hours of expert time per hand-authored
task. Each environment declares its toolchain (e.g., python3, sqlite3) in its public contract, and
the agent’s workspace is seeded only with its public tree.
A.3 COVERAGEAXES ANDCOVERINGARRAY
Every environment is labeled on 19 axes, the required axes of the corpus coverage policy: curriculum
layer, subdomain, generator revision, scale tier, the four horizon axes (semantic, action, operational,
verification), workflow stage, tool capability, artifact role, relation type, corruption class, source kind,
license class, reward component, observed reward band, outcome category, and failure category. The
corpus must satisfy a strength-2 covering array over these axes: for any two axes, every valid pair
of their values co-occurs in at least one admitted environment. Coverage is extended greedily by
choosing the generator, seed, and scale tier that fill the largest number of currently uncovered pairs,
so “diverse” is a checkable property of the corpus rather than a claim. Pairwise coverage is what
separates enforced from nominal diversity and rules outtemplate locking(Zeng et al., 2026a): a
corpus can be balanced on every axis taken alone while its axis values only ever appear in a few fixed
combinations; a strength-2 covering array rules this out for every pair of axes. Coverage is checked
on admitted environments only, after the gates of Appendix A.6. Appendix A.7 reports the resulting
balance across domains and capability categories.

Multi-format artifacts.Text-only tasks under-represent real terminal work, so each environment
ships concrete, heterogeneous artifacts inspected through standard tooling: relational databases,
columnar and delimited text, serialized model shards, compiled binaries, and service manifests. Some
environments are also multimodal: part of the latent world is rendered as an image, such as the
billing-dashboard screenshot of Example 1 (Appendix A.10).
Per-seed world variation.Re-seeding a generator varies entity identities, values, layouts, ten-
sor names, and the placement of every corruption, so no two environments share a public tree
(Appendix A.6). This is the mechanism behind both scale and decontamination.
A.4 SCALELADDER
Each generator exposes a scale axis that tunes the size of the world. For the warehouse environment
the tiers run from 30 customers and 48 transactions per month (small) to 480 customers and 960
transactions per month (large), with proportional growth in duplicates and missing values; for the
checkpoint-consolidation environment the ladder is the shard count crossed with the parallelism
topology (pure tensor parallelism up to combined tensor-, pipeline-, and expert-parallel layouts).
Because tasks are defined over the workflow DAG, typically five to six critical stages with cross-stage
dependencies, the action, operational, and verification horizons grow with the tier as first-class,
controllable quantities. We sample across the ladder so that the corpus is neither uniformly trivial nor
uniformly unsolvable. For the generators instantiated at all three scale tiers, the median input tree

A.6 QUALIFICATIONGATES
A synthesized environment is admitted only if it passes every gate below. All gates are benchmark-
independent; they are enforced while each generator is authored and checked automatically when
each environment is generated.
• Reward causality.Each reward component c must lose value when its cause is mutated in the
workspace:c(µ c(s⋆))<c(s ⋆)for a passing workspaces ⋆ and its cause-mutationµc.
• Exploit resistance.A probe s(k) for every one of 14 gaming strategies (empty output, minimal
schema-valid output, copied input, single-seed hard-coding, path traversal, private lookup, and oth-
ers) must score 0 under both the strict verifier and the progress scorer, verW (s(k)) = ΦW (s(k)) =
0.
• Role independence.Reference solver, alternative solver, strict verifier, and progress scorer have
disjoint, audited code closures; none imports another.
• Solver agreement.The reference solver πref, whose output scores exactly 1.0, verW (πref(s0)) =
ΦW (πref(s0)) = 1, and the independently authored alternative solverπalt must produce identical
output trees on every seed, πref(s0) =π alt(s0); a disagreement is treated as an unresolved
specification and the environment is rejected.
• Progress validity.The potential ΦW satisfies 0<Φ W (s)<1 on partially correct states, is
monotone to1.0along the reference trajectory, and produces negative increments on regression.
• Metamorphic invariance.Semantics-preserving transforms of a correct output do not change the
grade; stale-output counterfactuals fail.
• Six-seed diversity.At least six seeds yield distinct world identities, public-tree hashes, and task
ids.
• Public-contract hygiene.No private authority, reference output, or verifier code appears in the
promptxor the public trees 0.
Why we gate at generation time.The solver audit is independent of the verifier: neither πref nor
πalt imports verifier code, so their agreement is evidence about the specification rather than about
the grader. Unlike pipelines that skip validation and rely on downstream RL to soft-filter unsolvable
tasks (Ivison et al., 2026), we gate at generation time, because a dense progress signal is only useful
if it is causal and resists gaming. Procedural seeding also makes decontamination structural: no
two environments share a public tree, s0(E)̸=s 0(E′) forE̸=E ′, and none shares one with an
evaluation instance (Appendix A.9).

A.8 COMPARISONPROTOCOL
Agent time.“Agent time” in Table 1 is measured rather than estimated. The fixed evaluator of the
difficulty protocol below, Gemini 3.6 Flash, is run on a fixed 100-task subsample of each corpus,
and for every rollout we record the wall-clock time from the agent’s first action to its last step. The
interval includes every model call and retry and every command execution in between; it excludes
only sandbox setup before the first action and the separate test run after the last step (TEV-GYM’s
host-side grade at submission, 0.3 s at the median, falls inside the last step). The table reports
the median and mean over rollouts, in minutes. For the prior corpora these are the rollouts of the
difficulty measurement below (Harborterminus-2, 60 turns, 8 rollouts per task, timed by Harbor’s
agent_execution interval). That budget ends only 1–13% of their rollouts, and every rollout
it ends has already run longer than its corpus’s median, so the reported prior-corpus medians equal
those of an unlimited budget (only the means could rise). TEV-GYM’s rollouts run longer (28% use
more than 60 tool calls), so for TEV-GYMwe lift the budget until it no longer binds: we draw a fixed
100-environment subsample from all 1,170 environments (seed 20260915, stratified by domain
9.1–9.7) and run the evaluator in the single- bash harness of §4.1 with a budget of 300 tool calls
and 2 h of agent wall-clock per rollout, 2 rollouts per environment. No rollout reaches either limit
(median 41 tool calls, maximum 145), so the values are not truncated: median 12.4 min and mean
14.8 min, against a median of 0.5–2.0 min for the prior corpora. The measure compares corpora under
one evaluator and is not an estimate of human effort. Terminal-Universe releases no environments
and cannot be timed. “Progressive reward” marks a training signal defined on intermediate workspace

A.9 DECONTAMINATION
Structural cleanliness.Because each task is projected from a freshly seeded procedural world, no
two environments, and in particular no environment and no evaluation instance, share a public tree;
the six-seed diversity gate enforces this by hash. TEV-GYMtherefore contains no verbatim copy of
any evaluation task.
Measured overlap.We additionally measure lexical overlap between the task prompt of every one
of the 1,170 environments and our evaluation sets with a 13-gram sliding window over lower-cased
alphanumeric tokens, following standard contamination protocol. The evaluation texts are the task
cards of the 18 computing-and-math tasks (and, as a superset, all 23 tasks of that split; 9,010 distinct
13-grams), the instructions of the 74 TB 3.0/4.0 tasks (21,138) and of the 89 TB 2.1 tasks (13,292).
No environment shares a single 13-gram with any evaluation task (0 of 1,170 against each set;
maximum shared fraction 0.0%), and none shares an 8-gram; overlap appears only at 5-grams, in
generic phrasing such as “not modify files under input”. A control confirms that the comparator is
sensitive: the two TB sets share 156 13-grams with each other.

separated (full sets and the CM subsets of Table 3) and TB 2.1 included, and adds three statistics

A.10 THREEWORKEDTRAININGENVIRONMENTS
Two generalizations of §2.1 are easiest to see on concrete environments. First, the public trees0 need
not be text: Example 1, a cloud-operations task from one of TEV-GYM’s seven domains, stages a
billing-dashboard screenshot whose three findings appear in no CSV . Second, nothing in the pipeline
is specific to the seven computing-and-math domains: Examples 2 and 3 were synthesized by the
same pipeline for two other domains of Agents’ Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026), energy engineering
(closed-loop building control) and accounting (financial-statement reconstruction). For each we
present the training environment only, in two parts: thepublic view, the prompt x and the input tree
s0 that are all the agent ever receives, and theground truthsealed behind them, the latent world W ,
the reference deliverables derived from it, and what the grader compares. The three also span the two
ways a latent world grounds a reference: in Examples 1 and 3 the world is a generated record set and
the reference follows from it by construction; in Example 2 the world is a pinned simulator plus a
declared procedure, so the reference is atool oracle, produced by running that procedure once inside
the sealed image. Paths are relative to the agent’s working directory, the agent writes its deliverables
tooutput/, and all three run in a pinned container with the network disabled.
EXAMPLE1:MULTIMODAL CLOUD COST OPTIMIZATION(CLOUDOPERATIONS)
Public view.The container provides python3 and pandas. The agent receives the prompt below
and three inputs: an inventory CSV of 430 EC2, RDS, and S3 resources with utilization percentiles, a
pricing table, and a rendered billing-dashboard screenshot (Figure 6) whose lower panel lists three
findings, an idle NAT gateway, an unattached Elastic IP, and a stale CloudWatch log group, that
appear in no CSV . This is an extra-large instance of its generator.

You are an AWS cost optimization analyst working on Linux. Three inputs are staged under ‘

- ‘input/aws_billing_dashboard.png‘ - a synthetic AWS billing dashboard screenshot. It shows
a per-service cost breakdown AND three ’dashboard-only’ findings (an idle NAT gateway, an
unattached Elastic IP, and a stale CloudWatch log group) that are NOT present in the usage

- ‘input/resource_usage.csv‘ - the EC2/RDS/S3 inventory with columns ‘resource_id,
resource_type,name,state,instance_type,cpu_p95,mem_p95,connections_p95,size_gb,
ia_access_ratio‘.
- ‘input/aws_pricing_reference.csv‘ - the deterministic pricing table (‘sku,dimension,unit,
price_usd‘).
Apply these rules and price every saving from the pricing table:
- Downsize a running EC2 instance one tier when ‘cpu_p95 < 20‘ and ‘mem_p95 < 50‘.
- Downsize an available RDS instance one tier when ‘cpu_p95 < 25‘ and ‘connections_p95 < 10‘.
- Move an S3 bucket to Infrequent Access when ‘ia_access_ratio < 0.10‘ and ‘size_gb >= 100‘.
- Include the three dashboard-only findings (delete the idle NAT gateway, release the
unattached Elastic IP, delete the stale CloudWatch log group).
Write ‘output/optimization_report.json‘ with an ‘executive_summary‘ object and a ‘
recommendations‘ array, and ‘output/savings_summary.csv‘ with columns ‘resource_id,
resource_type,name,action,current_cost,projected_cost,monthly_savings‘.
Scoring is weighted: 30% coverage F1 over the hidden recommendation set (including the three
dashboard-only resources), 30% action correctness, 25% savings accuracy (full credit within
+/-20% relative error), and 15% report completeness.

Ground truth.The latent world is the pinned simulator together with the declared procedure:
the EnergyPlus model, the weather file, and the schedules, weights, and identification recipe of
instance.json fix a unique correct value for every field of the nine deliverables. The reference
is therefore produced by executing that procedure once, inside the same pinned image, by the
sealed reference builder, which the agent never sees. The builder (i) checks the SHA-256 of the
shipped 1ZoneUncontrolled.idf and Golden TMY3 weather file against the values pinned in
instance.json and applies the declared edits to the model (run period 1–7 July, four timesteps per
hour, an InternalMass of 48 m2, and a Schedule:Constant actuator driving a 2.0406 kW
OtherEquipment cooling sink); (ii) runs EnergyPlus twice through its Python API, once under
the two-position thermostat (declared setpoint schedule, deadband 0.5 ◦C, on-fraction 0.85) and
once under the prescribed 0.9/0.1 excitation schedule, reading the zone temperature and writing the
actuator at every zone timestep; (iii) fits the declared second-order input–output model
T[t] =a 1T[t−1] +a 2T[t−2] +b 0Tout[t] +b 1Tout[t−1] +c 0u[t] +c 1u[t−1] +d
by ridge least squares (λ= 10 −8) on the first 80% of each trace with the last 20% held out, and
asserts a negative cooling gain,c0 +c 1 <0 ; (iv) runs EnergyPlus twice more in closed loop, solving
at every zone timestep a 24-step cvxpy/OSQP receding-horizon problem with the policy’s declared
weights and actuating its first control; and (v) writes the nine artifacts with the declared rounding:
three 672-row traces, two 96-row action files over the final 24 hours, two logs exposing the seven
coefficients, training and held-out RMSE, closed-loop one-step RMSE, objective weights, and solver-
status counts, the 3×7 metrics table, and the summary. A round-trip self-check re-fits the model
and re-reads every artifact the way the grader will (coefficients within 10−7, row counts, distinct
policy weights) before the environment is published. The grader then compares the agent’s nine files
with these references cell by cell (CSV) and leaf by leaf (JSON) at a tolerance of 10−4, scoring each
artifact by its fraction of matching fields. Every artifact is a function of the closed-loop trajectories,
so a precomputed open-loop schedule, a first-order model, or a single policy cannot reproduce them.
