text: Preprint 2025,balance_sheet,cash,246,us-gaap:CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue,companyfacts.json ,→,#/facts/us-gaap/CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue/units/USD/1,"SEC Companyfacts ,→JSON, us-gaap:CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue, FY 2025, companyfacts.json#/ ,→facts/us-gaap/CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue/units/USD/1", ,→latest_exact_period_annual_structured_fact 2024,balance_sheet,cash,256,us-gaap:CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue,companyfacts.json ,→,#/facts/us-gaap/CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue/units/USD/2,"SEC Companyfacts ,→JSON, us-gaap:CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue, FY 2024, companyfacts.json#/ ,→facts/us-gaap/CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue/units/USD/2", ,→latest_exact_period_annual_structured_fact B DENSEREWARDDETAILS This appendix expands §3. Wasted groups under terminal reward.The all-fail fraction (1−p) G of §3.1 stays high even for larger groups, still 44% atp=0.05 withG=16, and even on synthesized terminal tasks Shen et al. (2026) find that only about half of all tasks yield any reward variance under binary reward. The same starvation afflicts actor-critic methods such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) in a softer form, since a critic fit to near-constant returns yields near-zero advantages everywhere; GRPO merely makes it exact. Relation to policy-invariant shaping.PPRS (Eq. (4)) is not policy-invariant shaping in the sense of Ng et al. (1999). Classical shaping zeroes the potential of the terminal state, so the shaping terms sum to the same constant−Φ(s0) = 0 on every trajectory and leave the objective unchanged. We keep the terminal potential, so the shaped return is terminal success plus λΦ(sT ) and defines a graded objective; zeroing it would give every all-fail group identical rewards again and reinstate the starvation of §3.1, which is why the term is kept. What is preserved is the ranking of trajectories: a passing trajectory earns 1 +λ and a failing one at mostλ, so a deterministic policy that maximizes one objective maximizes the other, and no trajectory is rewarded for trading completion against partial progress. What is not preserved is the ranking of stochastic policies in expectation. Let π1 andπ2 pass with probabilitiesp1

In training,R(τ) enters with per-turn credit (Appendix C): turnt receives the incrementλrt and the
final turn additionally receives the terminal term.
Relation to potential-based shaping.In the language of potential-based shaping (Ng et al., 1999),
Φis the potential andr t its difference. Classical shaping requires that the shaped objective have the
same optimal policies as the original; we deliberately do not, because the whole point is that the
shaped objective isnotindifferent to partial progress. What we retain is agreement on maximizers
(any passing rollout outscores any failing one) and anchoring ( Φ = 1 exactly when the verifier
passes), so the acceptance set of a task is unchanged. This is the opposite route from the usual
remedy for tasks beyond a learner’s frontier, which is to simplify, scaffold, or defer the task until
some rollout succeeds (Florensa et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2025b; Wolf et al., 2026; Zeng et al.,
2026a); we leave the task and the harness fixed and raise the resolution of the reward. We prefer a
task-aligned potential to the test-pass fraction of Shen et al. (2026) and the passing-assertion count of
Yang et al. (2026), which score only what the terminal tests probe and carry no notion of regression.
The signal is also denserwithina group that contains a success: the lone passing rollout is contrasted
not with an undifferentiated mass of failures but with a graded spectrum of near-misses. Because Φ is
produced by a scorer with a code closure disjoint from the verifier’s and has passed the causality and
exploit-resistance gates of Appendix A.6, none of the probed gaming strategies applied to the public
tree earns Φ>0 , and Φ rises only when the output tree matches more of the workflow’s correct
intermediate and final artifacts.

C.1 TRAININGRECIPE ANDHYPERPARAMETERS

policy ratio, and no KL anchor. Groups whose rewards have zero variance are discarded and refilled

applied with per-turn credit: turnt receives the incrementλrt, the final turn additionally receives the
terminal term, and each turn’s advantage is its return-to-go minus the group mean of that return at the
same turn index. Table 11 lists the recipe shared by every run; runs differ only in the corpus subset,
the reward mechanism, the model size, and the hardware they ran on.

D EXTENDEDRELATEDWORK
Synthetic corpora for coding and terminal agents.The first wave of agent training data mined real
repositories: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) and SWE-Gym (Pan et al., 2025) collect GitHub issues
with their tests, and SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025) and Skywork-SWE (Zeng et al., 2025)
automate the mining. The second wave synthesizes tasks: SWE-smith (Yang et al., 2025a) injects
bugs into working repositories, SWE-Flow (Zhang et al., 2025b) strips a repository along its runtime
dependency graph, and R2E-Gym (Jain et al., 2025) back-translates problem statements from commits.
Terminal corpora follow the same pattern at larger scale, either with a language model writing tasks,
containers, and tests that are then filtered for solvability, as in Endless Terminals (Gandhi et al., 2026),
SETA (Shen et al., 2026), and recursive solution extension (Li et al., 2026a) (TMAX (Ivison et al.,
2026) skips this filter and lets RL drop unsolved tasks), or by reconstructing environments from agent
trajectories, as in CLI-Gym (Lin et al., 2026) and Terminal-Universe (Wu et al., 2026). All of these
scale the number ofinstances: each instance is pull-request-sized or a single session, its verifier is a

must be validated after the fact. We scaleenvironments: a coding agent writes each generator once,
the authors review it, and instantiating it involves no model; verification is against the latent world
rather than a test suite. Closer in spirit is the programmatic synthesis of executable, stateful tool
environments, AutoForge (Cai et al., 2025), EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026), ScaleEnv (Tu et al., 2026),
Agent-World (Dong et al., 2026), EnvFactory (Xu et al., 2026), and LOGIGEN (Zeng et al., 2026b),
which also treats the environment as the unit of scale (Fang et al., 2025); these are API worlds for
short tool-use episodes, and only LOGIGEN emits a progress signal, a per-turn reward from the
database’s proximity to its target state. Two findings from that line carry over: more environments
alone do not help without difficulty control (Zhu et al., 2026b), and coverage rather than count is what
drives transfer (Chen et al., 2026a;b; Xu et al., 2026). Our environments differ from this family on
the two properties it largely lacks: each spans a long, multi-stage workflow across math and science,
ML, and coding and systems domains rather than a short tool-use episode, and every one ships the
progress potential ΦW of §3 rather than a bare success condition, so the difficulty control and dense
signal these two findings call for come from the same generator that supplies coverage.
Backward construction.Latent-world-first synthesis belongs to a long line of methods that derive a
task from its solution. Denoising objectives corrupt text and learn to restore it (Lewis et al., 2020);
the data-cleaning community injects errors of controlled repairability into clean databases to evaluate
repair algorithms (Arocena et al., 2015) and corrupts synthetic person records to benchmark record
linkage (Tran et al., 2013); mutation and bug injection corrupt working code (Yang et al., 2025a;
Hariharan et al., 2025); CLI-Gym rewinds a healthy environment to an earlier broken state (Lin
et al., 2026); instruction back-translation derives prompts from answers (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al.,
2024); and procedural generators with rule-based verifiers supply unlimited single-turn reasoning
problems whose answers are known by construction (Stojanovski et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Liu
et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). In every case the corrupted object is a single artifact graded by a pre-
existing oracle, or a one-step puzzle. We corrupt a rendering of an entire world into many mutually
constraining files of different formats, and the oracle is the world itself; this is what lets exactness, and
the ground truth of every intermediate stage, survive a multi-hour horizon. In the taxonomy of Zeng
et al. (2026a), generation pipelines anchor on the environment, the task, the trajectory, or a blueprint
that coordinates them; anchoring on the verified terminal state itself is what removes the artifact drift
among task, environment, and verifier that separately generated factors invite (Ivanov & Rana, 2026).
Concretely, we anchor one level earlier than any object in that taxonomy: the latent worldW itself,
so that the taskx, the input trees0, the strict verifier verW , and the progress potential ΦW (Eq. (1))

text:
Preprint
are four views of one object rather than four artifacts a blueprint must keep synchronized after the
fact. CLI-Gym is the closest of these in mechanism, but it rewinds a single running environment to
an earlier state and stops at one pass/fail check, with no signal over the stages in between.
World-state verification, environment scaling, and long-horizon benchmarks.Verifying an
agent against the final state of a simulated world rather than against its transcript is established in
AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024),τ-bench (Yao et al., 2025), WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024a), and
OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024), all with hand-authored tasks for evaluation. Recent work generates the
world too: AgentMercury (Jeong & Yoon, 2026) has a model author persistent business worlds with
executable invariants, and Zhang et al. (2026) derive dense rewards from progress predicates over
generated web sites; neither uses a declared corruption, and both depend on a model to write the
world. A growing literature argues that environments are the bottleneck of agentic RL (Xi et al.,
2025; Fang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a; Gandhi et al., 2026), with the caveat
that more environments alone do not help without difficulty control (Zhu et al., 2026b). Our thesis
is narrower: the environments worth scaling are those whose latent world supplies both the oracle
and the progress signal. Long-horizon benchmarks with partial credit, TheAgentCompany (Xu
et al., 2024), Long-Horizon Terminal-Bench (Li et al., 2026b), PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025),
MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025), and ALE-Bench (Imajuku et al., 2025), target the regime we train
for, but their checkpoints are written per task by hand or graded by a model, and at tens of instances
they are evaluation sets.
Sparse reward and dense signal in agentic RL.Group-relative methods discard rollout groups
with identical rewards (Yu et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Ivison et al., 2026), schedule prompts by
difficulty (Yang et al., 2025b; Sha et al., 2026), or seed groups with expert prefixes (Zhang et al.,
2025c); all assume enough solvable prompts to fill a batch. A complementary line moves the tasks
rather than the reward, generating or selecting them near the learner’s current success band (Florensa
et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Wolf et al., 2026); this keeps groups informative but
caps difficulty at what the current policy can sometimes finish. Denser signals come from learned or
judged step rewards (Cui et al., 2025; Choudhury, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; 2024b;
Gunjal et al., 2025), from advantages over recurring states (Feng et al., 2025), or from exact but proxy
quantities: similarity to an oracle patch (Wei et al., 2025), the fraction of tests passed (Du et al., 2025;
Shen et al., 2026), the count of passing assertions (Yang et al., 2026), compiler diagnostics (Zhang &
Lanser Contributors, 2025), path-centric credit for evidence gathering (Xia et al., 2026), or symbolic
oracles in closed domains (Yuan et al., 2026). Test-fraction rewards are the closest to ours and are
what lets SETA and T1 train on terminal tasks, but they score only what the terminal tests probe,
are not monotone in workflow progress, and carry no notion of regression. Our potential is exact
progress against the latent world at every workflow stage, anchored so that Φ = 1 exactly when the
verifier passes, and free for every seed. A recent finding shapes how such a signal should be used:
a shaping term that is not aligned with the task collapses GRPO agents, because in all-fail groups
it becomes the whole objective (Wang, 2026). Unlike the learned or judged step rewards above,Φ
needs no trained critic or LM judge; its relation to classical potential-based shaping (Ng et al., 1999)
is discussed in Appendix B.

Fig. 1.AXIS-Bench enables a systematic study of quality-aware VLA pretraining.We use 5,000 simulation demonstrations for controlled comparisons
and 19,250 for pretraining before real-world fine-tuning. The simulation study spans three VLAs, comparing reward definitions, label granularities, and
learning methods within each VLA. Green values show mean relative gains over plain behavioral cloning.
Abstract— How should demonstration quality be used during
vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve perfor-
mance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting,
filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label
granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demon-
strations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match
demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons
examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags dur-
ing fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that
approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success
over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor
episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-
dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves
mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged
or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support
these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simula-
tion demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact
states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories.
Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering
and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world
experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6% to
31.7%. Project page:https://axis-bench.github.io/.
I. INTRODUCTION
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly pre-
trained on multitask demonstrations and fine-tuned on target
tasks before deployment [1], [2], [3], [4]. During a demon-
stration, an operator may hesitate or move an object along an
unnecessary detour, producing action chunks that make little
progress toward the goal. Quality-aware pretraining [5], [6]
aims to learn effectively from naturally suboptimal demon-
strations. We evaluate its effect on performance after target-
task fine-tuning (FT).
Quality-based filtering, weighting, and conditioning have
been studied in robot learning [7], [5], [8], [9], [6]. Yet a
quality signal leaves several learning choices open. The same
quality information can be used to select which training ex-
amples to retain [8], [10], determine how strongly individual
actions contribute to the training loss [11], [10], or condition
the policy through explicit quality tags [6]. Quality can also
be defined at different granularities, describing local progress

over an action chunk or summarizing the quality of an
entire episode. For conditioned policies, additional choices
arise regarding how quality tags should be handled during
subsequent fine-tuning and inference. However, systematic
evidence comparing how these choices interact under shared
data and evaluation protocols remains limited. To address this
gap, we study how quality definitions, label granularities, and
learning methods jointly affect target-task performance, and
which findings are consistent across base VLA policies. We
compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across two
progress-based reward definitions, two label granularities,
and three VLAs (π0.5 [4], SmolVLA [12], and X-VLA [13]).
Using 5,000 pretraining demonstrations and 24 target tasks,
we further examine the effects of pretraining data size and
fine-tuning/inference protocols.
Three findings emerge (see Fig. 1). First, approach-aware
episode conditioning improves mean success over plain
behavioral cloning (plain BC) across the three evaluated
VLAs. Second, label granularity interacts with both the
learning method and base VLA: conditioning favors episode
labels and filtering favors chunk labels on average, but the
preferences can reverse. Third, after approach-aware episode
conditioning, constant-tag target-task FT yields higher mean
success than plain FT with tagged/untagged inference.
To support this study, we introduce AXIS-Bench (see
Fig. 2), a simulation and real-world benchmark built on the
crowdsourced AXIS simulation teleoperation dataset [14].
Recorded object and contact states let us recompute progress-
based quality labels on the same trajectories. Replayable
trajectories further enable researchers to re-render demon-
strations to align with target workspace and camera config-
urations and evaluate policies on their own real-world target
tasks. In our real-world reference experiment, simulation
pretraining raisesπ 0.5-base success rate from 9.6% to 31.7%.
Our main contributions are:
1)A systematic empirical study of quality-aware VLA
pretraining.We identify how quality definitions, label
granularities, learning methods, and adaptation proto-
cols interact across base policies, with matched data
and training budgets within each VLA.
2)AXIS-Bench for controlled comparison and real-
world validation.We provide shared human demon-
strations, configurable state-derived quality labels, and
standardized training and evaluation protocols, together
with replayable simulation trajectories and a real-world
setup for workspace adaptation.
II. RELATEDWORK
Robot demonstration datasets.Robot demonstration
datasets have expanded the diversity of tasks, environments,
and embodiments available for policy learning. Bridge-
Data V2 and DROID collect real-world demonstrations
across tasks and workspaces [15], [16], while Open X-
Embodiment aggregates data across robot embodiments [1],
supporting generalist policies such as Octo and OpenVLA
[2], [3]. Simulation provides complementary approaches
through crowdsourced teleoperation, as in RoboTurk [17],
and demonstration-based or procedural generation, as in
MimicGen and MolmoB0T [18], [19]. Real-world collections
naturally capture variation in human execution but generally
lack simulator states for directly recomputing progress-based
rewards. Generated simulation trajectories provide privileged
state information but need not preserve the natural execution
variability of human demonstrations. AXIS unifies crowd-
sourced human teleoperation with recorded object states,
contacts, and replayable trajectories [14].
Quality-aware VLA training.Studies of demonstration
proficiency motivate learning selectively from demonstra-
tions of varying quality [20]. Related data-curation methods
estimate training utility using state-action mutual informa-
2
title: What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study

text:
tion, target-task relevance, or rollout-based influence [7],
[21], [22], [23]. These methods also operate at different gran-
ularities: Re-Mix optimizes dataset-level mixture weights
[5], SCIZOR filters individual transitions for generalist pol-
icy training [8], and World Value Models (WVMs) use
chunk-level value changes for weighting and filtering [10].
Conditioning supplies quality information as an input to
the policy. Decision Transformer and RvS study return-
conditioned supervised learning for offline RL [24], [25].
In VLA training, RECAP applies advantage conditioning
during both pretraining and task-specific training [9], while
π0.7 conditions on quality, speed, and mistake metadata [6].
Related metadata- and quality-conditioning strategies have
also been explored in language-model pretraining and vision-
language learning [26], [27], [28]. We complement these
studies with a controlled comparison of reward definitions,
label granularities, and learning methods on shared demon-
strations across three VLAs.
III. BENCHMARKDESIGN ANDDATARESOURCE
A. Human demonstrations and replayable data
AXIS-Bench pairs human demonstrations with scene as-
sets and replayable simulation trajectories (see Fig. 2). Policy
observations comprise images, task instructions, and pro-
prioceptive states, paired with corresponding action targets.
Recorded object geometry, contacts, task progress, episode
boundaries, and validity masks support offline quality label-
ing (Sec. IV). We use two pretraining datasets: 5,000 simu-
lation demonstrations (about 35.3 hours) for the simulation
experiments and 19,250 simulation demonstrations (about
114.6 hours) for the real-world experiments. Both simula-
tion and real-world experiments use a DROID-compatible
interface [16], with actions comprising seven joint velocities
and a gripper command at 15 Hz. Pretraining observations
include both external-camera and wrist-camera views.
B. Controlled simulation benchmark
The simulation branch of Fig. 2 evaluates target-task per-
formance on 24 tabletop tasks spanning containment, support
placement, spatial relations, separation, and short sequences.
Pretraining uses the shared 5,000-demonstration dataset, in
which object meshes and poses, language goals, and visual
conditions vary across demonstrations. Visual randomization
varies room backgrounds, table textures, and lighting while
keeping the external-camera pose fixed. Target-task FT uses
354 demonstrations (about 2.4 hours). The embodiment,
renderer, and object library are shared between pretraining
and evaluation, so the benchmark evaluates target tasks and
initial object placements within this setting. Pretraining and
target task IDs are disjoint, although three target instructions
also occur under four pretraining task IDs (22 of the 5,000
demonstrations); the split therefore does not imply complete
semantic separation. Within each VLA configuration, method
comparisons use the same base-policy initialization, training
budget, target-task demonstrations, and evaluation layouts.

V. SIMULATIONEXPERIMENTS
We ask three questions: which quality-aware pretrain-
ing choices improve performance across VLAs, how label
granularity interacts with the learning method, and whether
quality tags should be retained during target-task FT. We also
examine how performance changes with dataset size.
A. Experimental overview
We compare plain BC, weighting, filtering, and condi-
tioning on 5,000 pretraining demonstrations, followed by
FT on 354 demonstrations covering 24 target tasks. Within
each VLA, comparisons share the initialization, data, training
budget, and evaluation layouts. We initializeπ0.5 [4] from the
releasedπ 0.5-DROID checkpoint and X-VLA [13] from its
released base policy; SmolVLA [12] uses a frozen pretrained
VLM and a randomly initialized action expert. Plain BC,
weighting, and filtering use plain FT and untagged inference;
conditioning uses constant-tag FT and tag-5 inference, with
stage-specific controls below. Matched FT-only controls omit
AXIS pretraining. For each of the 24 tasks, we evaluate all
configurations on the same set of 50 initial scene layouts
(1,200 trials per configuration) and report mean task success.
Error bars in Figs. 5–7 denote±1evaluation SE. Results
are plotted relative to each VLA’s plain-BC reference, with
absolute success rates given in the figure captions. Detailed
training, evaluation, and plotting protocols are in appendix.

VI. REAL-WORLDEXPERIMENTS
A. Experimental overview
We evaluate simulation pretraining on ten real-world ma-
nipulation tasks in a Franka FR3 workspace, with 25 real-
world demonstrations collected per task for target-task fine-
tuning. Each policy is evaluated with 24 trials per task (240
trials in total). All three configurations start fromπ 0.5-base
and use the same fine-tuning dataset. We compare an FT-
only control with plain BC and approach-aware episode con-
ditioning pretrained on 19,250 simulation demonstrations.
The FT-only and plain-BC configurations use plain FT and
untagged inference; conditioning uses tagged FT and tag-5
inference. Hardware, training, and evaluation details appear
in the appendix.
Fig. 8 illustrates workspace alignment: we first adjust
the simulated camera view, then configure the tabletop
and background to match the real workspace. Re-rendering
changes the observations while preserving recorded actions
and object states. Configuring our reference workspace took
approximately 30 minutes, after which recorded trajectories
could be re-rendered for pretraining.

VII. DISCUSSION ANDCONCLUSION
In the evaluated configurations, approach-aware episode
conditioning improves mean success over plain BC, and
constant-tag FT improves mean success after conditioned
pretraining under both tested inference protocols. Condition-
ing favors episode labels and filtering favors chunk labels on
average, with model-dependent reversals. The study covers a
shared tabletop simulation setting, with real-world validation
using one VLA in a reference workspace. Testing larger pre-
training budgets and additional workspaces and embodiments
would clarify how broadly the findings transfer. Initialization
and trainable modules vary across VLAs, so the comparisons
do not isolate the causes of their different method rankings.
Matched controls could test whether retaining data coverage
explains conditioning’s benefits, and which aspects of initial-
ization and adaptation explain the observed differences.
Our progress-based labels capture only part of demon-
stration quality and may undervalue necessary preparation
or recovery with little immediate progress. Preference-based
reward learning [33] and personalized policy condition-
ing [34] suggest ways to incorporate user-dependent objec-
tives beyond task progress. Demonstration decomposition for
planner alignment [35] also motivates examining quality over
meaningful subtasks. Whether such signals improve quality-
aware pretraining remains an open question.
Quality supervision could also complement task-relevant
visual attention [36] and semantic guidance for pretrained
policies [37]. Beyond nominal task success, deployment
requires evaluating robustness to sensory and instruction per-
turbations [38] and scene–task inconsistencies [39]. Safety
alignment through constrained learning [40] addresses a
further objective that progress-based quality labels do not
explicitly encode. These directions would extend the present
evaluation beyond task completion to the reliability and
safety of learned behavior. AXIS-Bench supports further
comparisons by enabling new quality labels to be computed
and trajectories to be re-rendered for user-defined workspaces
and tasks.

EXPERIMENTALPROTOCOLS
A. Simulation experiment details
Forπ 0.5, pretraining updates all parameters for 20,605
updates (batch 64, learning rate5×10 −5). FT starts from
the EMA checkpoint (decay 0.999) and runs for 13,580
updates (batch 32, learning rate2.5×10 −5), using LoRA
for language/action modules and a trainable vision encoder.
Pretraining and FT use 2,060 and 500 warmup updates,
respectively. Target demonstrations follow a fixed within-
task ranking by approach-aware progress established during
dataset curation. SmolVLA and X-VLA use 20,621 pretrain-
ing and 6,790 FT updates, with batch 64 and learning rate
10−4. SmolVLA starts from a pretrained SmolVLM2 with a
randomly initialized action expert and updates only the action
expert and state projection, keeping the VLM and vision
encoder frozen; X-VLA updates all parameters, with one-
tenth the learning rate for its VLM. Simulation normalization
statistics are fitted separately to each stage’s data and shared
across methods. All models receive five FT epochs, and we
evaluate the final checkpoint. Images use224×224center
crops forπ 0.5 and padding to512×512for SmolVLA or
224×224for X-VLA. SmolVLA uses AdamW with cosine
scheduling; X-VLA uses domain-prompt index 20.
Random-selection controls use a fixed sampling seed and
match the retained time steps and training updates of quality
filtering. Quality-tag dropout in simulation uses two inde-
pendent dropout operations with probabilities0.15and0.05
during both pretraining and tagged FT. Pretraining masks
are sampled once offline and shared across corresponding
experiments; tagged-FT masks are resampled each epoch.
For evaluation, the 24 tasks comprise six containment, six
support-placement, seven spatial-relation, two separation,
and three short-sequence tasks. The native prediction hori-
zons are 10, 50, and 30 actions forπ 0.5, SmolVLA, and
X-VLA, respectively. Policies return the first ten predicted
actions, and the client executes eight before replanning. The
H= 10labeling window is independent of the native
prediction horizon. Matched FT-only controls omit AXIS
pretraining while retaining the corresponding initialization.
Relative improvements use100(SR/SR BC −1)with
unrounded success rates; marginal SEs are scaled by
100/SRBC. The reference is each VLA’s 5K plain BC with
plain FT and untagged inference. Table I uses the same
BC reference for each VLA and training seed: we compute
100(SRA−SRB)/SRBC within each seed, then report the
mean and sample SD. Thus, row differences are expressed
relative to BC, including comparisons between two non-BC
configurations. The relative gains in Fig. 1 use the same
calculation for episode conditioning versus BC. Training-
seed SDs describe variation across three runs, not confidence
intervals or significance tests.
B. Real-world experiment details
The Franka FR3 setup uses a Robotiq gripper, ZED 2i
external camera, and ZED Mini wrist camera. Pretraining
and FT use 20K and 16K updates, respectively, with batch 64
and AdamW cosine learning rates from2.5×10 −5 to2.5×
10−6. Pretraining uses LoRA for language/action modules
and a frozen vision encoder; FT makes the vision encoder
trainable. The learning-rate schedules use 1,000 and 1,600
warmup updates for pretraining and FT, respectively. Both
stages use fixed DROID normalization statistics without re-
estimation,224×224center crops, and a 15-action prediction
horizon. Simulation observations are rendered at640×360
with workspace-aligned backgrounds and camera views. Ev-
ery checkpoint includes the same normalization statistics
for training and inference. Pretraining applies color jitter,
blur, posterization, sharpness, and grayscale augmentation
following MolmoB0T [19].
Conditioning assigns episode-score quintiles to 17,758
demonstrations and neutral tag 3 to 1,492 unscorable
episodes, without pretraining tag dropout. The ten real-world
tasks cover nesting, stacking, alignment, rotation, pressing,
closing, insertion, and extraction. Evaluation uses 12 layouts
per task and two trials per layout; equal trial counts make
task-averaged and pooled success rates identical.

title: What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study

text:
ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
Bingxin Xu1 Wenrui Bao2 Xinxin Liu2 Jiawei Zhou3 Yuzhang Shang2 Emilio Ferrara1
1University of Southern California 2University of Central Florida 3Stony Brook University
Abstract
Agentic robotics places a large language model
(LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where
it composes perception, motion, and vision-
language-action (VLA) tools under the guid-
ance of a memory and thereby generalizes to
new tasks without retraining. This generality
comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every prim-
itive requires a round of LLM reasoning over
the full interaction history, so the cost of an
episode grows with the number of primitives.
We find this reasoning largely redundant: once
a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a rou-
tine already prescribed by memory. We present
ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to
agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches
a chunk of chained primitives, which executes
autonomously and returns control only upon
failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the mem-
ory into these chunks, so execution is memory-
free at test time and the planner is reserved for
decisions that require reasoning. LLM com-
putation therefore scales with the number of
decisions rather than the number of primitives.
On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task suc-
cess by 5.0 points over the state of the art in
agentic robotics while requiring 2.9 × fewer
LLM calls, 4.4× fewer input tokens, and 2.3×
fewer output tokens.
1 Introduction
Agentic robotics has emerged as a new paradigm
for robot manipulation (Liang et al., 2023; Kumar,
2026; Fu et al., 2026; Tsui et al., 2026; Zhang et al.,
2026c; Jia et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b,a). Rather
than training a policy that maps pixels and language
directly to motor commands (Brohan et al., 2023a;
Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024), it places a
large language model (LLM) agent in the control
loop and equips it with perception, motion, and
vision-language-action (VLA) tools, together with
a memory of what has worked before. At each step,
the agent observes the scene, consults the mem-
ory, reasons, and issues a single tool call (Figure 1,
top). Because each task is composed by reasoning
rather than learned from demonstrations, the agent
handles new tasks without retraining and succeeds
where end-to-end policies break down. For exam-
ple, with no robot-specific training, GPT-6 Astra
driven through a generic agent harness completes a
real-arm pick-and-place task in 19 of 20 trials (Ope-
nAI, 2026; Menon et al., 2026) and ranks above
every public policy on the RoboDojo benchmark
(Zhang et al., 2026b), which illustrates the general-
ization this paradigm affords.
However, this generalization comes at a steep
price in efficiency. The planner acts through primi-
tives, i.e., robot skills invoked as tool calls, each of
which requires a dedicated round of LLM reason-
ing. Every such round reprocesses the full interac-
tion history, and reasoning models further consume
output tokens before responding (Sui et al., 2025).
Consequently, the number of calls and output to-
kens scales linearly with the number of primitives
in an episode, while input tokens scale quadrati-
cally (Kapoor et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026a), as
illustrated in Fig.1 Top. For instance, a single pick-
and-place task requires 24.2 LLM calls and 2.2M
input tokens on average, costing about $22 per
episode with GPT-6 Astra and still $11 even with
the cheaper GPT-5.5.1 As tasks grow longer, this
overhead quickly dominates the cost of execution,
hindering the scalability of LLM-based agents.
To address this inefficiency, we analyze the
agent’s behavior and find that LLM reasoning is
frequently redundant. Once a sub-goal is selected
and its targets are localized, the subsequent prim-
itives follow a fixed routine already encoded in
memory, such that each additional call merely re-
produces a decision that has already been made.
Although a single read of memory suffices to cap-
ture this routine, the LLM tends to deliberate over
each step and constantly returns to memory for

guidance. Furthermore, the memory retrieval and
LLM reasoning become less reliable as the context
grows (Liu et al., 2024; Laban et al., 2026). This
overhead could therefore be eliminated by compil-
ing memory into generalizable action sequences
that execute without the planner’s step-by-step in-
volvement. This concept also echoes the action
chunk (Zhao et al., 2023) in robotics.
Building on this observation, we propose
ChunkAct (Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics),
which consists of two complementary components:
chunked execution at test time and memory inter-
nalization offline.At test time, ChunkAct intro-
duces action chunking to agentic robotics.It
composes the primitives that realize a sub-goal into
an executable chunk, which the planner invokes
with a single call and which then runs to comple-
tion autonomously. This design confines the LLM
to where reasoning is genuinely required: under-
standing the physical scene, diagnosing failures,
and redirecting the plan. To support this, a failed
chunk returns a typed exit that specifies the failed
primitive along with an error log, providing the
planner with structured feedback for recovery. In
this way, LLM computation scales with the number
of decisions rather than the number of primitives
(See Fig.1 Bottom). Offline, ChunkAct builds these
chunks as generalizable routines with memory com-
piled into them. The parameters and procedural
knowledge that govern each chunk are compiled
from memory before deployment, making its ac-
tions inherently memory-conditioned. As a result,
chunks run memory-free at test time, eliminating
frequent memory retrieval and further improving
the efficiency of the LLM.
Together, these two components improve both
efficiency and performance. By substantially re-
ducing the number of LLM calls and the length
of the context, ChunkAct lowers the overall cost
of each episode. Meanwhile, because the plan-
ner reasons over a concise context and memory is
internalized throughout execution, ChunkAct also
achieves higher task success rates (See Fig.1 Right).
To summarize, our contributions are threefold.
• To our knowledge, ChunkAct is the first LLM
agent for robot manipulation that commits to a
chunk of chained perception and control primi-
tives per call rather than to a single primitive.
•ChunkAct compiles memory offline into gener-
alizable action chunks, enabling memory-free
execution at test time and reserving the LLM for
decisions that genuinely require reasoning.
• Compared with the previous SOTA agentic
robotics approach, ChunkAct improves success
by 5.0 points on LIBERO-Pro, while requiring
2.9× fewer LLM calls, 4.4× fewer input tokens,
and 2.3× fewer output tokens. It also exhibits
strong zero-shot transfer capability.
2 Related Work
Agentic robotics.Language models entered ma-
nipulation as planners that sequence a fixed reper-
toire of skills, grounded in affordances and closed
by textual feedback (Brohan et al., 2023b; Huang
et al., 2022). Code as Policies turned the plan
into a program over perception and control inter-
faces (Liang et al., 2023), and later work widened
2
title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics

text:
what the program could express with structured
prompts, foundation perception, and value maps
(Singh et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023a,b; Mu
et al., 2024). A parallel line places a reasoning
model above a learned policy rather than around
it (Belkhale et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025; Physical
Intelligence et al., 2025). The two lines have con-
verged inagentic robotics, where an LLM agent
sits in the control loop, calls perception, motion,
and VLA tools, and keeps a memory of what has
worked (Fu et al., 2026; Tsui et al., 2026; Kumar,
2026; Jia et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Xu et al.,
2026b,a). All of this work is measured by what the
agent can accomplish, and none of it addresses the
cost of consulting the planner before every primi-
tive, which has been approached only by caching
plans for tasks seen before (Zhang et al., 2026a;
Kim et al., 2026a). To our knowledge, we are the
first to improve efficiency in agentic robotics sys-
tems by consolidating recurring call sequences into
reusable action routines.
Action chunking in robotics.How many actions
a policy commits to per decision is a design choice
that trades reactivity against consistency and cost.
Policies that query the model once per control step
(Brohan et al., 2022, 2023a; Kim et al., 2024) tie
inference cost to control frequency and let errors
compound between queries. Action chunking, in-
troduced by ACT (Zhao et al., 2023) and adopted
by Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2025), predicts a
short sequence of actions per inference, and VLA
models have since built it into their action heads
and tokenizers (Black et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025;
Pertsch et al., 2025). Subsequent work tunes the
trade-off by interleaving chunks for closed-loop
reactivity (Liu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2026),
and world-action models extend chunked predic-
tion from actions to future observations (Du et al.,
2023; Wu et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026b). In all of
these, a chunk is a short sequence of motor com-
mands from a learned policy, and how much an
LLM agent should commit to per decision has been
asked only in text environments (Yang et al., 2026).
To our knowledge, we arethe first to explore ac-
tion chunking in agentic robotics, where a chunk
spans perception, control primitives, and internal-
ized memory rather than motor commands.
Memory in agentic robotics.Memory lets an
LLM agent improve without weight updates, and
its forms differ in what is stored rather than in
how it is used. Reflective memory stores trajecto-
ries or the lessons drawn from them and returns
relevant entries to the prompt (Park et al., 2023;
Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Packer et al.,
2023). Procedural memory stores what worked as
code, from skill libraries (Wang et al., 2023) to
induced workflows (Wang et al., 2024) and robot
programs adapted to new contexts (Kagaya et al.,
2025; Woods and Seifi, 2026). Robot harnesses
keep rule cards and task records written by the
planner itself (Zhang et al., 2026c), transition con-
ditions between subtasks (Xu et al., 2026b), or a
demonstration video navigated at a chosen gran-
ularity (Anonymous, 2026). In every form, the
planner decides what to retrieve and when, reads it
into context, and interprets it before acting, so the
memory is consumed at test time and its value is
bounded by the planner’s ability to use it (Zhang
et al., 2025). Li et al. (2025) comes closest to break-
ing this pattern by distilling recurring spans into
a datastore that is emitted rather than read, yet its
chunks remain text. We are the first work to ex-
plore compiling agentic memory offline into physi-
cal action, producing executable action chunks that
require no memory access at deployment.
3 Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
3.1 Preliminaries
We begin by formalizing agentic robotics, the set-
ting in whichChunkActoperates.
The agentic loop.An agentic system solves a
manipulation task with an LLM plannerG that se-
quentially composes primitives from a libraryP,
at = (p t,θ t) =G(c t), y t =p t(θt),
ct+1 =c t⊕(a t,y t). (1)
Herect denotes the context window of the planner
at step t, initialized with the task instruction as
c0 =ℓ . At each step, the planner reasons over
ct and outputs at, which specifies the primitive
to execute, pt ∈ P, and its arguments θt. The
primitive runs to completion and returns a result
yt, which is appended to the context withat. The
process repeats until the task is completed atT.
Notably, not every planner output is a robot ac-
tion. Action primitives alter the physical state of
the robot, whereas informational primitives leave
the scene intact and only return content, either from
perception or from a memoryM (Section B). Since
every result is appended toct, an informational call
is paid for not only once, but again as input at every
subsequent step.

We analyze the planner’s tool calls and reveal
two sources of inefficiency. ❶ The planner con-
flates deciding with executing. Every primitive in-
curs a full round of reasoning, even though, once
a sub-goal is fixed, the primitives that realize it
are largely determined by the memory; the plan-
ner is thus invoked far more often than the task
demands decisions. ❷ The planner spends most
of its calls gathering information rather than act-
ing. Only 20.5% of calls invoke an action primitive,
while memory reads and perception account for
31.7% and 44.3%, respectively (See Fig.2). Since
M is static across episodes, these reads retrieve the
same knowledge again and again, inflating the con-
text without informing new decisions. These two
findings motivate ChunkAct, whichbrings action
chunking to agentic roboticsthrough offline ac-
tion chunk building (Section 3.2) and online action
chunk triggering (Section 3.3).
3.2 Offline action chunk building
Targeting the ❶ issue, ChunkAct outputs action
chunks rather than single primitives. The planner
is reengaged only when the chunk fails, reserving
LLM reasoning for the decisions that require it.
The memory of an LLM agent already records
the general, reusable success rules and and pro-
cedural context for tasks. ChunkAct compiles all
memory once into executable chunk form rather
than letting the planner re-derive it at every step
(Figure 3(a)). Memory construction begins with
a partition over task categories. A manipulation
instruction decomposes into an ordered sequence
of typed sub-goals, and the space of such types
remains small even as the task set grows. For ex-
ample, two types suffice to cover a broad range of
tabletop manipulation: transport, which relocates
an object onto or into a receptacle, and fixture,
which actuates an articulated element of the scene.
All memory entries pertaining to a given type, from
general execution rules to task-specific records, are
therefore consolidated into a single source and com-
piled into a unified chunk, parameterized by the
object classes on which it operates.
Compilation retains only the procedural knowl-
edge that defines how a task type is executed: the
ordering of stages, the primitive assigned to each
stage, the stage-level parameters conditioned on
object class, the fallback strategies to attempt when
a stage fails, and the criteria used to verify each
stage. The primitive assignment, for instance, pre-
serves the division of labor recorded in memory,
delegating contact-rich stages such as grasping or
fixture actuation to the VLA policy and the remain-
ing stages to analytic primitives. Conversely, any
quantity unobservable at deployment time is ex-
cluded. Recorded coordinates and privileged sim-
ulator state are discarded, and all geometric quan-
tities are re-estimated from live perception of the
current scene. This decoupling allows a chunk to
transfer to scenes whose layouts differ from those
encountered during memory construction.
The resulting chunk is an executable routine that
captures the recurring procedure of its task type.
A single chunk covers every task of its type, with
class-dependent content resolved by lookup within
the chunk. The planner is thus relieved of both
memory retrieval and step-by-step primitive selec-
tion at run time. During execution, each stage is
verified before the next begins, and the library is
compiled once and kept frozen.
3.3 Online action chunk triggering
To sovle the ❷ problem, ChunkAct internalizes
the memoryM into executable chunks, allowing
memory-free execution at run time.
At test time the planner invokes chunks in place
of primitives, through a single tool call (Figure 3(b)
labels ChunkAct). The instruction is parsed into
its ordered sequence of typed sub-goals, each sub-
goal selects the chunk of its kind, and the planner’s

interface to execution narrows to two operations,
grounding a target in the current observation and
launching the chunks. An episode therefore begins
with the planner interpreting the task and the scene,
grounding the first target, and issuing one call, af-
ter which the chunks run the sub-goals until the
task is complete without any further request to the
planner. No memory is read along the way, since
everything the planner would have retrieved has
been compiled into the chunks, and the planner’s
context holds only the instruction, the observations
it has requested, and the exits it has received.
Chaining the stages under one call, rather than
exposing each stage as a separate call, follows from
where reasoning is actually needed. Compiling
memory and perception into chunks removes the
cost of retrieval and repeated observation, but a
per-stage interface would still return control to the
planner after every action, turning each step of
execution into a round of deliberation. Most of
these rounds involve no decision.
Once its target is grounded, the stages of a sub-
goal follow a fixed order, so a successful stage
already determines the next one and requires no
reasoning to select it. A chunk therefore chains the
stages directly and returns control to the planner
only when a stage fails.
Control returns to the planner only when a chunk
fails, and it does so through a typed exit. Every
stage of a chunk raises its own error code, so the
exit names the stage that failed and the reason it
failed, such as a perception call that cannot locate
its target, a policy call that loses the object, or a
verification that cannot confirm the sub-goal, and
it carries the error log with the robot state and
fresh observations (Section A). The planner then re-
perceives the scene from its true state, and chooses
among three responses, namely grounding the tar-
get again and re-invoking the chunk, redoing a
sub-goal whose verification failed, or falling back
to the primitives for a situation the library does not
cover. Each response is a decision that requires
understanding the task and the scene, and none is
a step of execution, so the planner is consulted at
decision points and nowhere else.
3.4 Role of LLM planner in agentic robotics
We examine how this design changes the role of
the planner, from stepwise executor to sub-goal
selector and failure handler.
Taken together, the two stages redefine the role
of the planner. In the per-primitive loop of Equa-
tion (1), the planner serves as both reasoner and
executor, treating every step alike regardless of
whether it requires judgment. ChunkAct separates
the two: execution is delegated to the chunks, while
the planner retains only what cannot be compiled,
namely understanding the task and scene and re-
sponding to failure. This separation reshapes both
sides of the loop.
On the input side, the dominant sources of con-
text are removed. Memory is internalized in the
chunks rather than retrieved online, and percep-
tion is performed within each chunk rather than
requested before every primitive. The context thus
stays compact across an episode, containing only

4 Experiments
4.1 Setup
Benchmarks.We evaluate on two benchmarks
from the LIBERO family. Our main experiments
use LIBERO-Pro (Zhou et al., 2025), which per-
turbs the four LIBERO suites (Liu et al., 2023),
Spatial, Object, Goal, and LIBERO-10, along ob-
jects, initial states, instructions, and environments.
Following Zhang et al. (2026c), we evaluate the
instruction and initial-state perturbations, denoted
instruction redirection (T) and position swap (S).
Each of the resulting eight suite and perturbation
combinations contains 10 tasks. As in that proto-
col, we run 10 seeds per task, so that each com-
bination aggregates 800 episodes. We further use
LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) benchmark, which
varies the LIBERO tasks along seven axes: object
layout, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, lan-
guage, lighting, background, and sensor noise. As
its 10,030 variants are too many to evaluate exhaus-
tively, we run a single seed on every task under
each of the seven perturbation axes, which covers
the full range of perturbations at a tractable cost.
Metrics.We measure performance by the task
success rate (TSR), as determined by the environ-
ment’s termination signal. We measure efficiency
by the number of planner calls and the numbers of
input and output tokens per episode.
Baselines.For the main experiment, we com-
pare with eight end-to-end VLA models, Open-
VLA (Kim et al., 2024), π0 (Black et al., 2024),
π0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), MolmoAct
(Lee et al., 2026), NORA (Hung et al., 2025), X-
VLA (Zheng et al., 2026), AtomVLA (Sun et al.,
2026), and the RLinf-fine-tuned π0.5 checkpoint
that serves as our VLA primitive, which we denote
πRLinf (Yu et al., 2026), and with CaP-X (Fu et al.,
2026), an agent that writes code over perception
and motion primitives without a VLA. Their re-
sults are those reported by Zhang et al. (2026c).
Harness VLA and ChunkAct are run by us. For
LIBERO-Plus experiment results, the VLA models’
performance are as reported by Fei et al. (2025).
Implementation.The planner is GPT-5.6-sol at
high reasoning effort running in Codex (OpenAI,
2025), with a budget of 100 LLM calls per episode.
The VLA primitive is πRLinf, and SAM 3 (Car-
ion et al., 2026) provides segmentation. ChunkAct
and Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026c) share the
same set-up and the same task-specific and global
memory. They differ only in how the memory is
used: Harness VLA reads it at test time, whereas
ChunkAct internalizes it offline into executable
chunks and reads no explicit memory at test time.

4.2 Main results
Task success performance.As shown in Ta-
ble 1, ChunkAct achieves the highest task suc-
cess rate on LIBERO-Pro, outperforming both end-
to-end VLAs and agentic robotic systems. It at-
tains an overall success rate of 83.8%, exceeding
the strongest prior method, Harness VLA, by 5.0
points. The perturbations in LIBERO-Pro, instruc-
tion redirection and position swap, require a policy
to act on instructions and object layouts that differ
from those seen in training, and end-to-end VLAs
largely fail under them. This failure extends to
πRLinf, the checkpoint that ChunkAct invokes as
its contact primitive, which trailsChunkAct by 43.8
points. Since the primitive alone does not gener-
alize to these perturbations, whatever success an
agent recovers must come from how it grounds the
task in the current scene before the primitive is
called. Placing an LLM planner above the VLA re-
covers much loss, as the agentic baselines show, yet
Harness VLA stops at 78.8% despite sharing the
same planner, primitive, perception, and memory
with ChunkAct. The two systems differ only in how
memory is used. Harness VLA retrieves memory
at test time and relies on the planner to reinterpret
past experience at every call, whereas ChunkAct
compiles it offline into executable chunks that en-
code how each task succeeds. The gap therefore
isolates the benefit of memory internalization.
Efficiency analysis.As shown in Table 2,
ChunkAct attains its higher success rate at a frac-
tion of the LLM cost. The first two rows corre-
spond to the Harness VLA and ChunkAct entries
in Table 1. Relative to Harness VLA, ChunkAct
issues 2.9× fewer LLM calls and consumes 4.4×
fewer input tokens and 2.3× fewer output tokens,
while improving success by 5.0 points. The third
and fourth rows repeat this comparison with rea-
soning disabled, and the efficiency advantage of
ChunkAct grows further. Both observations stem
from memory internalization. Harness VLA spends
most LLM calls on perception queries and mem-
ory reads, and each result is appended to the con-
text, so the context keeps growing over the episode.
ChunkAct folds these steps into the executable
chunks, so they run at test time without invoking
the LLM and their results never enter the context
window. The planner is called only at the decision
points that the chunks leave open. Fewer calls over
a shorter context reduce the input tokens, and fewer
planning decisions reduce the output tokens.
4.3 Analysis of LLM planner role in ChunkAct
Analyzing the LLM planner reasoning impact.
As shown in Table 2, ChunkAct remains robust
when the reasoning of LLM planner is disabled,
whereas Harness VLA does not. The task success
rate of ChunkAct stays stable across reasoning set-
tings, while Harness VLA degrades sharply once
reasoning is turned off. This contrast reflects how
heavily each system relies on the planner. Harness
VLA depends on the LLM at every step: each call
must interpret the retrieved memory, decide what
to perceive, and issue the correct next action, so
the errors of a weaker planner accumulate over
the episode. ChunkAct instead decouples the LLM
from the execution it does not need to perform.
With memory already internalized into the chunks,
the planner is consulted only for the remaining de-
cisions, which leaves a weaker planner far fewer
opportunities to fail.
Quantifying the LLM agent’s contribution.To
measure how much the planner contributes within
ChunkAct, the last row of Table 2 executes the
chunks under a scripted driver that makes no LLM
call. The chunks alone reach 57.5%, which cor-

ChunkAct without reasoning therefore accounts for

from recovery: when a chunk fails, the planner is
invoked to interpret the current scene and direct the
next step, which a scripted driver cannot. The LLM
thus serves not as a step-by-step executor but as a
recovery mechanism invoked where the compiled
routine falls short, which is why it adds substantial

4.4 Generalization to unseen perturbations
Out-of-distribution test.The memory of
ChunkAct is compiled on LIBERO-Pro and in-
cludes task-specific memory, which prior work
found necessary on that benchmark (Zhang et al.,
2026c). To test whether ChunkAct overfits to these
tasks, we apply it unchanged to LIBERO-Plus (Fei
et al., 2025), which perturbs the LIBERO tasks
along seven dimensions that the memory doesn’t
cover. The chunk library and planner prompt are
those of Section 4.2, so the evaluation is fully zero-
shot, whereas the VLA baselines, whose numbers
are taken from Fei et al. (2025), are fine-tuned on
the benchmark data.
Zero-shot transfer. ChunkAct achieves the best
overall success rate in Table 3, exceeding the
strongest prior method by 11.0 points and lead-
ing in six of the seven dimensions. The margin is
widest under camera and robot initial-state pertur-
bations, where ChunkAct stays above three quar-
ters while the best VLA falls to two thirds and one
half, respectively. Because a chunk recomputes
its targets from perception in every episode, such
changes alter the measured geometry but not the
procedure. These results show zero-shot transfer of
internalized memory to unseen perturbations rather
than overfitting to the tasks it was compiled from.
4.5 Qualitative analysis
Figure 4 follows a single LIBERO-Pro episode and
shows how the planner’s eight calls are distributed
over 22 seconds of execution. The planner is en-
gaged at two points only. At the start it views the
scene and launches a chunk, which grasps and lifts
the can without further LLM request. During the
move, however, the can slips out of the gripper, and
the chunk terminates with a typed exit. It returns a
hand-off block, a structured error report that adds
context to the error code. The planner resumes
from the true state of the scene rather than from
its expectation of it, spends four calls re-pointing
the can, and triggers ChunkAct again, which car-
ries the can to the basket, places it, and finishes
on its own once the environment reports success.
The episode makes visible the division of labor that
Table 2 quantifies. The planner is reserved for un-
derstanding, while the chunks handle execution. It
plans the next action chunk from the scene, and
re-plans when a chunk fails.
5 Conclusion
Agentic robotics generalizes to novel tasks with-
out retraining, but at a steep cost in efficiency. We
identify two bottlenecks: the LLM planner reasons
before every primitive, although the primitives of a
sub-goal follow a recurring pattern, and most of its
calls are spent on perception and memory retrieval
rather than action. ChunkAct is the first work to in-
troduce action chunking to agentic robotics, and it
internalizes memory into executable chunks offline.
The LLM is thereby decoupled from routine execu-
tion and engaged only where reasoning is genuinely
required, which improves LLM efficiency signifi-
cantly. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task
success by 5.0 points over the SOTA method with
2.9× fewer LLM calls, 4.4× fewer input tokens,
and 2.3× fewer output tokens, and it transfers zero-
shot to unseen tasks on LIBERO-Plus.
